Admittedly, the scrubber liquor is to be added to adjust viscosity of the sodium silicate. Such addition was in the factory of the assessee and before sale of sodium silicate. Modvat Rules allow ‘Credit of any duty of excise paid on the goods used in the manufacture on said final products" (Rules 57A). Rule 57B further clarifies that "Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 57A, the manufacturer of final products shall be allowed to take credit of the specified duty paid... on inputs used in or relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not". It was not reasonable to argue that materials used for maintaining viscosity at the required level were not used in relation to manufacture, particularly, when the viscosity control was by the manufacturer before the sale of goods. It is also to be noted that Modvat follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not. Correctness of payment is not relevant; only the fact of payment is. A view to the contrary also goes against the broad definition of ‘manufacture’ in section 2 of the Central Excise Act in a manner as to include "any process - incidental or ancillary to the completion of manufacture". Thus, a finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to the given factual situation and relevant legal provisions. Hence, the assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit as claimed. [Para 9]

Limitation--Demand for reversal of credit taken on molywire--Extended period and penalty are not sustainable, as there was no deliberate mis-statement of suppression. Hence we are of the view that though credit of duty paid on molywire is not admissible on merits, the demand even for this item cannot be confirmed by invoking the extended period under proviso to Rule 571 or Section 11A of the Central Excise Act in this context, the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Chemphar Drugs and Liniments [1989 (21) ECR 182 (SC)] appears to be squarely applicable. The applicant has submitted that the salt manufactured by them is required to be exported as per condition and undertaking given to the Government while taking land on lease basis. Therefore, the manufactured salt is 'Zero rated supply' under section 16 of the IGST Act for the applicant. [Para 6.1]

Section 16(2) of the IGST Act, 2017 states that 'subject to the provisions of sub-section (5) of section 17 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, credit of input tax may be availed for making zero-rated supplies, notwithstanding that such supply may be an exempt supply.' Whereas as per section 2(47) of the CGST Act, exempt supply includes nil rated supply and non-taxable supply. [Para 8]

As per section 16(2) of the IGST Act, Input tax credit is available on inputs and input services to make zero rated supplies (such supply may be an exempt supply), subject to the provisions of sub-section (5) of section 17 of CGST Act. As per clauses (c) and (d) of section 17(5) of the GST Act, input tax credit is not admissible in respect of works contract services or any goods and services for construction of immovable property (other than plant and machinery). This, a specific exception is made with regard to 'plant and machinery'. [Para 10]

Input tax credit of GST paid on goods and services used to construct the 'bunds' is admissible to applicant, provided that the bunds are used for making zero rated supplies and fulfil the conditions which are necessary for treating the bunds as 'plant and machinery'. [Para 11]

We have carefully considered the submissions from both the sides and perused the records. The Respondent manufactured PSF for which MEG is one of the inputs. Notification No. 225/86-CE dated 3/4/86 exempted PSF from Central excise duty chargeable thereon as it equivalent to the Central Excise Duty under Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty under Customs Tariff Act, 1975 paid on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF. This exemption notification provided similar duty concession in respect of other finished products mentioned in the table annexed to the notification and the duty concession was equal to the Central excise duty paid under Central Excise Act or additional Customs Duty paid under Customs Tariff Act, on the specified inputs used in the manufacture of the finished products. Though there is no explicit provision in this exemption notification regarding its applicability when the finished product is fully exempt from duty or is chargeable to nil rate of duty, it would be an obvious corollary that this exemption would not be applicable if the finished product is an exempted goods i.e. either fully exempt from duty by virtue of an exemption notification or chargeable to nil rate of duty. The point of dispute in this case is as to whether this exemption notification would be applicable when the finished goods - PSF in this case, have been cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export.

3.1 Rules 191BB permits removal of excisable goods from the place of manufacture or storage without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export, subject to the conditions prescribed in this Rule. The PSF, in question, in respect of which the set off of duty on MEG used in its manufacture is sought to be denied, had been cleared without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export in terms of the provisions of Rule 191BB. The Tribunal in the case of Orissa Synthetics Vs. CCE (supra) and CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. (supra), has with reference to exemption notification No. 225/96-CE, held that PSF cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of goods for export is not to be treated as exempted goods. It is not the contention of the Department that these judgments have been challenged before a higher court or have been set aside. Moreover when the Department has accepted the clearances of the PSF for export under bond without payment of duty, as eligible for the benefit of this exemption, there would be no justification in denying the same exemption to the goods cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of the finished goods for export.

3.2 The Notification No. 225/86-CE operates like Modvat scheme. Rule 57F (3) of Chapter V (AA) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 pertaining to Modvat scheme, provided that credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on any of the finished products in or in relation to manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used or for payment of duty on any waste arising in course of manufacture of finished products or for payment of duty on inputs themselves, if the same are allowed to be cleared as such. Proviso to this sub-Rule provided that the credit of the specified duty in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of final products cleared for export under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty and where for any reason such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations, as may be specified by the Central Government by notification in the official gazette. In the case of Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay (supra), the dispute arose as to whether the final products cleared under bond without payment of duty in terms of Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished product for export would be eligible for the benefit of the proviso to Rule 57F (3) and the Tribunal answered this question in the affirmative, holding that in respect of clearances of finished product without payment of duty under Rule 191BB, the benefit of proviso to Rule 57F (3) would be available. Same principle would apply in this case also and when the Department has accepted the applicability of the exemption in respect of the finished product exported under bond without payment of duty, the benefit of this exemption would also have to be extended in respect of the clearances without payment of duty under Rule 191B.

Per Rakesh Kumar :

The facts leading to filing of this appeal by Revenue are, in brief, as under.

1.1 The respondents are manufacturer of Polyester staple fiber (PSF) chargeable to Central Excise Duty under Chapter 55 of the Central Excise Tariff. One of the inputs used in the manufacture of PSF is Mono Ethlylene Glycol (MEG). The dispute in this case pertains to January 1987 to May 1991 period. During that period Notification No. 225/86-CE issued under the then Rule 8 (1) of Central Excise Rules, 1944 exempted "PSF including tops and polyester filament yarn (PFY)" from so much of duty of excise chargeable under the Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty chargeable under Customs Tariff Act, 1975, as the case may be, already paid on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF or PFY. During the period from May 1989 to August 1991, nine show cause notices were issued to the Respondent for recovery of allegedly wrongly availed input duty exemption amounting to Rs. 1,15,54,845/- on the following grounds :-

(a)

The Respondents are not eligible for set off of the duty paid on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF exported out of India without payment of duty;

(b)

set off of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for used in the manufacture of goods for export is not admissible;

(c)

set off of duty paid on MEG, which is contained in the bi-products or waste arisen in course of manufacture of PSF is not admissible;

(d)

set off of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared at nil rate of duty under Notification No. 191/85-CE is not admissible;

(e)

set off amounting to Rs. 6,50,090/-, which represents the duty on the quantity of MEG which was allegedly short received, is not admissible.

1.2 These show cause notices were adjudicated by the Assistant Commissioner by a common order dated 30th May 2003 by which the Assistant Commissioner while permitting the set off of duty on MEG contained in waste and by-products and also the set off of duty paid on MEG, used in the manufacture of PSF which was exported out of India under bond without payment of duty, disallowed -

(a)

set off of Rs. 15,63,263/- of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF which was cleared without payment of duty for manufacture under bond of finished goods for export under Rule 191BB;

(b)

the set off of Rs. 1,13,330/- of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared at nil rate of duty under Notification No. 191/85-CE dated 28/8/85, and

(c)

the set off of Rs. 6,50,090/- in respect of the quantity of MEG which was short received.

1.3 The Respondent filed the appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) challenging the Assistant Commissioner's order -

(a)

disallowing the set off of the duty of Rs. 15,63,263/- on MEG contained in the PSF cleared without payment of duty for manufacture in bond of finished goods for export under Rule 191BB; and

(b)

disallowing the set off of Rs. 6,50,090/- in respect of the quantity of the MEG held to have been short received. The Commissioner (Appeals) vide order-in-appeal No. 126-CE/LKO/04 dated 1/6/04 allowed the appeal on the following grounds :-

(i)

so far as set off of Rs. 15,63,263/- of the duty on the quantity of MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared without payment of duty for manufacture of finished goods for export under bond under Rule 191BB is concerned, this set off is admissible to the Respondent in view of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. Vs. CCE reported in 1989 (44) E.L.T. 794 (S.C.) and of the Tribunal in the cases of CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. reported in 1999 (107) E.L.T. 455 (Trib.) and Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay reported in 1995 (9) RLT 317 (CEGAT-WRB)=1995 (78) E.L.T. 595 (Trib.).

(ii)

BB which inter alia provided that a product can be cleared without payment of duty if it is meant to be used in the manufacture of final product which is to be exported. We note that this issue was examined at length in paras 7, 8 & 9 by this Tribunal (Final Order No. 477/97-NB dt. 15.4.97) in their own case of the appellants. For the sake of clarity, the same paras are reproduced as under:- "Heard the submissions of both sides. The facts of the case as narrated above are that the appellants are manufacturing POY. The appellants get a number of inputs for the manufacture of POY. Both polyester filament yarn and the inputs were specified under Rule 57A. The appellants filed a declaration under Rule 57G. During the month of May, June and July, 1992, the appellants cleared without payment of duty a particular quantity of POY under the provisions of Rule 191BB. The only dispute that arises is whether removal of the goods under the provisions of Rule 191BB can be treated as removal under an exemption notification. The notification covering the removal of the goods under Rule 191BB is the Notfn. No. 33/90-CE (NT). This notification inter alia provides that the goods can be removed without payment of duty under the provisions of Rule 191BB."

"We find that in the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited reported at page 599 of Reliance Industries Limited at para 6.2, this Tribunal held as under:-

"In the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited decided by the East Regional Bench, the man-made staple fibre was cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB of the Central Excise Rules and the department objected to the availing of Modvat Credit of duty on inputs used in these final products cleared under Rule 191BB of the Rules. The department's main contention was that such removals of final products without payment of duty under Rule 191BB were hit by Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules. The East Regional Bench, after considering all the arguments raised by the ld. SDR negatived the objection and allowed the appeal of Orissa Synthetics. For arriving at their conclusion, that Bench relied on the decision of the Delhi High Court in Hindustan Aluminium Corpn. reported in 1981 (8) ELT 642, wherein it was held by the Delhi High Court that the facility of removal without payment of duty under bond for export could not be equated with a general exemption from payment of duty of excise. That Bench also took note of the clarification issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs in consultation with the Ministry of Law about the scope of proviso (i) to sub-rule (2) of Rule 56A (analogous to the provisions of Rule 57C). In that clarification issued by the Board, the Board advised the field formations that the said proviso to Rule 56A (2) would not stand attracted, where the final products were exported under bond, since such removals could neither be construed to be exempted nor be regarded as goods charged to nil rate of duty. (Vide the extract of the advice of the Ministry of Law appearing in para 9 of the said order of the East Regional Bench). Thus we find that going by the allegation contained in the show cause notices involved in this appeal, the issue is identical in all respects and the ratio of that decision would apply to this case squarely."

"A careful reading of the above paragraph shows that the Tribunal had held that the goods manufactured from the inputs on which modvat credit has been taken which are cleared without payment of duty under Notfn. No. 33/90-CE (NT) does not mean that the goods are exempt from the whole of duty."

6. We find that the learned JDR has cited and relied upon the decision of this Tribunal in the case of East India Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. We have perused this decision. We find that this decision does not come under Rule 191BB but on the interpretation of Rule 57F (2) and 57F (3). Thus we find that this decision is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case. Following the ratio of the decision of this Tribunal in the case of the appellants themselves, we hold that the modvat credit is admissible to the appellants. In the result the appeals are allowed.

Per Shri G.R. Sharma :

The facts giving rise to the captioned appeal are that the appellants get PTA and convert it into polyester staple fibre (PSF). The PSF is sent to different parties who manufacture polyester fabrics from this and export it. The appellants for this purpose were following the procedure u/r 191-BB of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and transferring the PSF under Not. No. 33/90. The department alleged that PSF is being cleared at nil rate of duty under Not. No. 33/90. Rule 57C was attracted and the Asstt. Collector accordingly confirmed a demand of Rs. 1,54,472.26. In appeal, the ld. Collr. (Appeals) also agreed with the Asstt. Collr. observing that there is no denying the fact that particular clearance of PSF was at nil rate of duty vide Not. No. 33/90 dated 5.9.90. Therefore, such being the case, modvat claimed is not admissible and rejected the appeal of the appellants herein.

2. Shri Vinod Agarwal, ld. Advocate appearing for the appellants submits that the department has wrongly and erroneously interpreted the Not. Counsel that JCT Fibres Ltd. has since been changed to JCT Ltd. and therefore, prays for the change of cause title. The ld. SDR has no objection. The cause title is therefore, changed to M/s. 5. The short point for determination in this appeal is whether the provisions of Rule 57C are attracted when PSFs were sent to manufacturers of polyester fabrics for export. For this purpose, we have to see what the provisions of Not. No. 33/90 are Not. No. 33/90 inter alia stipulates "Transfer of excisable goods without payment of duty." It does not say that the duty shall be chargeable at nil rate etc. This notification also does not speak of exemption of the goods. Now let us examine the provisions of Rule 57C. Rule 57C lays down that modvat credit shall not be available in cases where the final product is exempt. Admittedly, in the instant case when these two rules are read together, I find that under Not. No. 33/90, the word `exempt' is not used nor nil rate of duty is used. Therefore, the goods were not exempt so as to attract denial of modvat credit on inputs under Section 57C. I get support for this view from the decision of the Tribunal in the case of J.K. Synthetics Ltd. cited above. In para 6, the Tribunal had held as under :

utilised towards payment of duty of excise,-

(i)

on any of the final products in or, in relation to the manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used in accordance with the declaration filed under sub-rule (1) of rule 57G; or]

(ii)

on the waste, if any, arising in the course of manufacture of the final products; or

(iii)

on the inputs themselves if such inputs have been permitted to be cleared under sub-rule(l)]: [Provided that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared for export under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export in accordance with sub-rule (2), shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption [or for export] on payment of duty and, where for any reason, such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations as may be specified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette:

Provided further that no such refund of credit of duty shall be allowed if the manufacturer avails of drawback allowed under the Customs and Central Excise Duties (Drawback) Rules, 1971, or claims rebate of duty under rule 12A, in respect of such duty.]

[Provided also that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared either to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a hundred per cent Export-Oriented Unit under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty,]

It is seen that earlier under the first proviso MODVAT credit taken in respect of the inputs contained in the goods exported under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export could be utilised for payment of duty towards goods cleared for home consumption or for any reason if this adjustment was not possible the cash refund has been provided for. With effect from 1.3.92, the second proviso has been added. Under this even where the final products in which the inputs have been utilised are cleared to a unit in a free trade zone or to a l00% export oriented unit under bond, the same benefit as in the case of the export of the goods has been provided for. We observe that as such in Rule 57F (3) there is no specific provision in regard to the clearances made to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, We observe that when the clearances are made to a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit of any finished product without payment of duty from a unit which has taken MODVAT credit in respect of the inputs, the benefit is given as ultimately in terms of these schemes the goods allowed manufacture are exported. The units which are manufacturing goods under Rule 191B in terms of notification issued under this Rule are in our view similarly placed as the unit located in the free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. We see no reason as to why the same benefit as provided under Rule 57F for these units cannot be extended to this unit. Interest of revenue is safeguarded by the specific provision under the notification issued under Rule 191B for recovery of duty both in respect of the finished goods and the non-duty paid goods out of which the same are manufactured in bond in case the goods are not exported. We therefore hold that notwithstanding the absence of any specific mention in the proviso to Rule 57F(3) in regard to the finished goods in respect of which input credit is taken and which are cleared without payment of duty to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, the second proviso to Rule 57F(3) would cover such units also, as we do not find any reason to differentiate the operations in the unit functioning under Rule 191B from the operations carried out in the unit functioning under a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. In view of above, we hold that the appellants plea has to be allowed and we order accordingly.

2. Shri Gopal Prasad, learned Consultant appeared for the Appellants. He stated that the impugned order has been passed by a wrong interpretation of Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules. They bring duty paid inputs Monoethylene Glycol which is used by them in the manufacture of MMSF which is cleared by them under Rule 191 BB and Notification 33/90 CEN.T. dated 5.9.90 to another manufacturer without payment of duty. The latter then manufacture the final product which is exported. The clearance of MMSF is without payment of duty on the strength of a suitable bond to ensure the utilisation of the said material for the manufacture of the final product which is exported. Ruie57C lays down that no credit to duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty. The Collector has held in his impugned order that they had made a very thin distinction between exemption and clearance without payment of duty, which is basically same. Shri Gopal Prasad submitted that this conclusion of the Collector is not correct. Notification 33/90, in terms of which they had cleared their product MMSF, permits goods to be removed without payment of duty for supply to manufacturers of final products which are exported. The expression (removal) without payment of duty is distinct and different from exempt from whole of the duty or chargeable to nil rate of duty. The Collector had referred to the amendment of Rule 57C by Notification 4/92 dated 1.3.92 and concluded that since by this amendment the final products cleared to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a 100 per cent Export oriented unit have been exempted from the effect of Rule 5 7C removal without payment of duty for supply to the ultimate exporter for manufacture of the resultant product will not get such a benefit in the absence of such exemption from the scope of Rule 57C being specifically extended to such non-duty paid removals. The learned Consultant contended that this interpretation of the Col lector is wrong. In the case of clearances of final products to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a 100 per cent Export Oriented Unit, these are exempt from the whole of the duty leviable and hence it was necessary to specifically provide for them as otherwise they would be hit by Rule 57C. Such is not the case with clearances without payment of duty under Notification 33/90 dated 5.9.90 issued under Rule 191 BB (1). That is not an exemption Notification. Such exemption Notifications were issued under Rule 8 of the Central Rules, 1944 earlier (now under Section 5A of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944). This vital difference has not been accepted by the Collector.

In this connection, he referred to the judgement of the Honourable Delhi High Court in Hindustan Aluminium Corporation Limited. Vs. Collector of Central Excise, reported in 1987 (8) ELT 642 where the facility of export under bond without payment of duty was held to be not the same as a general exemption from payment of any excise duty at all. Shri Gopal Prasad submitted that the ratio of this decision is equally applicable for clearance of goods in terms of Rule 191 BB and accordingly Rule 57C is not applicable to such cases.

1. SCENARIO PRIOR TO INTRODUCTION OF MODVAT CREDIT

The Supreme Court in its landmark judgment in the case of Swadeshi Polytex Limited vs. Collector of Central Excise 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC) was pleased to hold as follows :

This was a decision rendered under the proforma regime (set off duty on inputs) wherein provision similar to Rule 57D which permits retention of modvat credit on inputs even if the same is used in the manufacture of dutiable final products and emergence of by-products, waste or refuse is not to be denied.

Para 20

"It is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible.

It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. It is not possible to use a lesser quantum of ethylene glycol to prevent methanol from arising for producing a certain quantum of polyester fibre. Thus the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. It may be mentioned herein that it is not as if the appellants have used excess ethylene glycol wontedly to produce the methanol. It is clear that the appellants are not engaged in the production of methanol but in the production of polyester fibre. The Tribunal erred when it held that appellants were not entitled to a part of the credit of the duty since ethylene glycol when it reacts with DMT also gives rise to Methanol."

2. SCENARIO UNDER THE MODVAT REGIME BETWEEN 01/03/86 TO 03/09/94

Bearing the spirit of the decision of the Supreme Court in Swadeshi Polytex the lawmakers when they introduced Modvat Scheme, brought into force a specific provision in the form of Rule 57D(1) of the Central Excise Rules which reads as under :

Credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs shall not be denied or varied on the ground that part of the inputs is contained in any waste, refuse or by product arising during the manufacture of the final product, whether or not such waste, refuse or by product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty or is not specified as a final product under Rule 57A.

WHILE INTRODUCING RULE 57D CENTRAL GOVT ALSO BROUGHT INTO FORCE RULE 57C WHICH READS AS UNDER :

Credit to duty not to be allowed if final products are exempt. No credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty.

We have considered all the arguments from the revenue for coming to the conclusion that in the absence of specific legal provision either under Rule 57 C or under Rule 57 F (3) proviso, Modvat credit cannot be denied for utilisation in regard to clearance of similar final products. Rule 57 C seeks to deny Modvat credit, if the final products are either wholly exempted or are chargeable to Nil rate of duty. We have held that in the case of goods cleared under a Notification issued under Rule 191 BB for export purposes, such goods cannot be equated with goods exempted under an exemption Notification issued under Rule 8 (1) of the C.E. Rules or Section 5A of C.Ex. Act nor they can be construed as goods chargeable to Nil rate of duty. For arriving at this conclusion, we have taken note of the Board's own instructions issued in the context of identical provisions of Rule 56A of the C.E. Rules, after consulting the Ministry of Law. The argument of Shri Nair that irrespective of the fact that Rule 57C does not specifically provide for denying benefit in respect of clearances under Rule 191 BB, since Rule 57F (3) proviso can only cover direct exports from the factory and not removals under Rule 191 BB for further manufacture of export goods in another factory. We do not find any warrant to read such a restriction in Rule 57F (3) proviso; because proviso to Rule 57F (3) talks of "cleared for export under bond". In the absence of any specific restriction prescribed in that proviso, we are to go by what is meant by the term for export under bond' laid down in Rule 13 of the C.Ex. Rules. Under Rule 13, goods may be exported outside India without payment of duty from a warehouse or licensed factory, provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules and the owner enters into a bond for due performance. There is no dispute that Rule 191 BB is one of the relevant provision of Chapter IX of the Rules. Hence if the goods are cleared under Rule 191BB, they are goods cleared for export in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Viewed in this context, we could not persuade ourselves to agree that Rule 57F (3) proviso can he extended, only where the goods are cleared direct from the factory to the port of shipment. Hence, we find no reason to take any different view from the one we have already taken in the case of Reliance Industries. Hence we hold that objection from the Dept. on this ground is not sustainable and direct the authorities to allow the credit to be utilised in regard to clearance of similar final product.

The High Court in arriving at the above conclusion relied on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. Vs. C.C.E. - 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC). In this case, it is observed that the question for consideration was whether the appellants became ineligible to claim set-off of duty on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre to the extent it gave rise to methanol. In the premises, the Supreme Court held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ''The Supreme Court held that ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre, though methanol had arisen as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture, when ethylene glycol interacted with DMT to produce polyester fibre. Giving the reasoning, the Supreme Court says that it is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre and that the appellant was engaged in the production of polyester fibre and not methanol". (Emphasis supplied).

7. Accordingly, the High Court in its decision held that the entire quantity of sulphuric acid was necessary for manufacturing process and the modvat credit could not be denied simply because the entire input was not emerged in the final product in the manufacturing process.

8. The above ratio, in the judgments of the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court are applicable with the same force to the facts of the present case. It is therefore to be held that the entire quantity of pig iron is used in the manufacture of the exempted category of the P.D. Pumps and no quantity of the input is used in the manufacture of waste and scrap. In view of the provisions of Rule 57C, the modvat credit is not available to the appellants. Since in this case, I have relied on the ratio of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and that of the Allahabad High Court, specifically on the subject, there is no warrant to consider the other decisions cited before me by the appellants.

Roychowdhury submits that the appellants are engaged in the manufacture of Refined Rice Bran Oil which is chargeable to nil rate of duty as also the vegetable product which is a dutiable product. They availed the MODVAT Credit on the various inputs after declaring the same in their declaration under Rule 57G and all the inputs for Rice Bran Oil as also for vegetable product, were common inputs and as such, common RG-23A Part-I and II was being maintained by them. He submits that they are entitled to the MODVAT Credit even if a part of the inputs is used in the manufacture of Rice Bran Oil cleared by nil rate of duty in terms of proviso to Rule 57F(4) inserted by Notification No. 11/95 dated 16.3.95. He submitted that the said Rule permitted the assessee to utilise the MODVAT Credit towards the payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the fact whether such an iinput has actually been used in the manufacture of such a final product or not. In this view, he submits that the impugned Orders be set aside and Credit be allowed.

3. Shri T. Premkumar, learned S.D.R. appearing for the Revenue contends that the provisions of Rule 57F(4) are not applicable to the present situation inasmuch as the same are applicable when common inputs are being used in the manufacture of two different dutiable products, that is to say that one to one correlation is not required and Credit earned in respect of one final product can be utilised towards payment of duty on the other final product. As such he prays for rejection of the appeal.

4. I have considered the submission of both sides. The relevant proviso inserted in Notification No. 1/95-CE (NT) dated 16.3.95 is reproduced below for the sake of ready reference:-

"Provided also that, notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) of rule 57A and the notifications issued thereunder the credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty excise on any other final product, whether or not such inputs have actually been used in the manufacture of such other final product, if the said inputs have been received and used in the factory of production on or after the 16th day of March, 1995". (emphasis provided).

4.1 A reading of the above proviso shows that any credit of duty allowed in respect of any inputs can be utilised towards payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the input having been used in the said final product. As such, the first condition of the said proviso is that the credit of duty should have been allowed, i.e. the assessees are entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit of Duty on particular inputs and it is only after availing the said Credit that the manner of its utilisation has been laid down in the said proviso. In the instant case, the appellants were, at the first stage, not entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs used in the manufacture of Refind Rice Bran Oil because the said Oil was chargeable to nil rate of duty. As such the Rule 57C prohibited taking of Credit in such circumstances. When the availing of Credit is not permissible under the law, the question of its utilisation towards the payment of duty on any other final product does not arise. The proviso refers to a situation where the assessee manufacturer is entitled to availing the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs to be utilised in the manufacture of two different products and such accumulated availed Credit is allowed to be utilised towards the payment of the second final product, even though the input might not have been used in that final product. As such, I uphold the impugned orders passed by the authorities below in so far as the same relates to the denial of MODVAT Credit of Duty.

Per J.H. Joglekar:

Brief facts of the case are that the appellants herein are engaged in the manufacture of man-made fabrics. One of the raw materials used in the manufacture of polyester fibre is Mono Ethylene Glycol (MEG). The appellants had taken credit of duty paid on MEG. Polyester fibre although attracting duty under CET sub heading 5501/20 was exempted under Notification No. 191/85 dated 28.8.85 when used in the manufacture of fibres. The appellants were working under Notification 191/85. They paid duty and afterwards the files refund claim which was rejected on the ground that Notification 225/86 under which set off was available on Mono Ethylene Glycol used in the manufacture of polyester staple fibre, did not provide for refund of duty paid on inputs. The rejection of the claim by the Assistant Collector was upheld by the Collector of Central Excise (Appeals) against whose order the assessees have preferred the above appeal.

2. None appears for the appellants inspite of notice and therefore, we have heard Shri R.S. Sangia, learned DR, perused the records and pass the following order.

3. The appellants had paid duty on MEG used in the manufacture of polyester fibre supplied to NTC units under Notification 191/85. The appellants claimed that they were entitled to the set off of duty on MEG under Notification 225/86. This notification exempts polyester staple fibre etc. from so much of excise duty leviable thereon which is paid on inputs and used in or in relation to the manufacture of final product. In this case, since the product in which MEG is used i.e. polyester staple fibre is fully exempt, the set off of duty is not available on MEG. The exemption is not for MEG used in the manufacture of staple fibre but to polyester staple fibre to the extent of duty paid on MEG. The Collector (Appeals)'s finding that Notification 225/86 is a specially concessional provision and it does not provide for any refund of duty paid on the inputs namely MEG is correct in the case of the clear language of Notification 225/86. We therefore, uphold the impugned order and reject the appeal.

It has to be read in conjunction with other rules contained in that Section. The Section as a whole envisages the availability of credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of final products, the manner of utilisation of inputs and of credit so earned. If one is to confine himself to read only Rule57 A for determining the quantum of credit to be availed of, the provisions of Rule 57 B allowing higher notional credit in some cases has to be kept in operative. We are to read the entire scheme as a whole as envisaged in Rules 57A to 57 J. We are to consider whether in the case of removals of goods under bond in terms of Rule 191 B/191 BB would be hit by the Rule. Likewise, we are to consider whether in the case of utilisation of inputs and credit earned thereon, if the inputs have gone into the goods cleared for export under Rules 191 B/191 BB, whether there is a bar in availment of credit. Thus we are of the view that Rule 57A cannot be considered in isolation. In so far as this case is concerned, it has to be considered in conjunction with Rules 57C and 57 F (3).

Provisions of Rules 13, 191 B, 191 BB envisage the scheme relating to exports without payment of duty. But the scheme has been dovetailed with the Modvat scheme as is evident from the proviso to Rule 57F (3) which reads as below :-

From the above, it looks apparent to us, that even if the declared inputs are used in the declared final product, when some of final products are cleared for export under bond, credit earned from such inputs can be utilised for clearance of similar final products for home consumption and for any reason such adjustment is not possible, even cash refund to the manufacturer of final products is permitted. Now, we are to consider the meaning of the words "final products cleared for export under bond" (emphasised in the above proviso). POY & PSF are the final products in so far as the appellant is concerned. They are removed under bond in terms of Rules 191 B and 191 BB of the Central Excise Rules. Now let us look at the provisions governing the export of excisable goods. Rules 12 and 12 A govern the grant of rebate of Central Excise duty paid on these goods exported, as also on the excisable materials used in the production of goods, which are exported.

Rule 13 indicates that in like manner. Excisable Goods may be exported without payment of duly provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the C.Ex Rules and the owner of the goods to be exported enters into a bond undertaking to export the goods. From Rule 13. it is clear, that wherever rebate is permitted under Rules 12 & 12 A, goods in like manner can be exported without payment of duty in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Rules 191 B& 191 BB are the rules prescribing the export of excisable goods under bond figuring in Chapter IX of the C.Ex. Rules. Hence, we cannot give any other meaning to the words "final products cleared for export under Bond" figuring in the proviso to Rule 57 F (3), other than that is contained in Rule 13, which is the general provision permitting export of excisable goods for export under-bond. Hence we are not impressed with the argument of the Id. counsel for the Revenue that Modvat scheme is to be considered dehors export under bond, which is a separate scheme for exports.

Para 5 of the Larger Bench in the matter of Hunsur Plywood Works (P) Ltd. Vs. CCE (supra) is extracted below. 5. We have given a careful thought to the pleas made by both the sides. The commercial plywoods manufactured by the appellants were cleared free of duty in terms of Rule 191B after following the procedures prescribed thereunder. Rule 191B figures in Chapter IX which carries a heading "Export under claim for rebate of duty or under bond" and the Rule carries the heading "Manufacture in bond of articles from excisable goods on which duty has not been paid". This Rule is applicable to manufacture in bond of such articles from such excisable goods and subject to such conditions and limitations as may be specified in the notification issued in this regard. Under this Rule, the Govt. of India has issued a notification under which decorative plywood is covered for in bond manufacture out of commercial plywood as one of the items for the purpose of export outside India. It was under this notification that the appellants cleared commercial plywoods manufactured by them to the manufacturer of the decorative plywoods under proper central excise prescribed documents. It is nobody's case that the manufacturer has not manufactured decorative plywood for export purpose out of commercial plywood in question under Rule 191B of the Central Excise Rules. In terms of the notification, the manufacturer of the decorative plywood, i.e. the buyer of the commercial plywood, the appellants customer, would have therefore executed a bond for twice the amount of duty payable beyond the non-duty excisable goods i.e. commercial plywood in this case, used for the manufacture of decorative plywood for export purpose. The excisable goods therefore received by the decorative plywood manufacturer were also required to be kept in terms of this notification in a separate room. A procedure is also prescribed under this notification for disposal of the waste arising during the manufacture either on payment of duty or for recycling in the same factory. This notification also has a provision for allowing the manufacturer of the finished goods who has manufactured under bond under Rule 191B for clearance for home consumption on payment of excise duty leviable by them on such article as also on the excisable goods used in the manufacture thereof in the same manner as excisable goods intended for home consumption are cleared from the place of their production or manufacture or storage. It is thus seen that Rule 191B is a very comprehensive procedure under which finished goods manufactured out of non-duty paid goods have to be properly accounted for and in the event of the goods not being exported the levy of duty is provided both in respect of the finished goods manufactured in bond as also the inputs contained thereunder which was received without payment of duty. In view of this procedure prescribed under Rule 191B the question that has to be considered is whether goods cleared by the appellants under Rule 191B free of duty to the other unit which manufactured decorative plywood for export purposes could be taken to be export for Modvat purposes in terms of Rule 57F (3). We observe that Rule 57F (3) during the relevant period i.e. 1-3-1993 to 31-7-1993 providing for the manner in which the credit taken in respect of the inputs could be utilised read as under :

Per Jyoti Balasundaram :

The above appeal arises out of the order of the Commissioner of Central Excise, Allahabad who has confirmed a duty demand of Rs. 50,77,918/- against the appellants, holding that they had wrongly availed modvat credit of the above amount during the month of November 91 and imposed a penalty of Rs. 52 lakhs under Rule 173Q of the Central Excise Rules.

2. The brief facts of the case are that the appellants are engaged in the manufacture of polyester oriented yarn, polyester filament yarn and polyester textured yarn falling under Headings 54.02 and 54.03 of the Schedule to the CETA 1985. On 30.7.91, they filed a declaration under Rule 57G indicating POY, PFY and PTY as final products and poly ethylene terephthalate (polyester polymer chips) as inputs. On 31.7.91, they filed an application for permission to remove inputs or partially processed goods under Rule 57F (2) and/or Notification 214/86-CE along with an undertaking that the duty liability would be discharged on the finished goods. This application clearly mentioned that the inputs viz. DMT and MEG would be supplied directly to the job worker (M/s. Garware Plastics and Polyester Ltd.) for conversion into PP chips which would be returned to the appellants. By letter dated 19.8.91, the Range Superintendent sought clarification on certain points including maintenance of records and generation of waste. By reply dated 26.8.91, the appellants explained the procedure which would be followed by them for inputs to be directly supplied to job workers - they explained that the consignee's name would be shown as M/s. Garware Plastics and Polyester Ltd. A/c M/s. Raymond Synthetics. It was also explained that methanol and water would be generated as bye product during conversion of DMT and MEG into PP chips. The Assistant Commissioner granted permission to remove materials under Rule 57F (2) by his letter dated 11.10.91 the appellants took modvat credit of Rs. 50,77,918.90 on the basis of gate passes issued by M/s. Bombay Dyeing (supplier of DMT) and M/s. India Glycol (supplier of MEG) to the job workers on 11.1.95. The appellants were issued a show cause notice proposing recovery of modvat credit under the provisions of Rule 57I read with proviso to Section 11A on the grounds inter-alia that :

(a)

the appellants did not have permission under Rule 57F (2) read with Notification 214/86-CE during the period when DMT and MEG were received by job workers;

(b)

that the inputs were taken directly to the premises of the job worker without being brought into the appellants' premises.

(c)

authenticated challans were not issued for the movement of the goods;

(d)

payment of duty on methanol (bye product) by job workers is not in consonance with the provisions of the Notification 214/86;

(e)

job workers used catalysts and certain packing materials not supplied by the appellants and this was in violation of the condition of Notification 214/86.

(f)

appellants had not submitted a declaration under Rule 57G declaring PP chips as an intermediate product and POY, PFY, PTY as final products.

(g)

that the appellants had failed to produce proof that the job workers had supplied PP chips under Notification 214/86 in view of the job workers' letter that the chips were cleared without payment of duty in terms of Notification 53/88-CE;

(h)

that the appellants had wilfully misstated that they had received PP chips after conversion on job work under Notification 214/86.

The appellants replied to the notice denying the allegations, and pointing out that permission under Rule 57F had been applied for on 31.7.91 and since their application had not been turned down, they proceeded on the basis that permission had been granted, that there was no suppression of the fact that the inputs were directly sent to the job workers premises, that the job worker had cleared methanol (bye product) on payment of duty, that the receipt of inputs directly by the job worker was allowed since permission was granted on this basis by the Department on 11.10.91, etc.

XI (a) The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) denying the modvat credit on the aforesaid items are as under :

"These are the parts of the plant. These are the flameproof equipments fitted in the TEG and CP area of the POY plant.

These are basically safety equipments used to save the electrical and other equipment for flames and sparks and hence, are not used for producing, processing or for bringing about any change in any substance. Hence they are not qualified to become capital goods under Rule 57Q."

XI(b) Findings

The Commissioner (Appeals) has therefore accepted that these equipments are parts of the plant. The plant in question is undisputedly covered by the definition of capital goods in terms of Explanation 1 (a) to Rule 57Q. Therefore, these items are covered by Explanation 1 (b). Hence, denial of credit is incorrect.

XII S.S. Powder

XII(a) The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) denying the modvat credit on the aforesaid items are as under :

"This is part of the Spin Pack Assembly of the POY Plant. The SS Powder acts as a physical filter in extruding the molten polymer into yarn.

These goods aid in extruding the molten polymer into yarn and that S.S. Powder is more of the nature of raw material i.e. it is an input rather than capital goods and therefore not eligible for credit under Rule 57Q."

XII(b) Findings

Here also the Commissioner (Appeals) has specifically accepted that this is the part of spin pack assembly of the POY plant. Hence, the item is squarely covered by the Explanation of sub-Rule 1 (a) to Rule 57Q. In any event of the matter and without prejudice as per the interpretation of the Commissioner (Appeals) these items are in the nature of input. In such an event, the credit under Rule 57A ought to have been extended instead of denying the credit. The reasons mentioned already in respect of Molecular Sieves (under Sl. No. III) above are equally applicable to this case also.

XIII Hydraulic Pallet Truck/Spring Hangers Supports.

XIII(a) The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) denying the modvat credit on the aforesaid items are as under:

"This is an accessory of POY plant performing the function of handling the packed POY stacked on pallets for their storage/loading at the warehouse. The adjudicating authority rightly disallowed modvat credit on the said capital goods on the ground that it is not used for producing or processing or for bringing about any change in any substance because the role of item is after the goods are produced. This item does not fulfil the criteria laid down by the Supreme Court judgment in Rajasthan State Chemical Works. Therefore the citations quoted are not applicable."

XIII(b) Finding

The Commissioner (Appeals) had accepted that this is an accessory of POY plant and it performs the function of handling the packed POY stack for their storage/loading at warehouse. Hence, the item is covered by Explanation 1 (b) to Rule 57Q. In any event of the matter and the item itself is an equipment performing the functioning of handling of the goods in the factory. They are material handling equipments covered by the Explanation 1 (a) to Rule 57Q. In the following decisions, it has been held by the CEGAT that material handling equipments are capital goods and eligible for modvat credit: (a) CCE Vs. Cosmo Ferrites Ltd. 2002 (148) ELT 1232; (b) Malabar Cement Ltd. Vs. CCE 2002 (149) ELT 751 (Tri) maintained by Supreme Court in2003 (153) ELT A94; (c) CCE Vs. Vikram Cement 2001 (132) ELT 662 (Tri)

"This is part of the MEG Plant. It performs the function of supporting the catalyst inside the vessel to ensure optimum reaction during manufacturing the final product.

This item fitted at MEG plant performs the function of supporting the catalyst inside the vessel is only a support and cannot be capital goods. Credit has been rightly denied."

XIV (b) Findings

Here also the Commissioner (Appeals) accepts that it is part of MEG plant. Hence, the item is squarely covered by Explanation 1 (b) to Rule 57Q.

Levy of Purchase tax

10. 1[(1) Every dealer who in the course of his business purchases any goods specified in Schedule II from any person other than a registered dealer or 2[from a registered dealer who has opted for composition of tax under section 11 or from a registered dealer in the circumstances in which no tax u/s 9 is payable by the registered dealer on the sale price of such goods], shall be liable to pay tax on the purchase price of such goods if after their purchase,—

(a)

the goods other than those specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are not sold within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-State trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India but are sold or disposed of otherwise; or

4[(b)

the goods other than those specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are consumed or used,—

(i)

in the manufacture or processing of 5[goods declared tax free under section 16 other than the goods notified under sub-section (1B) of section 14] and the manufactured or processed goods are disposed of otherwise than by way of sale in the course of export out of the territory of India; or

(ii)

as plant, machinery, equipment and parts thereof in generation, transmission or distribution of electrical energy; or]

(c)

the goods other than those specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, after consumption or use in the manufacture or processing or mining of 6[any goods specified in Schedule II or the goods notified under sub-section (IB) of section 14], the manufactured or processed or mined goods are disposed off otherwise than by way of sale within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-State trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India; or

(d)

the goods specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are not sold within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-State trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India but are sold or disposed of otherwise; or

(e)

the goods specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are consumed or used in the manufacture or processing or mining of goods,

and such tax shall be levied,—

(i)

in respect of goods referred to in clauses (a), (b) and (c), at 3a[the rate of 5 per cent] or the rate specified in column (3) of Schedule II, whichever is lower; and

(ii)

in respect of goods referred to in clauses (d) and (e), at the rate specified in column (3) of Schedule II.

Explanation : The rate specified in Schedule II shall be the rate at which tax would have been levied on the sales of such goods within the State of Madhya Pradesh on the date of such purchase 7[:]]

8 [Provided that in respect of the goods referred to in clause (b) consumed in manufacture or processing of goods specified in Schedule I notified under second proviso to clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 14 and the goods so manufactured or processed are disposed off otherwise than by way of sale in the course of export out of the territory of India, such tax shall be levied at the rate of 2 per cent :

Provided further that in respect of the goods referred to in clause (c) consumed in manufacture of goods specified in Schedule II notified under first proviso to clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 14 and the goods so manufactured are disposed off otherwise than by way of sale within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-state trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India, such tax shall be levied at the rate of 2 per cent. ]

(2) No tax under this section shall be levied in respect of any year on—

(a)

a dealer whose turnover in a year does not exceed the limit prescribed under sub-section 9[(2)] of section 5;

(b)

any other dealer who has no turnover, if his aggregate of purchase prices of all the goods does not exceed such amount as may be prescribed.

(3) Every dealer who has no turnover and is liable to pay tax under sub-section (1) shall, for the purpose of sections 18, 20,21,24,25 and 39, be deemed to be a registered dealer.

2.1. Consequences of not computing total income as per Section 115BAA

The Ordinance provided an option to the domestic companies to pay tax at lower rates by opting for section 115BAA regime provided its total income is computed without claiming additional depreciation, prescribed allowancesand deductions. Further, while computing the taxable income, no loss or unabsorbed depreciation shall be allowed to set-off if such loss or unabsorbed depreciation is attributable to any of the prescribed deduction or allowance.

The Ordinance did not contain any provisions as to the consequences for subsequently not fulfilling any of the prescribed conditions. Thus, to remove the ambiguity, the Amendment Bill proposes that if a company, after opting for Section 115BAA, claims any of prescribed deduction or allowance in any previous year, then the option to pay tax at concessional rate shall become invalid for that year and for all subsequent assessment years.

2.2. Application of section 115BAA in case of amalgamation

It has been proposed in the Bill that in case of amalgamation, the successor co. shall not be allowed to set-off any loss or depreciation if such loss or depreciation is attributable to prohibited deduction or allowances as discussed earlier.

2.3. Allowability of deduction under section 80LA

One of the condition for opting for section 115BAA is that a domestic company shall not be allowed to claim any of the deduction as specified under Part-C of Chapter VI-A except deduction under section 80JJAA. In order to provide relief to the companies having a unit in the International Financial Services Centres (IFSCs), it has been proposed that deduction under 80LA shall be available even if such units opted for section 115BAA.

2.4. Adjustment of unabsorbed depreciation attributable to additional deprecation from block of asset

As companies opting for section 115BAA are not eligible to set-off the unabsorbed depreciation attributable to additional depreciation, a proviso has been proposed to be inserted in Section 115BAA(3) to clarify that if any unabsorbed depreciation, relating to additional depreciation, has not been given full effect, corresponding adjustment shall be made to WDV of the block of assets in prescribed manner. 4. A Plastic moulding company has developed a Mould for us and we have paid them for such mould. The mould will be used by the said company on our behalf for manufacture and supply of plastic parts exclusively for us. Please advise :

(1)

Since mould has not moved out of factory of the moulding company, would this be transaction of payment by us liable to excise and VAT ?

(2)

What will be treatment if after sometime we take back this mould ? Will duty or tax be leviable at that time ? If yes, on what value ?

In our view, the following shall be the consequences —

It is apparent that mould is being made/manufactured to be owned by your company. Hence, when charges for such mould are paid, it will have to be seen whether there is transfer of title of mould. As is apparent, mould becomes your property and accordingly, the same is a sale. Accordingly, the same is liable to excise duty and sales-tax. In our view, though there is no physical removal of goods from the factory of the moulding company; yet, since the title changes, it is a complete sale and would amount to 'removal' inasmuch as property belongs to you and any further use of moulds is only on your behalf. Viewed from another angle, when moulds are used inside the same factory for further manufacture, it amounts to 'captive use' and would be liable to duty in terms of the Explanation to rule 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The moulds must be shown as sold to you and received back on job-work basis under Rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Since both duty and tax stand paid at the time of sale of moulds to you, no further payment of duty or tax is warranted at the time when they are returned.

SERVICE TAX - TWO FOREIGN BRANCHES OF INDIA COMPANIES PROVIDED SERVICE TO EACH OTHER - TAXABILITY

5. A Ltd. and B Ltd. are two Indian companies (located in India). They have Branch X and Branch Y, respectively, outside India. Branch X provides services to Branch Y. Would this service be liable to service tax ? Please answer in light of applicability of rule 8 of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012.

Since Branch X of A Ltd. is located outside India, Branch X and A Ltd. would be deemed to be distinct persons under Explanations 3 and 4 to section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994. Similarly, Branch Y would also be a person separate person from B Ltd.

Since X and Y are separate persons and both are located outside India, Rule 8 of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012 would be inapplicable and furthermore, the service would be exempt under Entry 34(c) of the Notification No. 25/2012-ST.

The Lok Sabha passed the Finance Bill 2025 [hereinafter called 'Finance Bill (Lok Sabha)'] on March 25, 2025.While the Finance Bill,as passed by the Lok Sabha, largely retains the proposals made in the Finance Bill, certain noteworthy modifications have been made to the provisions relating to the block assessment, omission of equalisation levy and giving overriding powers to Section 44BBD over Section 115A and Section 44DA.

This article comprehensively analyses the changesmadeto the Finance Bill 2025 as passed by the Lok Sabha, highlighting their implications and the rationale behind these revisions.

1. The equalisation levy is withdrawn

Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 introduced the Equalisation Levy in respect of online advertisement services rendered to a specified person by a non-resident. The Finance Act 2020 expanded the scope of equalisation levy to the e-commerce supply of goods or services to a specified person by an e-commerce operator. However, the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 removed the equalisation levy on e-commerce supplies of goods or services with effect from 01-08-2024.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) amended Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 and the Income-tax Act ('ITA') to withdraw the equalisation levy from 01-04-2025 entirely. The following amendments have been made:

(a)

Amendments have been made to Sections 163 and 165 of the Finance Act 2016 to provide that the no equalisation levy shall apply to any consideration in respect of online advertisement services received or receivable by a non-resident on or after 01-04-2025.

(b)

A sunset date has been inserted in Section 10(50) of ITA to provide that this provision shall not apply from the assessment year 2026-27.

2. A Proviso has been inserted into Section 44BBD(2)

The Finance Bill 2025 proposed the insertion of Section 44BBD, which provides for the computation of income on a presumptive basis for non-residents engaged in the business of providing services or technology for setting up electronics manufacturing facilities in India. Section 44BBD(2) provides that a sum equal to 25% of the aggregate of the specified amounts shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of such business of the non-resident assessee.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) inserted a proviso to Section 44BBD(2), which provides that the provisions of Section 44DA or Section 115A shall not apply in respect of the amounts referred to in this subsection. This proviso will primarily impact the taxability of royalty and fees for technical services (FTS) earned by a non-resident.

The taxability of royalty and FTS depends upon the existence of the permanent establishment (PE) of a non-resident in India. If the PE exists in India and the royalty or FTS is connected to it, the income shall be taxable under the head "Business or Profession" as per Section 44DA. If the PE does not exist, the income shall be taxable under the head of other sources at the rate specified under Section 115A, subject to provisions of DTAA.

The impact of the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) is explained below.

2.1. No disallowance under Section 44DA

Section 44DA deals with the taxability of royalties and FTS connected to the PE in India. The first proviso to Section 44DA disallows the deduction in respect of the following:

(a)

Any expenditure or allowance that is not wholly or exclusively incurred for the business of such PE or fixed place of profession in India; or

(b)

Amount paid by the PE to its head office or to any of its other offices.

As the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 44DA, the above expenditure should not be disallowed if the royalty and FTS connected to the PE in India are taxable on a presumptive basis under Section 44BBD.

2.2. The concessional tax rate of Section 115A shall not be available

The proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 115A when the income is computed under Section 44BBD. Where the income is not computed under Section 44BBD, the tax rate under Section 115A will apply if the income is royalty or FTS. Therefore, the applicable tax rate for a non-resident providing services or technology in India shall be as follows:

(a)

Where the nature is business income, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income computed as per Section 44BBD shall be taxable at the applicable rate.

(b)

Issues

The sections 115BAA and 115BAB start with a non-obstante clause and overrides the other provisions of the Act. However, the sections are subject to the provisions of Chapter XII.

Owing to manner in which the sections have been introduced in the Act, certain issues have emerged which would need clarification, which are briefly discussed here-in-below:

1. Applicable tax rate on Long-term capital gains, short-term capital gains on listed securities and income under other heads

The sections do not override the provisions of Chapter XII of the Act i.e. provisions contained in the said chapter would hold forte. Hence special rates mentioned in sections 111A, 112, 112A, etc. would continue to apply.

Having regard to the language used in the sections, in our view, companies having income from House Property, Short-term capitals gains (other than on listed securities) and Income from Other Sources viz. bank interest, etc. should be taxed at 17.16%/ 25.168% if the reduced tax rate regime is opted for. A new manufacturing company holding sizeable rent yielding real estate and fixed deposits would stand to benefit (on account of lower tax rate of 17.16%) as compared to any other company having similar sources of income. The tax authorities may however, seek to dispute the adoption of section 115BAB by such companies by contending that the intention is not to extend benefit of lower taxes to non-business income.

2. Whether past MAT credit would be allowed

Sub-section 5A of section 115JB has been amended stating that provisions of section 115JB would not apply to companies which have exercised option to be governed by the aforesaid regime. It may be noted that no amendment has been made in section 115JAA of the Act which deals with utilization of MAT credit on account of MAT paid in earlier years. A plain reading of the provisions, in our view, suggest that past MAT credit available to an existing company should be allowed as a set-off against the tax liability under section 115BAA. There is no express prohibition in section 115BAA to deny MAT credit unlike several other deductions and losses specifically mentioned.

In our view, the MAT credit to be allowed in a year should be limited to the difference between the tax liability under section 115BAA and that under section 115JB which would have been payable. The fact that provisions of section 115JB are not applicable should not impact the computation of the credit which is separately provided in section 115JAA(5) and is an independent exercise for the purpose of determining and granting MAT credit only.

However, considering that the section seeks to override all the provisions of the Act, there may be litigation on the issue.

SHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and, therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

The Supreme Court held : The electricity is not an excisable item. In the instant civil appeal, the issue was with regard to the electricity which was generated inside the plant by heating of LSHS and which was captively consumed and used to manufacture cement/caustic soda. Rule 57A has an Explanatory clause (c) which states as to what inputs are included in Modvat credit. Explanation ( c) refers to ‘input used as fuel’. The said clause was introduced by Notification No. 4 of 1994. At that time, the Government made it clear that inputs used as fuel were entitled to MODVAT credit. That fuel, either utilized directly or for generating electricity, as an intermediary product, is integrally connected with several operations which result in the emergence of the final product, namely, cement/caustic soda. It is important to note that without utilization of LSHS, it is not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda. The electrolysis process is dependent on continuous flow of electricity. If there is disruption in the supply of electricity from the Electricity Board, then the entire plant of the assessee would fail and the manufacture of cement/caustic soda would not take place. Therefore, LSHS would come within the ambit of the expression ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product’. Electricity is one form of heat. It gets generated in several ways. LSHS is a fuel used in the generation of electricity. Since electricity is self-generated and since it comes into existence as an intermediary product, its utilization for production of final product is crucial. Hence, MODVAT credit on LSHS used in production of electricity could not be denied. Lastly, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced on behalf of the department, the expression ‘in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ was to be interpreted. The expression ‘in the manufacture of goods’ indicates the use of the input in the manufacture of the final product. The said expression normally covers the entire process of converting raw materials into finished goods such as caustic soda, cement, etc. However, the matter does not end with the said expression. The expression also covers inputs ‘used in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The said expression, namely, ‘in relation to’ also finds place in the extended definition of the word ‘manufacture’ in section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is for this reason that the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the expression ‘in relation to’ must be given a wide connotation. The Explanation to rule 57A shows an inclusive definition of the word ‘input’. Therefore, there is a dichotomy between inputs used in the manufacture of the final product and inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. The department gave a narrow meaning to the word ‘used’ in rule 57A. The department would have been right in saying that the input must be raw material consumed in the manufacture of final product. However, the expression ‘used’ in rule 57A uses the words ‘in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The words ‘in relation to’ which find place in section 2(f) of the 1944 Act have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover processes generating intermediate products and it is in this context that it has been repeatedly held by the Supreme Court that if manufacture of final product cannot take place without the process in question, then that process is an integral part of the activity of manufacture of the final product. Therefore, the words ‘in relation to the manufacture’ have been used to widen and expand the scope, meaning and content of the expression ‘inputs’ so as to attract goods which do not enter into finished goods. Where raw material is used in the manufacture of final product, it is an input used in the manufacture of final product. However, the doubt may arise only in regard to use of some articles not in the mainstream of manufacturing process, but something which is used for rendering final product marketable or something used otherwise in assisting the process of manufacture. This doubt is set at rest by use of the words ‘used in relation to manufacture’. In the instant case, the LSHS was used to generate electricity, which was captively consumed. Without continuous supply of such electricity generated in the plant, it was not possible to manufacture cement, caustic soda, etc. Without such supply, the process of electrolysis was not possible. Therefore, keeping in mind the expression ‘used in relation to the manufacture’ in rule 57A, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit on LSHS. The instant case fell in clause (c) and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) even before 16-3-1995
