Background

Amidst the prolonged slowdown in the economy, the government brought in the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019, promulgated by the President of India, to provide impetus to the ailing corporate sector. The ordinance inter alia provides to reduce the corporate tax rate on certain classes of companies; rationalise the current Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rates and withdraw the enhanced surcharge from certain incomes arising from investment in capital markets etc.

The key amendments that find focus in this article relate to reduction in effective corporate tax rate for certain class of domestic companies. Due to such tax rate reduction, India's lowest bracket of corporate tax rate of 17.16 percent1 is now competitive with that of other emerging economies such as Vietnam (20 percent), Thailand (20 percent), Singapore (17 percent), Hong Kong (16.5 percent)2.

The reduction in corporate tax rates has been made effective through insertion of two new sections in the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) i.e. section 115BAA and section 115BAB (collectively referred to as 'Beneficial sections'). These sections are still subject to other provisions of Chapter XII of the Act, such as section 111/111A/112/113 etc. and hence any income in nature of long term/short term capital gains etc. covered under other sections of Chapter XII will continue to be taxed at existing rates.

The sections providing concessional tax rates have been made effective from the current Financial Year (FY) i.e. FY 2019-20 itself. Hence, companies considering to opt for the beneficial sections should take a timely call taking into account the impact of the change in effective tax rates on the advance tax computations for the next quarter/s, on tax provisioning etc.

The amendments also include reduction of tax rate on book profit u/s. 115JB of IT. Act known as Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate from the existing effective tax rates of 20.20 percent to 17.47 percent for all companies.

Newly inserted section 115BAA and section 115BAB:

1.

Relief to existing Companies – Section 115BAA: Under this section, a domestic company can opt for a lower effective tax rate of 25.17 percent(22 percent basic plus 10 percent surcharge plus 4 percent cess) subject to certain conditions. This provision is applicable to all domestic companies (irrespective of activities, turnover or year of incorporation). If a company opts for this option then it would not be eligible for certain expenses /deduction as discussed later in subsequent paragraphs.

2.

Relief to new manufacturing Companies – Section 115BAB: Under this section, new domestic manufacturing companies can opt for a lower rate of tax of 17.16 percent (15 percent basic plus 10 percent surcharge plus 4 percent cess), subject to fulfilment of following conditions:

Company should be set-up and registered on or after 1 October 2019;

Manufacturing to be commenced on or before 31 March 2023 and the company is not formed by splitting up/reconstruction, of a business already in existence;

Company should fulfil certain conditions regarding use of plant and machinery.

However, a company willing to opt for beneficial sections would not be entitled various tax exemption/deduction available under the sections 10AA (tax holiday for SEZ units), 32(1)(iia) (additional depreciation), 32AD (additional deduction for investment in machinery), 33AB (deduction for tea/coffee/rubber development account), 33ABA (site restoration fund), 35(1)(ii) or (iia) or (iii), 35(2AA), 35(2AB)(weighted deduction for expenditure on scientific research), 35AD (capital expenditure for specified business), 35CCC (expenditure on agriculture extension projects) or 35CCD (skill development project) or any under any provision of Chapter VI-A under the heading "C - deductions in respect of certain incomes" other than section 80JJAA of the Act (henceforth collectively mentioned as deduction/exemption provisions).

Further, the Company will not be allowed any set-off of losses carried forward from earlier years if such losses are attributable to any of the deduction/exemption provisions referred in above paragraph.

Further MAT provisions u/s 115JB shall not be applicable to companies opting for sections 115BAA/115BAB.

The option to avail concessional rate of tax as per the aforesaid sections is available from FY 2019-20 onwards and should be exercised before the due date of filing tax return of the year from which such option is exercised. A company not opting for the beneficial provisions due to its existing tax exemptions/deductions, can avail the option for beneficial provisions in the future; however, such option once exercised cannot be revoked in subsequent years.

M.F.(D.R.) CIRCULAR NO. B-42/1/96-TRU, DATED 27-9-1996

REVERSAL OF MODVAT CREDIT TAKEN ON INPUTS UNDER RULE 57CC

Kind attention is invited to the provisions of Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules for reversal of Modvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods or goods chargeable to 'nil' rate of excise duty. The provision has been made that where a manufacturer uses inputs which are common to both dutiable goods as well as exempted goods, the manufacturer is required to debit the amount equal to 8% of the value of the exempted goods when they are cleared from the factory.

2. In some cases, the exempted goods cleared by one manufacturer are used as inputs by another manufacturer. The manufacturer of exempted goods indicates the amount of Modvat credit reversed on the invoices issued by him for such exempted goods. In this context, some doubts have been raised whether the amount of Modvat credit so reversed is available as Modvat credit to the user of such exempted goods when he uses them as inputs in his factory.

3. In this context, it is clarified that the amount reversed is not by way of payment of excise duty. Accordingly, the amount of Modvat credit reversed and shown in the invoice by the manufacturer of exempted goods cannot be taken as credit by the user of exempted goods.

- In Modi Plastics v. CCE (2007) 216 ELT 112 (CESTAT SMB), final products entered in DSA (that time RG-1) were found defective. These were reused within the factory. Waste was also recycled. Final products after processing were cleared on payment of duty. It was held that assessee is eligible for duty exemption under Notification No. 67/1995-CE dated 16-3-1995 on finished goods reprocessed. Provisions not applicable to matches as final products - The provisions of notification No 67/1995 dated 16.3.95 is applicable to all final products except matches [This item was excluded from Cenvat provisions. Now it has been included. However, corresponding change has not been made in notification No. 67/1995-CE].

Flushing of gas in air is not captive consumption ? - In BOC India v. CCE 2004 (173) ELT 89 (CESTAT), assessee was flushing gas and was allowing it to escape in atmosphere for cleaning, before new gas was produced. This was technical necessity. It was held that the gas is not used in further manufacture and such gas cannot be said to have been captively consumed. Hence, exemption under notification No. 67/1995-CE is not available [May be it is not used 'in manufacture of final product', but certainly it is used 'in relation to manufacture of final product', and should be eligible].

In fact, in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE 2000 (124) ELT 323 (CEGAT), Naphtha used in flushing pipelines was held eligible as flushing is a process integrally connected with manufacturing process of final product.

No duty on intermediate products if duty on final product remitted - Remission of duty does not mean goods are exempt from duty or chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty. Hence, no duty is payable on intermediate products used in the final products on which duty has been remitted - Pepsico India Holding v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 222 (CESTAT).

Proportionate reversal of credit taken on molasses used in exempted products sufficient - Molasses is used to manufacture rectified spirit and denatured spirit. Rectified spirit is exempted. Denatured spirit is dutiable. First rectified spirit is manufactured. While manufacturing rectified spirit, Carbon dioxide is manufactured, which is sold on payment of duty. Part of rectified spirit is used to manufacture denatured spirit, which is dutiable. In Ugar Sugar Works v. CCE (2007) 214 ELT 337 (CESTAT), it is held that on reversal of credit on molasses used in manufacture of rectified spirit, balance Cenvat credit taken on molasses cannot be denied.

In Godavari Sugar Mills v. CCE (2007) 212 ELT 234 (CESTAT), it was held that if proportionate Cenvat credit taken on molasses is reversed, it is sufficient - same view in SCI India v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 565 (CESTAT), though order is not worded happily - same view in Sakthi Sugars v. CCE (2008) 12 STT 174 (CESTAT). - view confirmed in CCE v. Sakhi Sugars (2016) 53 GST 149 = 64 taxmann.com 316 (SC).

No duty payable if some waste final products get produced - In Matsushita Lakhanpal Battery v. CCE 2005 (186) ELT 445 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturing battery cells for which intermediate products were manufactured within the factory. Some of the battery cells got rejected during manufacture. These were not marketable and no duty was paid on them. Department contended that since final product is 'exempt' duty should be paid on 'intermediate products' which were used in such waste battery cells. It was held that even if some final product becomes scrap and is not dutiable, it does not mean that intermediate products have not been captively consumed in manufacture of final product. Hence, demand is not sustainable.

Intermediate product exempt even if manufactured by third party - Intermediate product/input/capital goods are exempt even if they are manufactured by third party, as long as the captive consumption is within the factory - Tambraparani Containers v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 276 (CESTAT) (similar decisions in respect of capital goods discussed in a later paragraph).

Exemption to intermediate product if final product cleared on payment of 'amount' - If final product is exempt from duty, normally duty is payable on intermediate product. However, if final product is cleared as per provisions of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules [i.e. after paying 'amount' or after reversing Cenvat credit], intermediate product will be exempt from duty - proviso (vi) to Notification No. 67/1995-CE - clarified and confirmed in CCE, Cochin TN 68/2001 dated 24.7.2001] - noted and followed in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 287 ELT 102 (CESTAT).

The process of conversion of steel flats into loose leaf springs is that the steel flats are cut into pieces of defined sizes, holes are drilled into these pieces and then they are rolled. Loss of inputs during handling eligible - In or in relation to the manufacture covers the entire manufacturing process starting from initial stage of handling of inputs. Thus, if wastage of input at the initial handling from tank discharge due to various reasons like spillage, pipeline losses, handling losses etc., it is 'in or in relation to manufacture' and Cenvat (now ITC) cannot be denied. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE (2001) 136 ELT 943 (CEGAT) - followed in CCE v. Hydrogas Plg (I) P Ltd. 2006 (196) ELT 167 (CESTAT) - same view in Zeneca ICI Agro Chemicals v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 770 (CESTAT).

9.3-5 No credit on short received inputs but natural losses allowable

If inputs are short received and there is loss during transit, the goods short received cannot be termed as 'used in or in relation to manufacture'. Hence, Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such short received inputs is not available - Asea Brown Boveri Ltd. v. CCE 1994 (74) ELT 897 (CEGAT) - same view in Bombay Dyeing v. CCE 1999 (113) ELT 331 (CEGAT) * Sterlite Industries v. CCE (2007) 212 ELT 193 (CESTAT) * Carborandum Universal v. CCE (2008) 227 ELT 535 (CESTAT SMB).

Such price would have various components including Cost, Duties, Taxes, profits etc. The price is lump sum or composite price and cannot be divided into its components.

Further, the Duty, etc. embedded in purchase price is not incurred by the purchaser.

MODVAT Credit is not available as a consequence of payment. Finally, the credit available under the Rule is in respect of purchase price, which includes Duties. The credit is quantified with reference to the amount of Duty. That is only a basis for quantifying the amount.

Accordingly, it is not a credit for Duty. In this connection, a useful reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. P.J. Accordingly, in purchase cost of raw material, in spite of the amendment, there is no requirement to adjust MODVAT.

Exempted goods

As per Rule 2(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 'exempted goods' means goods which are exempt from whole of duty of excise leviable thereon and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 or under entries at serial numbers 67 and 128 of Notification No. 12/2012-CE, dated the 17th March, 2012 is availed.

[In Notification No. 12/2012-CE, Sr. No. 67 is coal falling under heading 2701 and Sr. No. 128 is fertilizers. Duty on these articles is 1% subject to condition that Cenvat credit should not be availed]

Thus, 'exempted goods' for purpose of Cenvat cover (a) Goods chargeable to 'Nil' duty as per Tariff and (b) Goods which are exempt by a notification issued under section 5A (c) Goods on which 2% excise duty has been paid under exemption Notification No. 1/2011-CE dated 1-3-2011 or 1% under Notification No. 12/2012-CE dated 17-3-2012.

Exempted goods include non-excisable goods - For purpose of rule 6(1), 'exempted goods' or exempted final products shall include non-excisable goods - Explanation 1 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Value of such goods shall be invoice value. If such invoice value is not available, then it will be determined by reasonable means - Explanation 2 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Waste, by products are exempted goods w.e.f. 1-4-2016 - Bagasse, dross and skummings of non ferrous metals or any such by-product will be treated as 'exempted goods' w.e.f. 1-3-2015 for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules - CBE&C circular No. 1027/15/2016-CX dated 25-4-2016.

Exempted goods mean non-excisable goods also w.e.f. 1-3-2015 for purpose of rule 6 - As per explanation 1 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 'exempted goods' or 'final products' shall include non-excisable goods cleared for a consideration from the factory.

Gas which escapes in atmosphere - rule 6 does not apply - Oxygen gas which escapes in atmosphere during manufacture of Nitrogen is not 'manufactured product'. Hence, rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not apply - CCE v. Air Liquid India Holding (2009) 238 ELT 122 (CESTAT SMB).

Electricity is 'exempted goods' w.e.f. 1-3-2015- As per explanation 1 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 'exempted goods' or 'final products' shall include non-excisable goods cleared for a consideration from the factory.

This should cover electricity sold outside and rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules shall apply.

Packing material in which inputs were received can be exempted goods w.e.f. 1-3-2015 - If packing material in which inputs were received was sold for price, such sale can be considered as sale of 'exempted goods' for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Pet Preform

The item in question, i.e., "pet preform", is moulded in such a way as to give it shape of containers of different sizes and styles. As the air is blown through it, it forms the shape of a container. Pet preforms cannot be used for any other purpose besides being used as a container. The fact that moulding is done to bring it in the shape does not take it away from the domain of plastic packing material. The fact that it is moulded into plastic containers would not take it outside the purview of the category of the materials intended for being used for the packing of plastic goods for sale. The process of moulding pet preform was required for putting it in shape with a view to adapt it for actual user. The process only facilitates the actual user for packing. Viewed from these aspects, the imposition of tax at 12.5 per cent is not justified. Being an item coming well under the purview of S1. No. 155 of Part III of Schedule C, tax is to be charged at four per cent. [Epitome Petrochemical Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, West Bengal and others, (2011) 41 VST 22; (2011) 58 S.T.A. 95, decided on 4.3.2011, by the Division Bench of West Bengal Taxation Tribunal; J.N.R.T. Commercial (P) Limited another v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, West Bengal Others, (2011) 58 S.T.A. 237, decided on 4.3.2011 by the Division Bench of West Bengal Taxation Tribunal]

Charcoal Iron Press / Machine Sewain / Domestic Grinder / Fruit Juice Machine / Mincer Hand Operated/ Puri Belna – manually operated: Whether covered within Hardware in Entry 45 of Schedule B of PVAT Act?

It was submitted on behalf of the applicant that all these items are made of iron and steel and no power is used while making use of these items, hence they should be classified within "hardware" under entry 45 of Schedule B of Punjab Value Added Tax Act, 2005.

Plaster of Paris (P.O.P.) – Whether it is same as Gypsum?

Entry 16 of Schedule – A which deals with tax free goods, reads as under:-"fertilizers including bio-fertilizers and organic fertilizers, gypsum, pesticides, weedicides, insecticides and fungicides"

As per the appellant, appellant is importing P.O.P. from outside Punjab and chemistry of P.O.P. and chemistry of gypsum was the same and therefore it fell in Entry 16 of Schedule A and was exempt from payment of tax. However, from bare perusal of Entry 16, it would come out that it relates to the fertilizers, pesticides, weedicides, fungicides relating to land and agriculture. The Gypsum in the entry will also relate to its use in reference to land and crops. Gypsum is stated to loosen soil structure and improve poor soil conditions. It is stated to be used when there is layer of hard soil in the field.

Appellant is dealing in P.O.P. which is used as a building material. It cannot be said to be relating to land or its use and cannot be an item covered in Entry 16 of Schedule A. I, therefore, agree with the order of the Commissioner dated 27.8.2008 where the Commissioner had determined the disputed question saying that P.O.P. was not gypsum covered in Entry 16 and not tax free. [*Prem Enterprises, Jalandhar v. State of Punjab, (2010) 35 PHT 67, decided on 14.9.2009 by Value Added Tax Tribunal, Punjab, Chandigarh]

*Note – The view taken in this case has been endorsed by the Division Bench of Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case reported as Prem Enterprises v. State of Punjab and another, (2013) 59 VST 237 (PH); VSTI 2013 (Delhi, Punjab and Haryana) …B-98; (2013) 44 PHT 62 (PH), decided on 9.1.2103 observing that-

"Though the chemical properties may be similar, but the fact remains that the uses of gypsum and POP are different. Entry 16 of Schedule A exempts fertilizers from tax. The definition is inclusive which includes gypsum as a fertilizer. Entry 16 exempts fertilizers from tax, whereas POP cannot remotely be used as fertilizer. Therefore, POP does not fall within entry 16 of Schedule A."

HEADNOTE: Section 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, read with section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 and section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Credit of duty not to be denied or varied in certain cases - Inputs - Whether section 11A Central Excise Act, would have no application, while construing impact of section 87 of Finance Act - Held, yes - Assessee, a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, paid specified duty - Relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE(NT) dated 1-3-1994 issued under rule 57A, assessee took MODVAT credit on inputs namely, Furnace Oil at rate of ‘15 per cent at valorem’ - This Notification was amended by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT) dated 3-5-1997 - By said amendment, rate of credit on above inputs was restricted to ‘10 per cent ad valorem’ - Said Notification was given retrospective effect from 23-7-1996 by virtue of provisions of section 87 of Finance Act - Whether demand for recovery of MODVAT Credit with interest was justified - Held, yes [Paras 17.2  18.1] [In favour of revenue]GST/Excise  Customs: Where specified duty was paid on inputs and relying upon Notification 5/94-CE (NT) dated 1-3-1994, assesse took MODVAT credit at rate of 15 per cent, in view of restriction imposed on rate of credit at 10 per cent via subsequent Notification 14/97 CE(NT) dated 3-5-1997 which was given retrospective effect, revenue’s demand for recovery was justified

FACT: The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

HEADNOTE: MODVAT follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not Rule 57A, read with rule 57B, of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - CENVAT Credit - One H produced sulphuric acid - During manufacture of sulphuric acid, waste material arises which is called scrubber liquor - Scrubber liquor, though normally a polluting material, can safely substitute for water in case of production of sodium silicate - Assessee, a manufacturer of sodium silicate, entered into an agreement with H for supply of scrubber liquor to assessee on condition that scrubber liquor would be supplied to assessee free, except for central excise duty and sales tax paid by H on scrubber liquor - Assessee availed MODVAT Credit of duty paid by it on scrubber liquor - Adjudicating Authority denied MODVAT Credit on ground that scrubber liquor could not be considered as input - Whether finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to factual situation and relevant legal provisions - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee was eligible for MODVAT Credit as claimed - Held, yes

FACT: One H was producing, sulphuric acid. During the manufacture of the said acid, waste material arises which is called "Scrubber Liquor". The scrubber liquor is polluting and its disposal is expensive. However, it can be used in manufacturing sodium silicate. Water is required to be added to adjust the viscosity of sodium silicate. The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of sodium silicate. The assessee entered into an agreement with H for the supply of scrubber liquor to the assessee. H was paying central excise duty and sales tax on scrubber liquor. It was agreed that the scrubber liquor would be supplied to the assessee free, except for the central excise duty and sales tax. In the invoices, the price (at which duty was calculated) was being shown as rebate. The assessee availed MODVAT Credit of duty paid by it on scrubber liquor. The adjudicating authority denied the MODVAT Credit availed by the assessee on the ground that the scrubber liquor could not be considered as input. On appeal, the appellate authority upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

HELD: Admittedly, the scrubber liquor is to be added to adjust viscosity of the sodium silicate. Such addition was in the factory of the assessee and before sale of sodium silicate. Modvat Rules allow ‘Credit of any duty of excise paid on the goods used in the manufacture on said final products" (Rules 57A). Rule 57B further clarifies that "Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 57A, the manufacturer of final products shall be allowed to take credit of the specified duty paid... on inputs used in or relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not". It was not reasonable to argue that materials used for maintaining viscosity at the required level were not used in relation to manufacture, particularly, when the viscosity control was by the manufacturer before the sale of goods. It is also to be noted that Modvat follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not. Correctness of payment is not relevant; only the fact of payment is. A view to the contrary also goes against the broad definition of ‘manufacture’ in section 2 of the Central Excise Act in a manner as to include "any process - incidental or ancillary to the completion of manufacture". Thus, a finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to the given factual situation and relevant legal provisions. Hence, the assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit as claimed. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Classification of goods - Madhya Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Heading No. 23099090 - Bio Processed Meal - Whether chapter heading 23099090 is exclusively meant for animal feed - Held, yes - Applicant is a renowned manufacturer of soya based products, both for general public, for animal feed as well as for industrial use - It has sought Advance Ruling on confirmation of classification of product 'Preparation of a kind used in Animal Feeding - Bio-Processed Meal' falling under HS Code 23099090 - However, applicant has not provided any evidence to prove that said product 'Bio-Processed Meal' is meant for animal feed for it to fall under Chapter heading 23099090 - Further, applicant has withdrawn comment 'and not fit for human consumption' from his application - Whether therefore, applicant's product 'preparation of a kind used in Animal Feeding - Bio-Processed Meal' is not entitled for classification under HSN 23099090 and accordingly applicant is not entitled to claim 'Nil' rate of duty under Notification No. 02/2017 - CT (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 - Held, yes [Paras 7.6 to 7.8]GST: Product 'preparation of a kind used in Animal Feeding - Bio-Processed Meal' is not entitled for classification under HSN 23099090 and accordingly applicant is not entitled to claim 'Nil' rate of duty under Notification No. 02/2017 - CT (Rate), dated 28-6-2017

FACT: The applicant is engaged in manufacturing and export of various soya processed food, used for human as well as animal consumption.

It seeks Advance Ruling on whether the product 'Preparation of a kind used in Animal Feeding - Bio-Processed Meal' will fall under HS Code 23099090 and applicable rate of GST on said product shall be 'Nil' as per Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017?

HELD: It is found that the applicant has sought confirmation of classification of their product to whom they term it 'Preparation of a kind used in Animal Feeding - Bio-Processed Meal' and also informed that the said product falls under the HS Code 23099090. Further, it is noted that the main raw material for the said preparation is 'Meal of Soyabean'.

Further, the applicant has provided the following reasoning to establish that the said product is meant for Animal Feeding:

'The protein content of the feed grade is less than 50 per cent and not fit for human consumption. During the manufacturing process soya meal undergoes through fermentation process. The process uses biotechnology to convert protein structure to smaller molecular weight to increase efficiency digestion and absorption. It also breaks down and reduce antigens or anti-nutrient substance due to fermentation'. [Para 7.2]

It is noted that the applicant is renowned manufacturer of soya based products used for the consumption of general public namely Soya Flakes/Grits, Soya Flour, Soya lecithin, Soya Protein/TVP etc. They are also engaged in the manufacturing of various products meant for animal feeding namely GMO Soyabean meal, non-GMO Soya Grits etc. They are also manufacturing soya products for industrial use. The products meant for industrial use and for consumption of general public are leviable to various rates of GST whereas the applicant has claimed the chapter heading of 23099090 which is exclusively meant for animal feed and attracts Nil rate of duty. In such a situation, a critical analysis is required to establish that the said product is meant only for animal feed. [Para 7.4]

The applicant has claimed the classification under HSN Code 23099090 which is exclusively meant for animal feed and attracts Nil rate of GST. Further, the Notification No. 17-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 and corresponding notification issued under MPGST Act has exempted intra-State supplies of goods, the description of which is specified in column (3) of the Schedule appended to the said notification. Falling under the tariff item, sub-heading, heading or Chapter, as the case may be, as specified in the corresponding entry. [Para 7.5]

HEADNOTE: Section 14, read with  section 26A, of the Madhya Pradesh Value Added Tax Act, 2002 - Input tax - Rebate of - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was in business of manufacture of edible oil - It purchased soya seeds after payment of VAT and consumed same in manufacture of edible oil - In addition to edible oil, by-products de-oiled cake (DOC), sludge, etc. were also produced in course of manufacturing process - By-product DOC was tax free - Assessee claimed benefit of set off as provided under sections 14(1)(a), (2) and 26A(7) - Assessing Authority held that since DOC, a by-product, was not taxable goods, assessee was not entitled to benefit of set off on entire purchase of soya seeds - Whether in view of judgment of Supreme Court in case of Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Bharat Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. 1992 taxmann.com 38, assessee was eligible to set off on entire purchase of soya seeds - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]CST  VAT : Madhya Pradesh VAT - Where assessee purchased soya seeds after payment of VAT and consumed same in manufacture of edible oil and by-products de-oiled cake (DOC), sludge, etc. were also produced in manufacturing process, even though DOC was not taxable goods, assessee was entitled to benefit of set off, as provided under sections 14(1)(a), (2) and 26A(7), on entire purchase of soya seeds

FACT: The assessee was in the business of manufacture of edible oil. It purchased soya seeds from the registered dealers after payment of VAT and consumed the same in the manufacture of edible oil. In addition to the edible oil, by-products de-oiled cake (DOC), sludge, etc. were also produced in the course of manufacturing process. The by-product DOC was tax free.

The assessee claimed benefit of set off as provided under sections 14(1)(a),(2) and 26A(7).

The Assessing Authority opined that the assessee used soya seeds in the manufacture of edible oil. The DOC, a by-product, was not taxable. Hence, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of set off as provided under sections 14(1)(a), (2) and 26A(7) on entire purchase of soya seeds. He apportioned the tax liability after deducting the percentage of proportionate manufacture of DOC.

On writ:

HELD: The Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Bharat Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. 1992 taxmann.com 38 has considered the question of set off and applicability of principle of apportionment in the event of raw material purchased by dealer be used in manufacture of taxable goods and a by-product which is not taxable. It has held that a refinery would be entitled to set off to the entire tax paid by it on the purchase of raw material. [Para 11]

From a reading of the judgment of the Supreme Court, it is clear that manufacturer is eligible the benefit of set off on the entire amount of tax paid on purchase of raw material and principle of apportionment could not be invoked. The judgment of the Supreme Court is applicable to the instant case, because the DOC, a by-product, is tax free and another by-product sludge and main product oil are taxable. Hence, the authority cannot apportion the tax liability after deducting the percentage of proportionate manufacture of DOC. [Para 13]

In view of the aforesaid, the assessee was eligible to set off on entire purchase of soya seeds. [Para 19]

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Modvat credit - Inputs - Appellant-job-worker manufactured plastic half round rain water system out of raw material supplied by manufacturer-supplier - Benefit of notification 1/93 was denied to appellant because as per appellants goods were classifiable under head 32.26.90 and according to department goods were fall under head 39.17.00 - On appeal Tribunal denied said benefit and remitted back matter for revaluation of duty by classifying manufactured goods under head 39.17.00 and directed for allowing Modvat credit accordingly - However, on readjudication, Modvat credit was denied - Whether since supply of goods by manufacturer to job-worker was well established, Modvat credit would have to be granted - Held, yes [Matter remanded for redetermine value] Circulars & Notifications: Notification No. 1/93

FACT: The appellant-job-workers manufactured ‘Plastic half round rain water system’ using raw material supplied by the manufacturer. The appellants claimed benefit of notification No. 1 of 1993 which was denied because the goods manufactured were bearing brand name of manufacturer. Classification of goods manufactured as well as turnover limitation and valuation of goods were in dispute. The Tribunal held that goods manufactured were classifiable either under heading 39.25.99 or under heading 39.17.00 and remitted the matter back to redetermine the valuation and eligibility of Modvat after denying benefit of Notification as well as plea of limitation. On readjudication the Modvat credit was denied. The Commissioner determined demand and imposed penalty.

On appeal :

HELD: The limitation issue was settled by the earlier order of the Tribunal and it was not open to reopen that issue. However, the question of classification in the instant case was annexed issue. The imposition of penalty, therefore, was not called for. There was no cause for imposition of penalty in these appeals. More so when, section 11AC penalty for certain period, in this case could not be invoked, being period earlier to introduction of that section. As regards the plea made on interest under section 11AB, the application of Board Instruction No. 655/46/2002-CX, dated 26-6-2002 would govern and be applicable in this case to levy interest. The valuation was to be redetermined as per the formula prescribed by the Apex Court in the case of Ujjagar Print. The CA certificate had to be considered to determine the valuation and duty. As regards the plea of Modvat, there was no valid reasons to deny the same as arrived at in the order impugned. Since goods have been supplied by manufacturer to the job-workers, the Modvat credit would have to be granted and thereafter duty demand was to be reverted. [Para 4]

In view of the finding, these appeals were partly allowed after setting aside the penalty as imposed and the matter was remitted back to the Commissioner to re-determine the valuation of goods and quantum of duty and interest. [Para 5]

By section 12A, there is no deduction permissible from turnover of certain sales except on a certificate. The difference in the language of the two provisions is clear inasmuch as both may be providing deductions from turnover, but one provides for deduction on declarations and other provides on certificate. [Para 32] By section 17, there is a power conferred in the State Government which shall be exercised by issuance of a Notification in the Official Gazette to reduce rate of tax and to amend Schedules. By section 17A, there will be no deductions under section 8 in certain cases. Thus, section 17A deals with the situation where any entry, or part thereof, is transposed whether under section 17 or otherwise, by its deletion from one of the Schedules and its insertion in or addition to another Schedule, then, if no tax on any sale or purchase of the goods specified in that entry, or part thereof, is leviable, the deductions provided in clause (ii) or clause (iii) of section 8 shall not apply to the resale of those goods. Therefore, there has to be a fulfilment of the pre-condition, namely, transposition, whether under section 17 or otherwise. Secondly, there ought to be no tax on any sale or purchase of the goods specified in that entry or part thereof. It is only upon such situation that there will be no deduction provided in clause (ii) or clause (iii) of section 8 and which provision deals with resale of the goods. In other words, the deductions under these clauses shall not apply to the resale of those goods. The reason for that is obvious, for the Government has exercised a power, either in terms of section 17 and clause (a) and (b) thereof, or otherwise. [Para 33]

In-show cause notice, it has been alleged that APSEZ has availed CENVAT Credit on services-Goods Transport Agency, Cargo Handling Services, Clearing & Forwarding Agent services, Manpower Recruitment & Supply Agency Service, Steamer Agent Services etc. These services have no relationship/nexus with the provisions of output service of Port service inasmuch as the said services had been directly provided to the cargo imported by others. it was to be held that phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’ were the intentionally manufactured products. [ No benefit could be extended to] the mother liquor which emerges during the course of processing of bones with HCl and is used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’. If the entire process from start to end is examined, undoubtedly HCl had to be held as having been used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’. [Para 9] Rule 57CC (rule 6) applies to the final product, dutiable or exempted and makes no distinction between an intended final product or unintended emergence of by-product. The said rule in simple terms requires the assessee to pay an amount equal to 8 per cent of the value of the goods cleared at nil rate of duty, even where the inputs have been used directly or indirectly in the manufacture of such final product. As HCl had been used in the instant case in the manufacture of final product phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, which attract nil rate of duty, the provisions of rule 57CC would apply. It was impossible to obtain the mother liquor or the resultant phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’ without the use of HCl. As long as HCl is used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, the applicability of provisions of rule 57CC cannot be ruled out. [Para 12]

The appellant’s reference to the provisions of rule 57D in support of their contention that Modvat credit was not to be denied if a part of the same was contained in the by-product, was indicative of the legislative intent that reversal of 8 per cent amount of the value of the by-product in terms of provisions of rule 57CC would not apply. The expression ‘by-product’ occurring in rule 57D has to be examined and interpreted in the context of the said rule, which uses the other expression ‘waste’ or ‘refuse’, etc. It is in this scenario that the rule provides for non-reversal of Modvat credit, even if waste, refuse or by-product has emerged during the course of manufacture. The effect of the said rule would be that if waste product, which may not be excisable, e.g. , floor sweepings during the course of manufacture of biscuits, then the quantum of credit originally taken is not to be varied. Similarly, if iron and steel scrap arises during manufacture of iron products, the Modvat is not to be varied, but iron and scrap being excisable products, [the manufacturers] have to discharge duty burden. If the same are exempted, provisions of rule 57CC will apply. As such, it is to be concluded that rule 57D refers to waste scrap and by-product, which are not excisable at all. The said provision cannot be pressed into service in support of the plea that even if the by-product is excisable, but exempted, amount of 8 per cent is not required to be paid. The appellant was not being directed to reverse the credit amount equivalent to the inputs contained in the said exempted final products. Further, taking an hypothetical example of electrolysis of water, which an assessee may undertake to obtain oxygen, he cannot take the plea that hydrogen which also emerges during such electrolysis is an unintended product and even if the same is being sold as an exempted product, the same should be treated as a by-product and rule 57CC would not apply. [Para 13]

The issue in the instant case was not relatable to reversal of the credit originally taken by the appellant on the ground of emergence of any by-product. The issue was a straight and simple interpretation of rule 57CC, which as already held does not make any distinction between exempt final product or exempt by-product. As long as the excisable product cleared from an assessee’s factory enjoys exemption or attracts nil rate of duty, provisions of rule 57CC will come into play. The straight answer to the above question lies in the literal interpretation of the language employed in the said rule without straining to find out the legislative intent, especially when the language used is unambiguous. As already observed, the provisions of rule 57CC or rule 6 envisage common use of inputs in two final products, i.e., one dutiable and other exempted, for the applicability of the same. As such, as long as two final products emerging out of use of common inputs are excisable and one of them is exempted, the provisions of rule 57CC will apply. The exempted final product may be intended manufacture or unintended by-product. [Para 14]

Prior to 1-7-2017, the sale of natural gas was governed by the residuary Entry of the MVAT Act, namely, Schedule-E and, hence, the applicable rate of tax on 30-6-2017 was 13.5 per cent. Furthermore, the petitioner was eligible to claim set off of the input MVAT paid by it subject to a reduction of 3 per cent on account of the provisions of Rule 53(1) and Rule 53(1A) of the MVAT Rules. In other words, the net effective rate of MVAT on natural gas was only 3 per cent prior to 1-7-2017 if the natural gas was consumed domestically as fuel or as an input for manufacture.

With effect from 1-7-2017, when any person purchased natural gas domestically, the seller would charge and collect full tax from him at the rate of 13.5 per cent. However, since the person was no longer a dealer under the MVAT Act due to section 16(6A), he could not claim set-off or refund of the input MVAT collected from him. Furthermore, he would be liable to pay GST on his outputs at the full rate since the GST Act only provided for adjustment of GST paid and not of VAT paid. Hence, such a person would be taxed at the full rate on his outputs without adjustment of the input tax paid by him. Whilst the effective rate of taxation on natural product prior to 1-7-2017 was 3 per cent, the effective rate after 1-7-2017 rose to 13.5 per cent.

Realizing the above, the respondents sought to provide relief to the taxpayers. The net effective rate of tax on natural gas prior to 30-6-2017 was 3 per cent. Hence, vide Notification No.VAT1517/ CR136( A)/Taxation1 dated 24-8-2017, with effect from 24-8-2017, Entry 16 was inserted into Schedule-B of the MVAT Act which made provisions for a concessional rate of 3 per cent on the sale of natural gas. In other words, the Notification dated 24-8-2017 sought to maintain quo ante.

The Notification dated 24-8-2017 also provided that for a seller to be eligible to avail the 3 per cent concessional rate, the purchasing dealer must be certified by the Respondents in Proforma-A. The petitioners duly applied and received from the respondents Proforma with effect from 24-8-2017.

However, unfortunately, there existed anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017. While sub-clause (i) of Entry 16 used the phrase 'dealer', the main body of the entry uses the phrase 'registered dealer'. The word 'dealer' continued to be defined under the MVAT Act as a person who is involved in buying or selling goods. Hence, a person who was involved in purchase of natural gas, but not in the sale of natural gas would still be considered as a dealer. However, such a person would not be a 'registered dealer' on account of the provisions of section 16(6A). It was submitted that it was never the intention of the respondents at the time of the enactment of the Notification dated 24-8-2017 to restrict the benefits to only registered dealers. That was clear from the fact that no goods as defined in the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, ('MGST Act') can be manufactured from natural gas as well as the usage of the phrase 'of any other goods whatsoever.'

It was further supported by the issuance of Notification No.VAT-1517/ CR-136 (a)/Taxation 1 dated 13-10-2017 by the respondents. This Notification dated 13.10.2017 sought to cure the anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017 and amended Entry 16 of Schedule B to do so. Explanations (b) and (c) as inserted by the Notification dated 13-10-2017 expanded the scope of terms 'goods' and 'registered dealers' to include goods covered by the MGST Act and persons registered under the MGST Act respectively. This effectively cured the anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017.

iii.

The section provides for taxation with reference to preordained criteria which are mentioned in provision itself-amounts received or payable to an assessee non-resident, whether in India or outside India, had to be included for purpose of calculating income under section 44 BB.

iv. There is no compelling reason to assign a narrow and restricted meaning to the expression 'services' in section 44BB and confine it to services other than technical, consultancy or managerial services. In the absence of any words of limitation or exclusion, the word 'services' shall be understood in its plain and ordinary sense. If the legislature wanted to give a restricted meaning to the expression 'services', explicit words to that effect would have been deployed. The contextual setting and the company in which the expression 'services' is found is suggestive of inference that far from excluding technical/consultancy services, they were also intended to be brought within the ambit of section 44BB.The word 'services' followed by an expansive phrase 'in connection with' are relatable to prospecting for and exploration of mineral oil. That means, all services associated with prospecting for and exploration activities are brought within the scope and reach of section 44BB.

v.

Another category of assessees governed by section 44BB are those supplying plant and machinery on hire. Both these two categories of assessees covered by section 44BB engage themselves in core activities pertaining to prospecting and exploration of oil and gas and the Parliament thought it fit to accord a special treatment to the income derived by these two categories of non-residents in India.

vi.

Between the competing provisions, namely section 9(1)(vii) read with sections 44DA and 44BB,section 44BB being a more specific provision, will prevail for the purposes of computation. Section 44DA provides for method of computation of income by way of fees for technical services received by a non-resident or a foreign company carrying on business through a PE in India. If the non-resident is engaged in the business of providing services in connection with the prospecting etc. of mineral oils, the computation provisions relating to fees for technical services will have to yield to section 44BB. In a case of business governed by section 44BB, normally, the enterprise concerned would be having a PE in India. It is difficult to envisage a situation of a person being engaged in providing services or facilities in connection with prospecting and extraction of mineral oils not having a fixed place of business from where the operations are carried on. Thus, the existence of PE is a common feature in both the sections, though there is an explicit reference to PE under section 44DA. Rendering of technical services through PE may be a common feature of both the sections, although in the case of section 44DA,it is explicitly mentioned. But, what is important is the nature of business and it is that factor which serves as an indicator to apply one of the two sections. If the business is of the specific nature envisaged by section 44BB, the computation provisions therein would prevail over the computation provisions in section 44DA.In other words, the income received by a non-resident entity for the technical services provided in relation to prospecting and extraction of mineral oil, will be wholly governed by section 44BB for the purposes of computation.

vii.

Explanation appended to section 44BB provides that for the purpose of this section, plant includes ships, aircrafts, apparatus and equipments used for the purpose of said business and mineral oils include petroleum and natural gas. Thus, the amount received by the assessee on account of supply of spare parts of ships, aircrafts, apparatus and equipments used for the purpose of the business is squarely covered under section 44BB.

viii.

If an assessee does not claim benefit of section 44BB(3),it cannot claim that amount, which it receives by way of mobilisation advance outside India, should not be included for purpose of calculating income under section 44BB.

ix.

Services provided by non-resident in connection with movement of offshore rigs set up by assessee on high seas for exploration, prospecting and production of mineral oil from the seabed is assessable under section 44BB and not as fees for technical services under section 9(1)(vii).

x.

The Hon'ble Calcutta High Court in the case of Schlumberger Sea Co. Inc. are paid is effectively connected with the permanent establishment or fixed place of profession. Such income would be computed and assessed under the head "business" in accordance with the provisions of the Act, subject to the condition that no deduction would be allowed in respect of any expenditure or allowance which is not wholly or exclusively incurred for the business of such permanent establishment or fixed place of profession or in respect of amounts, if any, paid by the permanent establishment to its head office or to any of its other offices.

• Under section 44BB one does not find any reference to a permanent establishment in India. The type of services contemplated by the provision is more specific than what is contemplated by section 44DA. Section 44BB refers specifically to "services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of mineral oils". Revenues earned by the non-resident from rendering such specific services are covered by section 44BB.

•

If as contended by the Revenue, section 44DA covers all types of services rendered by the non-resident, that would reduce section 44BB to a useless lumber or dead letter and such a result would be opposed to the very essence of the rule of harmonious construction. [Para 11]

Effect of amendment w.e.f. 1-4-2011

•

The second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44DA inserted by the Finance Act, 2010 w.e.f. 01.04.2011 makes the position clear. Simultaneously, a reference to section 44DA was inserted in the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44BB.

•

It should be remembered that section 44DA also requires that the non-resident or the foreign company should carry on business in India through a permanent establishment situated therein and the right, property or contract in respect of which the royalty or fees for technical services is paid should be effectively connected with the permanent establishment. Such a requirement has not been spelt out in section 44BB; moreover, a flat rate of 10 per cent of the revenues received by the non-resident for the specific services rendered by it are deemed to be profits from the business chargeable to tax in India under section 44BB, whereas under section 44DA, deduction of expenditure or allowance wholly and exclusively incurred by the non-resident for the business of the permanent establishment in India and for expenditure towards reimbursement of actual expense by the permanent establishment to its head office or to any of its other offices is allowed from the revenues received by the non-resident.

•

Because of the different modes or methods prescribed in the two sections for computing the profits, it apparently became necessary to clarify the position by making necessary amendments. That perhaps is the reason for inserting the second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44DA and a reference to section 44DA in the proviso below sub-section (1) of section 44BB.

•

A careful perusal of both the provisos shows that they refer only to computation of the profits under the sections. If both the sections have to be read harmoniously and in such a manner that neither of them becomes a useless lumber then the only way in which the provisos can be given effect to is to understand them as referring only to the computation of profits, and to understand the amendments as having been inserted only to clarify the position.

•

So understood, the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44BB can only mean that the flat rate of 10 per cent of the revenues cannot be deemed to be the profits of the non-resident where the services are of the type which do not fall under that section, but are more general in nature so as to fall under section 44DA. Similarly, the second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44DA can only be interpreted to mean that where the services are general in nature and fall under the sub-section read with Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii), then an assessee rendering such services as provided in section 44BB cannot claim the benefit of being assessed on the basis that 10 per cent of the revenues will be deemed to be the profits as provided in section 44BB [Para 12].

Conclusion

•

In other words, the amendment made by the Finance Act, 2010 with effect from 1-4-2011 in both the sections, cannot have the effect of altering or effacing the fundamental nature of both the provisions or their respective spheres of operation or to take away the separate identity of section 44BB.

•

Therefore, these amendments would not assist the Revenue's contention in the present case. Therefore, in the present case the profits shall be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 44BB and not section 44DA. [Para 12]

"As regards MEG, this item is a chemical added to water for use as an anti freezing agent in the chilling plant so that the solution does not get solidified and the process does not come to a stand still. Since it is an input used in the plant for maintaining the solution at 0°C to enable chemical reaction to take place, it has to be construed as an input used in relation to the manufacture of the final product. It has become a settled law that the inputs need not be physically present in the final product. So long as its usage is necessary for the manufacture of the final product and they are not excluded under Rule 57A, they are to be allowed Modvat credit. Even the said rule has been amended in June 95, making this position explicit in the context of these judicial pronouncements. Hence, we hold that M.E.G. is an input used in the chilling medium for maintaining the temperature at the desired level for chemical reaction to take place and can therefore be construed to be used in relation to the manufacture of final product." [Para 8.2]

facts.text: The issue is whether proforma credit can be availed of by the manufacturers in terms of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE on inputs even if the end product (tyres) listed is liable to nil rate of duly.

The appellants receive duly paid bi-metal strips for use in the manufacture of I.C. Engines and parts thereof. They avail of Modvat Credit for the inputs. The appellants cleared certain parts like plain shaft bearings at nil rate of duty by following Chapter X procedure. The Assistant Collector held that credit could not be allowed on inputs used in the manufacture of parts cleared at nil rate of duty as per provisions of Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. This was upheld by the Collector (Appeals).

The Tribunal by its order No. A 722-723/Cal/91 dt. 31.10.1991. had allowed the respondents the benefit of modvat credit in respect of (i) Wire netting of stainless steel and phosphor bronze and felts (articles of textile material) which are not machine, machinery etc. and (ii) Chemicals and resins used in water treatment treating them to be inputs for paper. The Collector has filed these applications under Rule 35 G(1) for reference to High Court of certain questions of law as arising out of Tribunal's order.

The appellants claimed Modvat benefit for Nitrogen Gas as an input used in relation to their final product MMA Monomer. The gas was used as it was inert, did not react with other chemicals, and was an essential technological necessity to create an inert atmosphere. The Assistant Collector held that such a use of Nitrogen gas cannot be held to be in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product and therefore disallowed the credit. The Collector (Appeals) concurred with this view.

Appellants manufacture Pumpable Slurry Explosives (PSE) and supply the same free of duty to a 100% Export Oriented Unit (EOU). The appellants want to be allowed to accumulate Modvat credit on inputs of PSE for utilisation later as and when they start clearing the goods on payment of duty.

The appellant manufactured during the material period, "Metrosyl DM Silicone Fluid" classified under CETA sub-heading 3910.00 from imported Chlrosilanes. They were denied benefit of Notfn. 132/86-CE which provided for concessional rate of duty for silicone in primary form if produced out of duty paid Chlrosilanes, on the ground that they had availed Modvat credit on Chlrosilane and hence it could no longer be considered as duty paid.

One H was producing, sulphuric acid. During the manufacture of the said acid, waste material arises which is called "Scrubber Liquor". The scrubber liquor is polluting and its disposal is expensive. However, it can be used in manufacturing sodium silicate. Water is required to be added to adjust the viscosity of sodium silicate. The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of sodium silicate. The assessee entered into an agreement with H for the supply of scrubber liquor to the assessee. H was paying central excise duty and sales tax on scrubber liquor. It was agreed that the scrubber liquor would be supplied to the assessee free, except for the central excise duty and sales tax. In the invoices, the price (at which duty was calculated) was being shown as rebate. The assessee availed MODVAT Credit of duty paid by it on scrubber liquor. The adjudicating authority denied the MODVAT Credit availed by the assessee on the ground that the scrubber liquor could not be considered as input. On appeal, the appellate authority upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

The assessee used Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS) and furnace oil as fuel for generating electricity which in turn was captively consumed for production of final products such as caustic soda and cement. The assessee claimed MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) of rule 57A on LSHS. In civil appeal challenging the entitlement of assessee to MODVAT Credit on LSHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

The Appellants/Petitioners manufacture Ingots, Billets, Bars, Rounds, Rods, flats etc. of Steel from waste and scrap of steel/iron. On introduction of Modvat scheme w.e.f. 1.3.1986, Govt. by its order dated 7.4.1986, issued directions under the 2nd proviso to Rule 57G(2), allowing deemed credit in respect of specified inputs purchased from outside and lying in stock on or after 1.3.1986, with the manufacturers of specified final products Without production of documents evidencing payment of duty. On 29.8.1986, the Govt. issued another order directing that deemed credit shall not be admissible in respect of waste and scrap of steel which are exempt from payment of duty or are chargeable to nil rate of duty. The Central Excise authorities disallowed the deemed credit in respect of such waste and scrap and directed deposit of the credit already availed. Hence these petitions.

The appellants manufacture MS steel products in which lead, along with zinc was used in the process of galvanisation. Both the inputs and the final products have been notified in Notification No. 177/86-CE and are entitled to Modvat credit. The Assistant Collector denied them Modvat credit on the ground that lead was neither consumed in the process of manufacture of final product, nor can it be termed as input. Hence the appeal against the order of CCE (Appeals).

The appellants manufacture cement, and declared some 41 inputs which were claimed to be used in or in relation to the manufacture of cement. Modvat was denied by the Assistant Collector; Collector (Appeals) allowed the benefit in respect of only 'grinding media' and rejected the appeal otherwise.

Modvat credit was disallowed for scrap arising in the appellants' steel plant in the course of manufacture of E.R.W. and SW pipes from duty-paid H.R. Coil. The scrap is useful only for melting. The Collector (Appeals) upheld the Assistant Collector's order that deemed credit cannot be granted because the scrap was exempt from duty and the facility was available only for inputs clearly recognisable as being non-duty-paid or chargeable to nil rate of duty.

The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

In this background, on 1-11-1997, a show cause notice was issued to the Appellant/Assessee raising a demand in the sum for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 2-5-1997, along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent to be calculated on the said amount for the period commencing from 12-8-1997 and ending on the date of payment. Furthermore, via the very SCN, a proposal was also made for imposing penalty.

In the reply, the assessee took stand that, for the period falling between 3-5-1997 and 19-6-1997, it had already 'expunged' MODVAT credit, in consonance with Notification No. 14/97 CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. In so far as the demand for interest was concerned, it was stated that it was premature, as under section 87(2)(c) of the Finance Act, interest would be payable, only, if, the amount demanded was not paid within ninety (90) days of the enactment of the Bill.

The stand, which, the Appellant /Assessee appeared to have taken with respect to penalty was that the alleged infraction was not an offence prior to the enactment of the Finance Act.

The Adjudicating authority sustained the demand in sum, equivalent to the excess credit availed of by the Appellant/Assessee for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 to 3-5-1997. Furthermore, the Appellant/Assessee was directed to pay interest at the rate of 18 per cent.

The Commissioner (Appeals), allowed the appeal of the Appellant/Assessee, albeit, partially. While the Commissioner (Appeals), confirmed the demand of duty for the period 23-7-1996 to 28-2-1997, along with interest, he set aside the demand of duty for the period spanning between 1-3-1997 and 3-5-1997.

The appellant-assessee, a private limited company engaged in manufacture and export of perfumery compounds and essential oils, had set up a 100% EOU at Nilakottai in FY 2002-03. For AY 2009-10, it claimed deduction under Section 10B on the EOU's profits of about Rs. 2.32 crores. It filed a return declaring income of about Rs. 7.13 lakhs, which was assessed at about Rs. 3.79 crores.

■

The AO disallowed the claim under Section 10B(7) read with Sections 80-IA(8) and 80-IA(10), alleging that profits were inflated through non-market factors. The AO recorded substantial purchases from related/group entities without establishing market value, large interest-free funding from partners/group entities without arm’s length interest, an abnormally high gross profit of about Rs. 2.33 crores on sales of about Rs. 5.84 crores, and no clear correlation between inputs and outputs, characterizing the activity as mere processing rather than manufacturing. On these bases, the AO concluded that the course of business was arranged to produce more than ordinary profits and denied the full deduction under Section 10B.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) partly allowed relief. It noted that the AO had not substantiated allegations regarding non-market purchases or related-party pricing, observed that interest-free loans may still attract Section 80-IA(10) if they lead to excess profits, held that invocation of Section 80-IA(10) was proper but that reasonable/ordinary profits must be determined using comparables, benchmarked the assessee against its sister concern Pragati Aroma Oil Distillers Pvt. Ltd. (engaged in the same activity), and restricted the Section 10B deduction to 19.06% of sales (the sister concern’s net profit rate), taxing the balance at normal rates.

■

On further appeal, the ITAT recorded that the AO’s conclusions based on low manufacturing expenses and high margins were largely presumptive and unsupported by proper evidence or comparables, yet noted that the assessee and the sister concern operated in the same line of business under common management and that the assessee had disclosed higher profits. The ITAT upheld the CIT(A)’s approach of using the sister concern as a benchmark and sustained the restriction of the eligible profits to about 19% for the purpose of Section 10B.

The petitioner company was engaged in the manufacture of fertilizers at its factory. These fertilizers were thereafter subsequently sold.

The first respondent was the State of Maharashtra, whereas the respondent Nos.2, 3 and 4 were the Officers and the Authorities exercising powers under the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 ('MVAT'). The respondent No.5, GAIL had been impleaded as a respondent simply because the petitioner stated that for the purposes of manufacture of fertilizers, the petitioner purchased natural gas from respondent No.5. This was an intra-state purchase. The purchase was under various gas purchase agreements. The purchase in natural gas was either utilized as fuel or as an input in the manufacture/processing of fertilizers/chemicals.

With effect from 01-07-2017, the GST regime had been implemented in India. As a matter of policy, the Central and the various State Governments chose to leave petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and alcoholic liquor for human consumption outside GST regime and continue to levy VAT/Central Sales Tax on the said commodities.

Various amendments were made to the MVAT Act vide Maharashtra Act No.XLII of 2017 to make the MVAT compatible with the GST regime. In and amongst the said amendments, was the insertion of section 16(6A) into the MVAT Act which provided that any person who was not involved in the sale of the six commodities, i.e., petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and alcoholic liquor for human consumption would no longer have a valid registration under the MVAT Act. However, the proviso to section 16(6A) provided that any person who was affected by section 16(6A), but wished to continue to do business in the aforementioned six commodities would have to apply to the respondents in the prescribed manner to have the cancellation of his registration revoked.

Prior to 1-7-2017, the sale of natural gas was governed by the residuary Entry of the MVAT Act, namely, Schedule-E and, hence, the applicable rate of tax on 30-6-2017 was 13.5 per cent. Furthermore, the petitioner was eligible to claim set off of the input MVAT paid by it subject to a reduction of 3 per cent on account of the provisions of Rule 53(1) and Rule 53(1A) of the MVAT Rules. In other words, the net effective rate of MVAT on natural gas was only 3 per cent prior to 1-7-2017 if the natural gas was consumed domestically as fuel or as an input for manufacture.

With effect from 1-7-2017, when any person purchased natural gas domestically, the seller would charge and collect full tax from him at the rate of 13.5 per cent. However, since the person was no longer a dealer under the MVAT Act due to section 16(6A), he could not claim set-off or refund of the input MVAT collected from him. Furthermore, he would be liable to pay GST on his outputs at the full rate since the GST Act only provided for adjustment of GST paid and not of VAT paid. Hence, such a person would be taxed at the full rate on his outputs without adjustment of the input tax paid by him. Whilst the effective rate of taxation on natural product prior to 1-7-2017 was 3 per cent, the effective rate after 1-7-2017 rose to 13.5 per cent.

Realizing the above, the respondents sought to provide relief to the taxpayers. The net effective rate of tax on natural gas prior to 30-6-2017 was 3 per cent. Hence, vide Notification No.VAT1517/ CR136( A)/Taxation1 dated 24-8-2017, with effect from 24-8-2017, Entry 16 was inserted into Schedule-B of the MVAT Act which made provisions for a concessional rate of 3 per cent on the sale of natural gas. In other words, the Notification dated 24-8-2017 sought to maintain quo ante.

The Notification dated 24-8-2017 also provided that for a seller to be eligible to avail the 3 per cent concessional rate, the purchasing dealer must be certified by the Respondents in Proforma-A. The petitioners duly applied and received from the respondents Proforma with effect from 24-8-2017.
