Modvat--Cleaning reducer, coating reducer and vinyl reducer used in the manufacture of pilfer-proof caps & crown corks are eligible for Modvat because the goods are used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and are not specifically excluded from the benefit of Modvat credit. "There is no requirement that the inputs used should be present in the final product in order to qualify for Modvat benefit. As long as they are used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and are not specifically excluded from the scope of the benefit like machines, machinery appliance etc. in the explanation clause in Rule 57A or by the exclusion in Notification 177/86 dated 1.3.1986, modvat credit has to be allowed."

Reference--Modvat--Inputs--As the Tribunal's decision is in accordance with the provisions relating to grant of Modvat benefit and in conformity with the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the Eastend Paper Inds. Ltd. case 1990 (26) ECR 10 (SC) = ECR C 1535 SC reference to the High Court is not required to be made. "......our finding from the stand point of Tinplates being packaging materials in the manufacture of vegetable product is also in conformity with the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the East End Paper Industries Ltd. case. ....For all these reasons, the decision taken would be in accordance with the relevant provision granting Modvat benefit and particularly in conformity with the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the East End Paper Industries' case. ...there is no point of law required to be referred to the High Court."

Modvat--Rule 57A--Explanation--Modvat credit allowed as long as inputs are used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products and are not specifically excluded from the scope of the benefit in the explanation clause in Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 or by exclusion in Notification No. 177/86-CE. "There is no requirement that inputs should be present in the final product or it should be consumed in order to qualify for modvat benefit. It is clear that to become input it must be used in or in relation to the manufacture of goods. If lead is used in the process of manufacture of final product, there cannot be any doubt in availing modvat credit as per Explanation to Rule 57-A. As long as they are used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final products and are not specifically excluded from the scope of the benefit......in the explanation clause in Rule 57-A of the Central Excise Rules or by exclusion in Notification No. 177/86-CE, dated 1st March, 1986, modvat credit has to be allowed."

Modvat credit--availment of Modvat credit cannot be permitted when the inputs have not been specifically mentioned in the declaration filed under Rule 57G [ratio of earlier decision in Paro Food Products v. CCE 1988 (19) ECR 127]. "........in interpreting the scope and ambit of Rule 57G(2) the Tribunal has in a number of decisions taken the view that the manufacturer who fails to file a declaration under Rule 57G specifying the particular input would not be entitled to take credit of duty paid on the inputs received by him under the MODVAT Scheme. .......in view of the decisions quoted above........the appeal is allowed."

As ramming mass and fireclay are used for lining the furnace for heat resistance, they are on par with refractory materials and are not eligible for Modvat. (ratio of Cegat decision). "...ramming mass and fireclay...are used for lining the furnace and ladles for heat resistance and they are also on par as refractory materials... following the ratio of the decision in this Bench Order ...we hold that magnesite ramming mass, fireclay and refractory bricks are not eligible for Modvat credit and demands issued denying the Modvat credit on these three inputs by the department are therefore sustainable."

2. Modvat credit allowed on Acetylene gas as it is not a tool. It is used in an essential process in the manufacture of the final product. Unless Oxygen is mixed with it, it cannot perform function of metal cutting. It can be construed as consumable for operation of the torch to produce high flame. "Since the process of removal of unwanted material from the castings is an essential process to the completion of the manufacture of final product, namely casting, we hold that acetylene gas has been used in relation to the manufacture of the final product. ... acetylene gas by itself cannot be said to perform the function of metal cutting, unless ...oxygen gas also gets mixed. ...Admittedly acetylene gas is stored in a cylinder from which the gas is drawn and passes through the torch and in that process it gets consumed. ...At the most, they can be construed as a consumable gas for operation of the fool...therefore,...Modvat credit is required to be extended in respect of acetylene gas."

3. Binders (Foundry Chemicals) are not eligible for Modvat credit as they are used in the preparation of sand moulds which are essential for the manufacture of castings and cannot be considered to have come into existence during the coarse of manufacture of the final product. "...we are convinced that the sand moulds are in the nature of equipment or apparatus used for the purpose of castings...they are produced independently and used for castings ...moulds cannot be considered to have come into existence during the course of manufacture of the final product. Hence the benefit of Rule 57P cannot also be extended. We, therefore, hold that binders and foundry chemicals are not eligible for Modvat credit."

4. Modvat credit not allowed on Sleeves, Graphite, Stopper head as these are used either in the mould or ladles which have also been denied Modvat credit. "...from the...nature of the inputs, we observe that ...they are used either in the mould or the ladle. We have held that moulds and ladles come under the category of equipment or apparatus. These sleeves and stopper heads could at the most be construed as fittings in those equipments, for a specific purpose required to be replaced after each heat. In this view of the matter, we hold that Modvat benefit is not admissible with regard to these two inputs."

5. Flourspar--is eligible for Modvat benefit as it is used directly in the manufacturing process in removing impurities. "The 'function of the flour spar is to remove impurities. ...flourspar is fed into the furnace after the scrap is melted.........In view of the aforesaid position, this item of input goes directly in the manufacturing process and cannot be denied Modvat benefit."

Modvat--Transitional facility under Rule 57 H available on inputs lying in stock on 1.3.1986 and prior to filing of declaration under Rule 57G. "...inputs lying in stock as on 1.3.1986 and which were used in the manufacture of the finished product which were cleared on payment of duty, should be eligible for MODVAT in terms of Ride 57H of the Central Excise Rules.....the Assistant Collector can allow the MODVAT facility on the input lying in stock with the manufacturer prior to the fifing of declaration under Rule 57G and which are used in the manufacture of final products which arc cleared from the factory on or after 1.3.1986."

MODVAT--declaration by letter is a proper declaration for availment of Modvat in respect of inputs brought under gate passes, if the letter contains clearly (i) input to be used and (ii) finished product in which it will be used. Set off Since Notfn. No. 95/79-CE does not contain a clause to the effect that proforma credit on inputs should be correlated to the duty payable on outputs, non-payment of duty on finished goods does not make the manufacturer ineligible to proforma credit. "Read by itself this notification does not have any condition that there should be any nexus between the inputs and outputs.... The Ld. JDR's argument that goods mentioned in column 5 (final products) are only those which pay duty is not supported by the wordings of the notification. No condition regarding payment of duty is contained any where in the notification. We are further supported in this view by a judgment of the Cegat (SRB) (CCE Bangalore v. Wipro Information Technology, Bangalore) reported in 1988(14) ECR 490 wherein it was held that proforma credit once allowed cannot be recovered subsequently even if finished goods are exempted later on, making proforma credit ineligible, since no interlinking account is provided for in rule."

Minority view:--Interpretation--as per proviso 2 of the Notfn. availability of proforma credit on inputs is directly proportional to the duty payable on the finished product and since tyres were cleared without payment of duty, set off cannot be allowed on the inputs used in the manufacture of tyres. Proviso 2 of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE ".....the extent of the credit that could be taken in respect of the duty paid on the inputs shall be restricted to the duty payable on the end product if it happens to be less than the credit of duty taken on the inputs. What follows from this therefore, is that if the duty payable on the end product is nil, then the extent of exemption that will be available will also be nil........In as much as, no duty in respect of these tyres has been paid, in terms of proviso 2 to the notification, the availability of the credit on the inputs in respect of these tyres will have therefore, to be nil."

Modvat Credit available only on such inputs as have actually suffered duty. "......the common objective of sub-paras (ii) &(iii) of Explanation to Rule 57A is that where that portion of the value of the goods which relates to the value of the packing materials has not suffered any duty, then there will he no question of availing of any credit of duty thereon at all. This is because only if the inputs which are used in or in relation to the manufacture of final products have actually Suffered any duty, then only the question of taking MODVAT credit thereon arises."

Modvat--Soda lye/flakes used for washing bottles before filling aerated water are eligible. Cleaning is part of manufacture. Modvat credit is admissible in respect of the inputs in question.."

Modvat - Phospheric acid added to cane juice to make up deficiency of phosphate is an input for quality sugar--Eligible. CE Rule 57A. "Modvat scheme does not restrict input duty relief only to essential raw materials or components. It is available to any item used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. The only restriction is that it is not to be an item of machinery/tool, appliance etc. Here the undisputed fact is that phosphoric acid is required to be added, where-ever P. 205 content is low in the cane juice for achieving whiteness of sugar. Hence, it is an input needed in the manufacture of the desired quality sugar......It is a chemical added to the product mix for achieving proper clarification of cane juice. Hence it goes as an input for the clarification of cane juice. Hence we cannot appreciate the stand taken by the Collector (Appeals) that the phosphoric acid is a tool or appliance. We also carefully considered the Boards' clarification......in a case where the cane juice does not have the desired level of P. 205 content and on account of that phosphoric acid is necessarily to be added for purpose of clarification, it cannot be dismissed as not an input.....Viewed in this context, the addition of phosphoric acid is a necessity and hence we could not agree with the clarification given by the Board."

Modvat--Input credit is not allowable to aluminium castings received without payment of duty. "It is observed that the learned Collector (Appeals), while taking note of this has also taken note of the fact that in the same notification issued by the Govt. of India it has also been stated that no such credit shall be allowed if such inputs are clearly recognisable as being non-duty paid or charged to nil rate of duty or wholly exempt from duty. The learned Collector (Appeals) in his order has observed that since the Aluminium castings in respect of which input credit has been claimed were received without payment of duty, in view of the proviso to the Notification in F. No. 822/5/86-TRU dated 7.4.1986 the appellants were not eligible for the benefit of the input credit as claimed..........In the MODVAT Scheme since the benefit of credit is sought to be given for that quantum of duty which has been paid towards the goods or which is otherwise directed to be given in terms of the Rules, it has to be held the term "non-duty paid" refers to the goods where numerically no duty has been paid. As it is under Rule 57C no credit of duty is to be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of excise duty leviable thereon or if chargeable to Nil rate of duty. Thus if the inputs are used for the exempted goods, the inputs are not eligible for the benefit of MODVAT credit and the question of carrying forward the duty paid on the inputs, which resulted in the production of the exempted goods and which in turn are used in the manufacture of specified finished product, cannot arise."

MODVAT for lactose: Ch. 17 of the CET Act, 1985 was not included in 1986 for Modvat credit under Notfn. 177/86-CE, but was included in 1987 by the amending Notfn. 83/87-CE. So the declaration filed in 1986 for obtaining Modvat credit will not cover lactose which was declared only in June 1987. Under Rule 57G credit can only be taken from the date of obtaining acknowledgement of the declaration, not prior to that date. "It is an admitted position that in 1986 goods falling under Chapter XVII were not included in the Notification, although admittedly the finished products of the appellants were notified. Therefore, in 1986, the materials falling under Chapter XVII were not specified as input and they were therefore clearly outside the purview of MODVAT Scheme, ft was only in 1987 by virtue of Notification 83/87 dated 1.3.1987 materials like Lactose became eligible by being specified in the Notification as input for the purpose of MODVAT,.......in terms of Rule 57G they are eligible to take credit only from the date of obtaining the acknowledgement of the declaration and not prior to that date.....The contention that since they had already included the material in their declaration filed in 1986, and that therefore, they were eligible to take credit without any further declaration in 1987, does not have much force."

MODVAT--Detailed description in the prescribed manner of inputs is necessary to avail of MODVAT credit. "......the proforma for declaration to be filed under Rule 57G also has specific columns for the description of the final product and its Tariff classification as well as description of the inputs and its Tariff classification, besides the column to indicate the nature of the inputs whether raw material or component etc. When such is the legal position, and such is the requirement of the proforma for the declaration prescribed for the purpose, the contention of the appellants that broad description of the inputs will suffice for the purpose of availing MODVAT credit, is not tenable.'

Modvat--Hylam Sheets are used to avoid burring of glass epoxy sheets while drilling, to ensure the quality of PCBs-Not by itself a processor or machine. CE Rule 57. The sheets by themselves are not bringing about any change in the epoxy sheets being drilled. In view of above, we hold that Hylam sheets will not fall within the excluded category. We observe that the items excluded have to perform specified functions as set out in the explanation as above before the same can be taken to be excluded from the purview of the term 'inputs' as set out in Rule 57A of the Modvat Rules. In the present case as seen from the facts placed before us the Hylam sheets do not perform any one of the functions as set out in the explanation which would disqualify these for the purpose of being considered as input for Modvat purpose."

Production Incentive : Epoxy resins even if not excisable during the base year 1975-76 and not included in base clearances, are eligible for exemption. "The applicability of the ratio of that decision to the facts of the present cases would not get diluted because of the fact that unlike in the decided case (where the goods were not excisable during the base period, but were excisable in the incentive period), the goods in the present cases were not excisable under 15A(1) CET during the base period but were nevertheless excisable under Item 68 CET."

2. Product to product linkage not envisaged for Production Incentive; only a computation of base clearances of goods falling under Item 15A(1) CET as it stood during the incentive years is required. "On a plain reading of the Notification, the base clearances would be the clearances of all the products which fell for classification under 15A(1) CET as it stood during the base period and the excess clearances of all the products which fell within the scope of 15A(1) CET during the incentive period. The fact that the coverage and scope of Item 15A(1) CET was not the same but was different in the base period and the incentive period would not in our opinion, make any difference to the above petition. Nor is a product to product linkage envisaged in the Notification. It only calls for a computation of the clearances of all goods which fell under 15A(1) CET as it stood during the base period and similar a computation of the excess clearances for all the goods which fell under 15A(1) CET as it stood during the incentive period."

In an identical issue in application filed by the same applicant in AAR/823 of 2009 which was disposed of on 21-12-2009, it was held that the second limb of section 44BB was clearly attracted for the reason that the 'plant and machinery', which includes a ship or a vessel, has been supplied on hire for being used in the prospecting operation. Following the ruling in the said case, it is to be ruled that : (1) the income derived by M&C ought to be computed in accordance with computational mechanism under section 44BB; (2) as per section 44BB, read with Part II of the First Schedule, the effective rate at which the tax has to be withheld from the payments made by the applicant to M&C would be 4.223 per cent; and (3) as the amounts falling under section 44BB have been excluded from the purview of the definition of royalty, the consideration for services provided by M&C cannot be construed to be in the nature of royalty under section 9(1)(vi ). Once section 44BB is attracted, the computation has to be made in accordance with that provision and no other special provision, viz., section 44DA or section 115A would come into play in view of the fact that the payment is being made by a non-resident to another non-resident. [Para 3]

As per Trade Notice No. 83/89 dt. 26.4.1989, the appellants are entitled to deemed Modvat credit, irrespective of the fact whether the goods were actually purchased from the market or received from third parties unless the inputs are clearly recognisable as non-duty paid or chargeable to nil rate of duty. "...we do not find any warrant at all on a plain reading of the Rule disentitling the appellants to deemed Modvat credit in respect of the inputs in question. We are also fortified in this respect by the statutory instructions issued by the Government of India dated 74.1986 in Order F. No. B/22/5/86-TRU read with the Trade Notice No. 83/89 dated 26.4.1989......Since in terms of the above Trade Notice deemed credit is permissible on all inputs whether purchased or otherwise received by the manufacturer unless such inputs are clearly recognisable as non-duty paid or chargeable to nil rate of duty, we are inclined to hold that the appellants would be entitled to take deemed credit in respect of the inputs in question."

case in the manufacture of final product phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, which attract nil rate of duty, the provisions of rule 57CC would apply. It was impossible to obtain the mother liquor or the resultant phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’ without the use of HCl. As long as HCl is used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, the applicability of provisions of rule 57CC cannot be ruled out. [Para 12] The appellant’s reference to the provisions of rule 57D in support of their contention that Modvat credit was not to be denied if a part of the same was contained in the by-product, was indicative of the legislative intent that reversal of 8 per cent amount of the value of the by-product in terms of provisions of rule 57CC would not apply. The expression ‘by-product’ occurring in rule 57D has to be examined and interpreted in the context of the said rule, which uses the other expression ‘waste’ or ‘refuse’, etc. It is in this scenario that the rule provides for non-reversal of Modvat credit, even if waste, refuse or by-product has emerged during the course of manufacture. The effect of the said rule would be that if waste product, which may not be excisable, e.g. , floor sweepings during the course of manufacture of biscuits, then the quantum of credit originally taken is not to be varied. Similarly, if iron and steel scrap arises during manufacture of iron products, the Modvat is not to be varied, but iron and scrap being excisable products, [the manufacturers] have to discharge duty burden. If the same are exempted, provisions of rule 57CC will apply. As such, it is to be concluded that rule 57D refers to waste scrap and by-product, which are not excisable at all. The said provision cannot be pressed into service in support of the plea that even if the by-product is excisable, but exempted, amount of 8 per cent is not required to be paid. The appellant was not being directed to reverse the credit amount equivalent to the inputs contained in the said exempted final products. Further, taking an hypothetical example of electrolysis of water, which an assessee may undertake to obtain oxygen, he cannot take the plea that hydrogen which also emerges during such electrolysis is an unintended product and even if the same is being sold as an exempted product, the same should be treated as a by-product and rule 57CC would not apply. [Para 13]

The issue in the instant case was not relatable to reversal of the credit originally taken by the appellant on the ground of emergence of any by-product. The issue was a straight and simple interpretation of rule 57CC, which as already held does not make any distinction between exempt final product or exempt by-product. As long as the excisable product cleared from an assessee’s factory enjoys exemption or attracts nil rate of duty, provisions of rule 57CC will come into play. The straight answer to the above question lies in the literal interpretation of the language employed in the said rule without straining to find out the legislative intent, especially when the language used is unambiguous. As already observed, the provisions of rule 57CC or rule 6 envisage common use of inputs in two final products, i.e., one dutiable and other exempted, for the applicability of the same. As such, as long as two final products emerging out of use of common inputs are excisable and one of them is exempted, the provisions of rule 57CC will apply. The exempted final product may be intended manufacture or unintended by-product. [Para 14]

Modvat--Benefit cannot be extended as the acid is not used for bringing into existence the final product, but to take care of environmental hazards created by the effluents. "The Notification envisages the benefit only if it is established that the use of the input is in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. Legally, going by the words of the Notification what it states is that the use should be such that it can be related to the emergence of the final end-product. In the present case the use of the acid is not for bringing into existence the final product but for taking care of the hazards involved by way of generation of effluents as a result of the process of manufacture of the final product. We observe that the treatment of effluent has to be taken to be a separate process where a totally different chemistry is involved."

2. Modvat--Input--Processes which are indispensible to the emergence of the end-product are to be held as used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. "With a view to draw line as to what constitutes the input in or in relation to the manufacture of a product, it can be safely held that the process which are indispensible to the emergence of the final product and which are inextricably linked up with the production stream of the end-product up to the stage of its emergence and the inputs which are so used in those processes without which the end-product may be difficult to be manufactured have to be held as used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. Inputs which are used after the emergence of the final product and which may be required to be used in the process at the post manufacturing stage of the end-product will have to be considered as a separate process for a different purpose."

Semi-finished Poy which is taken to another unit for texturising in the mode prescribed by Rule 56B, held to be base yarn, eligible for exemption vide Notification dated 11th May, 1982. Exemption cannot be denied by classifying the same as semi-finished yarn. Item 18 II(i)(a). "Rule 56B applies to semi-finished goods which are excisable. The Poy that is produced by the petitioners is excisable. It is used for the purposes of being texturised. It is, therefore, base yarn for the purposes of being texturised. It falls within the definition of base yarn in the notification dated 11th May, 1982 because it falls within the particular provision of the tariff that is therein referred to."

Modvat - Inputs--Molybdenum sheets and Tungsten Nozzles are not inputs.--Molybdenum sheets act as electrodes to conduct electricity to generate heat, have a long life, and are thus a part of the furnace. Similarly, Tungsten nozzles are in the nature of a die or a tool/used for processing the materials--Credit inadmissible. CE Rule 57A. "In the present case the electrodes conduct the electricity to generate the heat. These stand on a different footing. The electrodes have a very long life and can be taken to be only as a part of the furnace rather than as an input used as an in-process material. ........ In view of the above we hold that so far as Molybdenum plates are concerned, the same are not eligible for the benefit of the Modvat Credit in regard to Tungsten nozzles we hold these help in giving shape to the end-product and have to be held to be an item in the nature of a die or a tool used for processing the materials. Total set-off of duty paid on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre must be allowed even if some part of it is contained in the methanol which is a by-product of the chemical reaction during manufacture. Since the formation of methanol cannot be prevented by using less ethylene glycol, it is obvious that the final product is polyester fibre, not methanol. ".....it is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ......ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre. It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. It is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol from arising for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre. Thus, the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. It may be mentioned herein that it is not as if the appellants have used excess ethylene glycol wantonly to produce the methanol. It is clear that the appellants are not engaged in the production of methanol but in the production of polyester fibre. That position is undisputed. Therefore, it appears that the Tribunal erred when it held that the appellants were not entitled to a part of the credit of duty since ethylene glycol when it interacts with DMT also gives rise to methanol."

2. Set-off of duty paid on inputs can only be denied if the final product is totally exempt from duty. So credit of duty cannot be denied on non-excisable methanol which arose during the manufacture of dutiable polyester fibre. "....the only situation where the credit of the duty paid on the inputs could be denied was only where the final products were wholly exempt from the duty of excise or chargeable to nil rate of duty. In the present case, the excisable goods, namely, polyester fibre were not wholly exempt from duty nor chargeable to nil rate of duty. It cannot be read in the notification that the notification would not be available in case non-excisable good arise during the course of manufacture. In fact, the Tribunal seems to have erred in not bearing in mind that exemption notification was pressed in service in respect of polyester fibre which is excisable goods and not in respect of methanol which arises as a by-product as a part and parcel of chemical reaction."

Section 16(2) of the IGST Act, 2017 states that 'subject to the provisions of sub-section (5) of section 17 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, credit of input tax may be availed for making zero-rated supplies, notwithstanding that such supply may be an exempt supply.' This, a specific exception is made with regard to 'plant and machinery'. [Para 10]

Input tax credit of GST paid on goods and services used to construct the 'bunds' is admissible to applicant, provided that the bunds are used for making zero rated supplies and fulfil the conditions which are necessary for treating the bunds as 'plant and machinery'. [Para 11]

We have carefully considered the submissions from both the sides and perused the records. The Respondent manufactured PSF for which MEG is one of the inputs. Notification No. 225/86-CE dated 3/4/86 exempted PSF from Central excise duty chargeable thereon as it equivalent to the Central Excise Duty under Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty under Customs Tariff Act, 1975 paid on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF. This exemption notification provided similar duty concession in respect of other finished products mentioned in the table annexed to the notification and the duty concession was equal to the Central excise duty paid under Central Excise Act or additional Customs Duty paid under Customs Tariff Act, on the specified inputs used in the manufacture of the finished products. Though there is no explicit provision in this exemption notification regarding its applicability when the finished product is fully exempt from duty or is chargeable to nil rate of duty, it would be an obvious corollary that this exemption would not be applicable if the finished product is an exempted goods i.e. either fully exempt from duty by virtue of an exemption notification or chargeable to nil rate of duty. The point of dispute in this case is as to whether this exemption notification would be applicable when the finished goods - PSF in this case, have been cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export.

3.1 Rules 191BB permits removal of excisable goods from the place of manufacture or storage without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export, subject to the conditions prescribed in this Rule. The PSF, in question, in respect of which the set off of duty on MEG used in its manufacture is sought to be denied, had been cleared without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export in terms of the provisions of Rule 191BB. The Tribunal in the case of Orissa Synthetics Vs. CCE (supra) and CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. (supra), has with reference to exemption notification No. 225/96-CE, held that PSF cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of goods for export is not to be treated as exempted goods. It is not the contention of the Department that these judgments have been challenged before a higher court or have been set aside. Moreover when the Department has accepted the clearances of the PSF for export under bond without payment of duty, as eligible for the benefit of this exemption, there would be no justification in denying the same exemption to the goods cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of the finished goods for export.

3.2 The Notification No. 225/86-CE operates like Modvat scheme. Rule 57F (3) of Chapter V (AA) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 pertaining to Modvat scheme, provided that credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on any of the finished products in or in relation to manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used or for payment of duty on any waste arising in course of manufacture of finished products or for payment of duty on inputs themselves, if the same are allowed to be cleared as such. Proviso to this sub-Rule provided that the credit of the specified duty in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of final products cleared for export under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty and where for any reason such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations, as may be specified by the Central Government by notification in the official gazette. In the case of Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay (supra), the dispute arose as to whether the final products cleared under bond without payment of duty in terms of Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished product for export would be eligible for the benefit of the proviso to Rule 57F (3) and the Tribunal answered this question in the affirmative, holding that in respect of clearances of finished product without payment of duty under Rule 191BB, the benefit of proviso to Rule 57F (3) would be available. Same principle would apply in this case also and when the Department has accepted the applicability of the exemption in respect of the finished product exported under bond without payment of duty, the benefit of this exemption would also have to be extended in respect of the clearances without payment of duty under Rule 191B.

Per Rakesh Kumar :

The facts leading to filing of this appeal by Revenue are, in brief, as under.

1.1 The respondents are manufacturer of Polyester staple fiber (PSF) chargeable to Central Excise Duty under Chapter 55 of the Central Excise Tariff. One of the inputs used in the manufacture of PSF is Mono Ethlylene Glycol (MEG). The dispute in this case pertains to January 1987 to May 1991 period. During that period Notification No. 225/86-CE issued under the then Rule 8 (1) of Central Excise Rules, 1944 exempted "PSF including tops and polyester filament yarn (PFY)" from so much of duty of excise chargeable under the Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty chargeable under Customs Tariff Act, 1975, as the case may be, already paid on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF or PFY. During the period from May 1989 to August 1991, nine show cause notices were issued to the Respondent for recovery of allegedly wrongly availed input duty exemption amounting to Rs. 1,15,54,845/- on the following grounds :-

(a)

The Respondents are not eligible for set off of the duty paid on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF exported out of India without payment of duty;

(b)

set off of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for used in the manufacture of goods for export is not admissible;

(c)

set off of duty paid on MEG, which is contained in the bi-products or waste arisen in course of manufacture of PSF is not admissible;

(d)

set off of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared at nil rate of duty under Notification No. 191/85-CE is not admissible;

(e)

set off amounting to Rs. 6,50,090/-, which represents the duty on the quantity of MEG which was allegedly short received, is not admissible.

1.2 These show cause notices were adjudicated by the Assistant Commissioner by a common order dated 30th May 2003 by which the Assistant Commissioner while permitting the set off of duty on MEG contained in waste and by-products and also the set off of duty paid on MEG, used in the manufacture of PSF which was exported out of India under bond without payment of duty, disallowed -

(a)

set off of Rs. 15,63,263/- of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF which was cleared without payment of duty for manufacture under bond of finished goods for export under Rule 191BB;

(b)

the set off of Rs. 1,13,330/- of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared at nil rate of duty under Notification No. 191/85-CE dated 28/8/85, and

(c)

the set off of Rs. 6,50,090/- in respect of the quantity of MEG which was short received.

1.3 The Respondent filed the appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) challenging the Assistant Commissioner's order -

(a)

disallowing the set off of the duty of Rs. 15,63,263/- on MEG contained in the PSF cleared without payment of duty for manufacture in bond of finished goods for export under Rule 191BB; and

(b)

disallowing the set off of Rs. 6,50,090/- in respect of the quantity of the MEG held to have been short received. The Commissioner (Appeals) vide order-in-appeal No. 126-CE/LKO/04 dated 1/6/04 allowed the appeal on the following grounds :-

(i)

so far as set off of Rs. 15,63,263/- of the duty on the quantity of MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared without payment of duty for manufacture of finished goods for export under bond under Rule 191BB is concerned, this set off is admissible to the Respondent in view of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. Vs. CCE reported in 1989 (44) E.L.T. 794 (S.C.) and of the Tribunal in the cases of CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. reported in 1999 (107) E.L.T. 455 (Trib.) and Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay reported in 1995 (9) RLT 317 (CEGAT-WRB)=1995 (78) E.L.T. 595 (Trib.).

(ii)

BB which inter alia provided that a product can be cleared without payment of duty if it is meant to be used in the manufacture of final product which is to be exported. We note that this issue was examined at length in paras 7, 8 & 9 by this Tribunal (Final Order No. 477/97-NB dt. 15.4.97) in their own case of the appellants. For the sake of clarity, the same paras are reproduced as under:- "Heard the submissions of both sides. The facts of the case as narrated above are that the appellants are manufacturing POY. The appellants get a number of inputs for the manufacture of POY. Both polyester filament yarn and the inputs were specified under Rule 57A. The appellants filed a declaration under Rule 57G. During the month of May, June and July, 1992, the appellants cleared without payment of duty a particular quantity of POY under the provisions of Rule 191BB. The only dispute that arises is whether removal of the goods under the provisions of Rule 191BB can be treated as removal under an exemption notification. The notification covering the removal of the goods under Rule 191BB is the Notfn. No. 33/90-CE (NT). This notification inter alia provides that the goods can be removed without payment of duty under the provisions of Rule 191BB."

"We find that in the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited reported at page 599 of Reliance Industries Limited at para 6.2, this Tribunal held as under:-

"In the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited decided by the East Regional Bench, the man-made staple fibre was cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB of the Central Excise Rules and the department objected to the availing of Modvat Credit of duty on inputs used in these final products cleared under Rule 191BB of the Rules. The department's main contention was that such removals of final products without payment of duty under Rule 191BB were hit by Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules. The East Regional Bench, after considering all the arguments raised by the ld. SDR negatived the objection and allowed the appeal of Orissa Synthetics. For arriving at their conclusion, that Bench relied on the decision of the Delhi High Court in Hindustan Aluminium Corpn. reported in 1981 (8) ELT 642, wherein it was held by the Delhi High Court that the facility of removal without payment of duty under bond for export could not be equated with a general exemption from payment of duty of excise. That Bench also took note of the clarification issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs in consultation with the Ministry of Law about the scope of proviso (i) to sub-rule (2) of Rule 56A (analogous to the provisions of Rule 57C). In that clarification issued by the Board, the Board advised the field formations that the said proviso to Rule 56A (2) would not stand attracted, where the final products were exported under bond, since such removals could neither be construed to be exempted nor be regarded as goods charged to nil rate of duty. (Vide the extract of the advice of the Ministry of Law appearing in para 9 of the said order of the East Regional Bench). Thus we find that going by the allegation contained in the show cause notices involved in this appeal, the issue is identical in all respects and the ratio of that decision would apply to this case squarely."

"A careful reading of the above paragraph shows that the Tribunal had held that the goods manufactured from the inputs on which modvat credit has been taken which are cleared without payment of duty under Notfn. No. 33/90-CE (NT) does not mean that the goods are exempt from the whole of duty."

6. We find that the learned JDR has cited and relied upon the decision of this Tribunal in the case of East India Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. We have perused this decision. We find that this decision does not come under Rule 191BB but on the interpretation of Rule 57F (2) and 57F (3). Thus we find that this decision is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case. Following the ratio of the decision of this Tribunal in the case of the appellants themselves, we hold that the modvat credit is admissible to the appellants. In the result the appeals are allowed.

Per Shri G.R. Sharma :

The facts giving rise to the captioned appeal are that the appellants get PTA and convert it into polyester staple fibre (PSF). The PSF is sent to different parties who manufacture polyester fabrics from this and export it. The appellants for this purpose were following the procedure u/r 191-BB of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and transferring the PSF under Not. No. 33/90. The department alleged that PSF is being cleared at nil rate of duty under Not. No. 33/90. Rule 57C was attracted and the Asstt. Collector accordingly confirmed a demand of Rs. 1,54,472.26. In appeal, the ld. Collr. (Appeals) also agreed with the Asstt. Collr. observing that there is no denying the fact that particular clearance of PSF was at nil rate of duty vide Not. No. 33/90 dated 5.9.90. Therefore, such being the case, modvat claimed is not admissible and rejected the appeal of the appellants herein.

2. Shri Vinod Agarwal, ld. Advocate appearing for the appellants submits that the department has wrongly and erroneously interpreted the Not. No. 33/90 to hold that the goods were exempt and therefore, Rule 57C comes into play. The ld. Counsel submitted that Not. No. 33/90 dated 5.9.90 only allows the transfer of goods without payment of duty in terms of the procedure set out under Rule 191 BB. The ld. Counsel also submits that Rule 57C comes into play only when the goods are exempt. He submits that no exemption notification is issued either under sub-rule (1) of Rule 8 or Section 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944. He submits that reading the notification along with the provisions of Rule 57C, there is nothing to show or to come to the conclusion that the goods were exempt. He submits that since the goods were not exempt, therefore, Rule 57C is not applicable to the facts of the present case. In support of his contention, he cited and relied upon the decision of this Tribunal in the case of J.K. Synthetics Limited Vs. C.C.E., Jaipur reported in 1996 (87) ELT 389 =1996 (15) RLT 462 (T). He submits that their case was squarely covered by the decision of the Tribunal in the above case and therefore, prays that the appeal may be allowed.

3. Shri Satnam Singh, ld. SDR appearing for the respondent Commr. submits that transfer of excisable goods are governed by the provisions of Rule 191 BB; that this Rule inter alia requires bond, permission etc. He submits that from the record, it is not evident whether such permission was taken. He also submits that the goods in actuality were transferred without payment of duty and therefore, they should be deemed to be cleared from the factory at nil rate of duty. He submitted that nil rate of date means an exemption, therefore, the provisions of Rule 57C shall be attracted, and therefore, justifies the decision of the lower authorities in view of his observation.

4. Heard the submissions of both sides. The first point that was made by the ld. Counsel regarding permission for change in cause title. It was submitted by the ld. Counsel that JCT Fibres Ltd. has since been changed to JCT Ltd. and therefore, prays for the change of cause title. The ld. SDR has no objection. The cause title is therefore, changed to M/s. JCT Limited.

5. The short point for determination in this appeal is whether the provisions of Rule 57C are attracted when PSFs were sent to manufacturers of polyester fabrics for export. For this purpose, we have to see what the provisions of Not. No. 33/90 are Not. No. 33/90 inter alia stipulates "Transfer of excisable goods without payment of duty." It does not say that the duty shall be chargeable at nil rate etc. This notification also does not speak of exemption of the goods. Now let us examine the provisions of Rule 57C. Rule 57C lays down that modvat credit shall not be available in cases where the final product is exempt. Admittedly, in the instant case when these two rules are read together, I find that under Not. No. 33/90, the word `exempt' is not used nor nil rate of duty is used. Therefore, the goods were not exempt so as to attract denial of modvat credit on inputs under Section 57C. I get support for this view from the decision of the Tribunal in the case of J.K. Synthetics Ltd. cited above. In para 6, the Tribunal had held as under :

utilised towards payment of duty of excise,-

(i)

on any of the final products in or, in relation to the manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used in accordance with the declaration filed under sub-rule (1) of rule 57G; or]

(ii)

on the waste, if any, arising in the course of manufacture of the final products; or

(iii)

on the inputs themselves if such inputs have been permitted to be cleared under sub-rule(l)]: [Provided that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared for export under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export in accordance with sub-rule (2), shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption [or for export] on payment of duty and, where for any reason, such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations as may be specified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette:

Provided further that no such refund of credit of duty shall be allowed if the manufacturer avails of drawback allowed under the Customs and Central Excise Duties (Drawback) Rules, 1971, or claims rebate of duty under rule 12A, in respect of such duty.]

[Provided also that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared either to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a hundred per cent Export-Oriented Unit under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty,]

It is seen that earlier under the first proviso MODVAT credit taken in respect of the inputs contained in the goods exported under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export could be utilised for payment of duty towards goods cleared for home consumption or for any reason if this adjustment was not possible the cash refund has been provided for. With effect from 1.3.92, the second proviso has been added. Under this even where the final products in which the inputs have been utilised are cleared to a unit in a free trade zone or to a l00% export oriented unit under bond, the same benefit as in the case of the export of the goods has been provided for. We observe that as such in Rule 57F (3) there is no specific provision in regard to the clearances made to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, We observe that when the clearances are made to a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit of any finished product without payment of duty from a unit which has taken MODVAT credit in respect of the inputs, the benefit is given as ultimately in terms of these schemes the goods allowed manufacture are exported. The units which are manufacturing goods under Rule 191B in terms of notification issued under this Rule are in our view similarly placed as the unit located in the free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. We see no reason as to why the same benefit as provided under Rule 57F for these units cannot be extended to this unit. Interest of revenue is safeguarded by the specific provision under the notification issued under Rule 191B for recovery of duty both in respect of the finished goods and the non-duty paid goods out of which the same are manufactured in bond in case the goods are not exported. We therefore hold that notwithstanding the absence of any specific mention in the proviso to Rule 57F(3) in regard to the finished goods in respect of which input credit is taken and which are cleared without payment of duty to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, the second proviso to Rule 57F(3) would cover such units also, as we do not find any reason to differentiate the operations in the unit functioning under Rule 191B from the operations carried out in the unit functioning under a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. In view of above, we hold that the appellants plea has to be allowed and we order accordingly.

The Collector has held in his impugned order that they had made a very thin distinction between exemption and clearance without payment of duty, which is basically same. Shri Gopal Prasad submitted that this conclusion of the Collector is not correct. Now coming to the objection that Modvat credit cannot be utilised in regard to duty payable on similar final products, where some of the final products are cleared under bond in terms of Rule 191 BB of the Central Excise Rules, the issue is squarely covered by the decision of the East Regional Bench in the case of Orissa Synthetics and also by our decision in the case of Reliance Industries. We have considered all the arguments from the revenue for coming to the conclusion that in the absence of specific legal provision either under Rule 57 C or under Rule 57 F (3) proviso, Modvat credit cannot be denied for utilisation in regard to clearance of similar final products. Rule 57 C seeks to deny Modvat credit, if the final products are either wholly exempted or are chargeable to Nil rate of duty. We have held that in the case of goods cleared under a Notification issued under Rule 191 BB for export purposes, such goods cannot be equated with goods exempted under an exemption Notification issued under Rule 8 (1) of the C.E. Rules or Section 5A of C.Ex. Act nor they can be construed as goods chargeable to Nil rate of duty. For arriving at this conclusion, we have taken note of the Board's own instructions issued in the context of identical provisions of Rule 56A of the C.E. Rules, after consulting the Ministry of Law. The argument of Shri Nair that irrespective of the fact that Rule 57C does not specifically provide for denying benefit in respect of clearances under Rule 191 BB, since Rule 57F (3) proviso can only cover direct exports from the factory and not removals under Rule 191 BB for further manufacture of export goods in another factory. We do not find any warrant to read such a restriction in Rule 57F (3) proviso; because proviso to Rule 57F (3) talks of "cleared for export under bond". In the absence of any specific restriction prescribed in that proviso, we are to go by what is meant by the term for export under bond' laid down in Rule 13 of the C.Ex. Rules. Under Rule 13, goods may be exported outside India without payment of duty from a warehouse or licensed factory, provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules and the owner enters into a bond for due performance. There is no dispute that Rule 191 BB is one of the relevant provision of Chapter IX of the Rules. Hence if the goods are cleared under Rule 191BB, they are goods cleared for export in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Viewed in this context, we could not persuade ourselves to agree that Rule 57F (3) proviso can he extended, only where the goods are cleared direct from the factory to the port of shipment. Hence, we find no reason to take any different view from the one we have already taken in the case of Reliance Industries. The sulphuric acid (duty paid input) can be said to have been used by the petitioner in the manufacture of final product when the entire relevant quantity thereof was applied or subjected to the manufacturing process". 6. The High Court in arriving at the above conclusion relied on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. Vs. C.C.E. - 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC). In this case, it is observed that the question for consideration was whether the appellants became ineligible to claim set-off of duty on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre to the extent it gave rise to methanol. In the premises, the Supreme Court held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ''The Supreme Court held that ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre, though methanol had arisen as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture, when ethylene glycol interacted with DMT to produce polyester fibre. Giving the reasoning, the Supreme Court says that it is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre and that the appellant was engaged in the production of polyester fibre and not methanol". (Emphasis supplied).

7. Accordingly, the High Court in its decision held that the entire quantity of sulphuric acid was necessary for manufacturing process and the modvat credit could not be denied simply because the entire input was not emerged in the final product in the manufacturing process.

8. The above ratio, in the judgments of the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court are applicable with the same force to the facts of the present case. It is therefore to be held that the entire quantity of pig iron is used in the manufacture of the exempted category of the P.D. Pumps and no quantity of the input is used in the manufacture of waste and scrap. In view of the provisions of Rule 57C, the modvat credit is not available to the appellants. Since in this case, I have relied on the ratio of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and that of the Allahabad High Court, specifically on the subject, there is no warrant to consider the other decisions cited before me by the appellants.

9. The appeal thus fails and the same is accordingly rejected.

2. The appellants duly represented by Shri S.K. Roychowdhury submits that the appellants are engaged in the manufacture of Refined Rice Bran Oil which is chargeable to nil rate of duty as also the vegetable product which is a dutiable product. They availed the MODVAT Credit on the various inputs after declaring the same in their declaration under Rule 57G and all the inputs for Rice Bran Oil as also for vegetable product, were common inputs and as such, common RG-23A Part-I and II was being maintained by them. He submits that they are entitled to the MODVAT Credit even if a part of the inputs is used in the manufacture of Rice Bran Oil cleared by nil rate of duty in terms of proviso to Rule 57F(4) inserted by Notification No. 11/95 dated 16.3.95. He submitted that the said Rule permitted the assessee to utilise the MODVAT Credit towards the payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the fact whether such an iinput has actually been used in the manufacture of such a final product or not. In this view, he submits that the impugned Orders be set aside and Credit be allowed.

3. Shri T. Premkumar, learned S.D.R. appearing for the Revenue contends that the provisions of Rule 57F(4) are not applicable to the present situation inasmuch as the same are applicable when common inputs are being used in the manufacture of two different dutiable products, that is to say that one to one correlation is not required and Credit earned in respect of one final product can be utilised towards payment of duty on the other final product. As such he prays for rejection of the appeal.

4. I have considered the submission of both sides. The relevant proviso inserted in Notification No. 1/95-CE (NT) dated 16.3.95 is reproduced below for the sake of ready reference:-

"Provided also that, notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) of rule 57A and the notifications issued thereunder the credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty excise on any other final product, whether or not such inputs have actually been used in the manufacture of such other final product, if the said inputs have been received and used in the factory of production on or after the 16th day of March, 1995". (emphasis provided).

4.1 A reading of the above proviso shows that any credit of duty allowed in respect of any inputs can be utilised towards payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the input having been used in the said final product. As such, the first condition of the said proviso is that the credit of duty should have been allowed, i.e. the assessees are entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit of Duty on particular inputs and it is only after availing the said Credit that the manner of its utilisation has been laid down in the said proviso. In the instant case, the appellants were, at the first stage, not entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs used in the manufacture of Refind Rice Bran Oil because the said Oil was chargeable to nil rate of duty. As such the Rule 57C prohibited taking of Credit in such circumstances. When the availing of Credit is not permissible under the law, the question of its utilisation towards the payment of duty on any other final product does not arise. The proviso refers to a situation where the assessee manufacturer is entitled to availing the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs to be utilised in the manufacture of two different products and such accumulated availed Credit is allowed to be utilised towards the payment of the second final product, even though the input might not have been used in that final product. As such, I uphold the impugned orders passed by the authorities below in so far as the same relates to the denial of MODVAT Credit of Duty.

Per J.H. Joglekar:

Brief facts of the case are that the appellants herein are engaged in the manufacture of man-made fabrics. One of the raw materials used in the manufacture of polyester fibre is Mono Ethylene Glycol (MEG). The appellants had taken credit of duty paid on MEG. Polyester fibre although attracting duty under CET sub heading 5501/20 was exempted under Notification No. 191/85 dated 28.8.85 when used in the manufacture of fibres. The appellants were working under Notification 191/85. They paid duty and afterwards the files refund claim which was rejected on the ground that Notification 225/86 under which set off was available on Mono Ethylene Glycol used in the manufacture of polyester staple fibre, did not provide for refund of duty paid on inputs. The rejection of the claim by the Assistant Collector was upheld by the Collector of Central Excise (Appeals) against whose order the assessees have preferred the above appeal.

2. None appears for the appellants inspite of notice and therefore, we have heard Shri R.S. Sangia, learned DR, perused the records and pass the following order.

3. The appellants had paid duty on MEG used in the manufacture of polyester fibre supplied to NTC units under Notification 191/85. The appellants claimed that they were entitled to the set off of duty on MEG under Notification 225/86. This notification exempts polyester staple fibre etc. from so much of excise duty leviable thereon which is paid on inputs and used in or in relation to the manufacture of final product. In this case, since the product in which MEG is used i.e. polyester staple fibre is fully exempt, the set off of duty is not available on MEG. The exemption is not for MEG used in the manufacture of staple fibre but to polyester staple fibre to the extent of duty paid on MEG. The Collector (Appeals)'s finding that Notification 225/86 is a specially concessional provision and it does not provide for any refund of duty paid on the inputs namely MEG is correct in the case of the clear language of Notification 225/86. We therefore, uphold the impugned order and reject the appeal.

(iii) Rule 57A is no doubt the Rule prescribing the applicability of the provisions of the Section relating to Modvat credit. But that rule cannot be read in isolation. It has to be read in conjunction with other rules contained in that Section. The Section as a whole envisages the availability of credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of final products, the manner of utilisation of inputs and of credit so earned. If one is to confine himself to read only Rule57 A for determining the quantum of credit to be availed of, the provisions of Rule 57 B allowing higher notional credit in some cases has to be kept in operative. We are to read the entire scheme as a whole as envisaged in Rules 57A to 57 J. The relevant Rule for denying credit is Rule 57 C, which stipulates that no credit shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to 'nil' rate of duty. We are to consider whether in the case of removals of goods under bond in terms of Rule 191 B/191 BB would be hit by the Rule. Likewise, we are to consider whether in the case of utilisation of inputs and credit earned thereon, if the inputs have gone into the goods cleared for export under Rules 191 B/191 BB, whether there is a bar in availment of credit. Thus we are of the view that Rule 57A cannot be considered in isolation. In so far as this case is concerned, it has to be considered in conjunction with Rules 57C and 57 F (3).

Provisions of Rules 13, 191 B, 191 BB envisage the scheme relating to exports without payment of duty. But the scheme has been dovetailed with the Modvat scheme as is evident from the proviso to Rule 57F (3) which reads as below :-

Quote "Provided that credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared for export under bond for used in the intermediate products cleared for export in accordance with sub rule (2), shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty on similar rinal products cleared for home consumption or for export on payment of duty and where for any reason, such adjustment is not possible by refund to the manufacturer, subject to such safeguards, condition and limitations as may be prescribed by the Central Govt, in the Official Gazette". Unquote (emphasis supplied)

From the above, it looks apparent to us, that even if the declared inputs are used in the declared final product, when some of final products are cleared for export under bond, credit earned from such inputs can be utilised for clearance of similar final products for home consumption and for any reason such adjustment is not possible, even cash refund to the manufacturer of final products is permitted. Now, we are to consider the meaning of the words "final products cleared for export under bond" (emphasised in the above proviso). POY & PSF are the final products in so far as the appellant is concerned. They are removed under bond in terms of Rules 191 B and 191 BB of the Central Excise Rules. Now let us look at the provisions governing the export of excisable goods. Rules 12 and 12 A govern the grant of rebate of Central Excise duty paid on these goods exported, as also on the excisable materials used in the production of goods, which are exported.

Rule 13 indicates that in like manner. Excisable Goods may be exported without payment of duly provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the C.Ex Rules and the owner of the goods to be exported enters into a bond undertaking to export the goods. From Rule 13. it is clear, that wherever rebate is permitted under Rules 12 & 12 A, goods in like manner can be exported without payment of duty in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Rules 191 B& 191 BB are the rules prescribing the export of excisable goods under bond figuring in Chapter IX of the C.Ex. Rules. Hence, we cannot give any other meaning to the words "final products cleared for export under Bond" figuring in the proviso to Rule 57 F (3), other than that is contained in Rule 13, which is the general provision permitting export of excisable goods for export under-bond. Hence we are not impressed with the argument of the Id. counsel for the Revenue that Modvat scheme is to be considered dehors export under bond, which is a separate scheme for exports.

The commercial plywoods manufactured by the appellants were cleared free of duty in terms of Rule 191B after following the procedures prescribed thereunder. Rule 191B figures in Chapter IX which carries a heading "Export under claim for rebate of duty or under bond" and the Rule carries the heading "Manufacture in bond of articles from excisable goods on which duty has not been paid". This Rule is applicable to manufacture in bond of such articles from such excisable goods and subject to such conditions and limitations as may be specified in the notification issued in this regard. Under this Rule, the Govt. of India has issued a notification under which decorative plywood is covered for in bond manufacture out of commercial plywood as one of the items for the purpose of export outside India. It was under this notification that the appellants cleared commercial plywoods manufactured by them to the manufacturer of the decorative plywoods under proper central excise prescribed documents. It is nobody's case that the manufacturer has not manufactured decorative plywood for export purpose out of commercial plywood in question under Rule 191B of the Central Excise Rules. In terms of the notification, the manufacturer of the decorative plywood, i.e. the buyer of the commercial plywood, the appellants customer, would have therefore executed a bond for twice the amount of duty payable beyond the non-duty excisable goods i.e. commercial plywood in this case, used for the manufacture of decorative plywood for export purpose. The excisable goods therefore received by the decorative plywood manufacturer were also required to be kept in terms of this notification in a separate room. A procedure is also prescribed under this notification for disposal of the waste arising during the manufacture either on payment of duty or for recycling in the same factory. This notification also has a provision for allowing the manufacturer of the finished goods who has manufactured under bond under Rule 191B for clearance for home consumption on payment of excise duty leviable by them on such article as also on the excisable goods used in the manufacture thereof in the same manner as excisable goods intended for home consumption are cleared from the place of their production or manufacture or storage. It is thus seen that Rule 191B is a very comprehensive procedure under which finished goods manufactured out of non-duty paid goods have to be properly accounted for and in the event of the goods not being exported the levy of duty is provided both in respect of the finished goods manufactured in bond as also the inputs contained thereunder which was received without payment of duty. 2. The brief facts of the case are that the appellants are engaged in the manufacture of polyester oriented yarn, polyester filament yarn and polyester textured yarn falling under Headings 54.02 and 54.03 of the Schedule to the CETA 1985. On 30.7.91, they filed a declaration under Rule 57G indicating POY, PFY and PTY as final products and poly ethylene terephthalate (polyester polymer chips) as inputs. On 31.7.91, they filed an application for permission to remove inputs or partially processed goods under Rule 57F (2) and/or Notification 214/86-CE along with an undertaking that the duty liability would be discharged on the finished goods. This application clearly mentioned that the inputs viz. DMT and MEG would be supplied directly to the job worker (M/s. Garware Plastics and Polyester Ltd.) for conversion into PP chips which would be returned to the appellants. By letter dated 19.8.91, the Range Superintendent sought clarification on certain points including maintenance of records and generation of waste. By reply dated 26.8.91, the appellants explained the procedure which would be followed by them for inputs to be directly supplied to job workers - they explained that the consignee's name would be shown as M/s. Garware Plastics and Polyester Ltd. A/c M/s. Raymond Synthetics. It was also explained that methanol and water would be generated as bye product during conversion of DMT and MEG into PP chips. The Assistant Commissioner granted permission to remove materials under Rule 57F (2) by his letter dated 11.10.91 the appellants took modvat credit of Rs. 50,77,918.90 on the basis of gate passes issued by M/s. Bombay Dyeing (supplier of DMT) and M/s. India Glycol (supplier of MEG) to the job workers on 11.1.95. The appellants were issued a show cause notice proposing recovery of modvat credit under the provisions of Rule 57I read with proviso to Section 11A on the grounds inter-alia that :

(a)

the appellants did not have permission under Rule 57F (2) read with Notification 214/86-CE during the period when DMT and MEG were received by job workers;

(b)

that the inputs were taken directly to the premises of the job worker without being brought into the appellants' premises.

(c)

authenticated challans were not issued for the movement of the goods;

(d)

payment of duty on methanol (bye product) by job workers is not in consonance with the provisions of the Notification 214/86;

(e)

job workers used catalysts and certain packing materials not supplied by the appellants and this was in violation of the condition of Notification 214/86.

(f)

appellants had not submitted a declaration under Rule 57G declaring PP chips as an intermediate product and POY, PFY, PTY as final products.

(g)

that the appellants had failed to produce proof that the job workers had supplied PP chips under Notification 214/86 in view of the job workers' letter that the chips were cleared without payment of duty in terms of Notification 53/88-CE;

(h)

that the appellants had wilfully misstated that they had received PP chips after conversion on job work under Notification 214/86.

The appellants replied to the notice denying the allegations, and pointing out that permission under Rule 57F had been applied for on 31.7.91 and since their application had not been turned down, they proceeded on the basis that permission had been granted, that there was no suppression of the fact that the inputs were directly sent to the job workers premises, that the job worker had cleared methanol (bye product) on payment of duty, that the receipt of inputs directly by the job worker was allowed since permission was granted on this basis by the Department on 11.10.91, etc.

Therefore, the apparatus in question is covered by the Explanation 1 (b) of Rule 57Q. The findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that these are excluded from Rule 57Q are incorrect for the reasons mentioned in respect of item No. IV above. XI Flame Proof Equipment

XI (a) The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) denying the modvat credit on the aforesaid items are as under :

"These are the parts of the plant. These are the flameproof equipments fitted in the TEG and CP area of the POY plant.

These are basically safety equipments used to save the electrical and other equipment for flames and sparks and hence, are not used for producing, processing or for bringing about any change in any substance. Hence they are not qualified to become capital goods under Rule 57Q."

XI(b) Findings

The Commissioner (Appeals) has therefore accepted that these equipments are parts of the plant. The plant in question is undisputedly covered by the definition of capital goods in terms of Explanation 1 (a) to Rule 57Q. Therefore, these items are covered by Explanation 1 (b). Hence, denial of credit is incorrect.

XII S.S. Powder

XII(a) The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) denying the modvat credit on the aforesaid items are as under :

"This is part of the Spin Pack Assembly of the POY Plant. The SS Powder acts as a physical filter in extruding the molten polymer into yarn.

These goods aid in extruding the molten polymer into yarn and that S.S. Powder is more of the nature of raw material i.e. it is an input rather than capital goods and therefore not eligible for credit under Rule 57Q."

XII(b) Findings

Here also the Commissioner (Appeals) has specifically accepted that this is the part of spin pack assembly of the POY plant. Hence, the item is squarely covered by the Explanation of sub-Rule 1 (a) to Rule 57Q. In any event of the matter and without prejudice as per the interpretation of the Commissioner (Appeals) these items are in the nature of input. In such an event, the credit under Rule 57A ought to have been extended instead of denying the credit. The reasons mentioned already in respect of Molecular Sieves (under Sl. No. III) above are equally applicable to this case also.

XIII Hydraulic Pallet Truck/Spring Hangers Supports.

XIII(a) The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) denying the modvat credit on the aforesaid items are as under:

"This is an accessory of POY plant performing the function of handling the packed POY stacked on pallets for their storage/loading at the warehouse. The adjudicating authority rightly disallowed modvat credit on the said capital goods on the ground that it is not used for producing or processing or for bringing about any change in any substance because the role of item is after the goods are produced. This item does not fulfil the criteria laid down by the Supreme Court judgment in Rajasthan State Chemical Works. Therefore the citations quoted are not applicable."

XIII(b) Finding

The Commissioner (Appeals) had accepted that this is an accessory of POY plant and it performs the function of handling the packed POY stack for their storage/loading at warehouse. Hence, the item is covered by Explanation 1 (b) to Rule 57Q. In any event of the matter and the item itself is an equipment performing the functioning of handling of the goods in the factory. They are material handling equipments covered by the Explanation 1 (a) to Rule 57Q. In the following decisions, it has been held by the CEGAT that material handling equipments are capital goods and eligible for modvat credit: (a) CCE Vs. Cosmo Ferrites Ltd. 2002 (148) ELT 1232; (b) Malabar Cement Ltd. Vs. CCE 2002 (149) ELT 751 (Tri) maintained by Supreme Court in2003 (153) ELT A94; (c) CCE Vs. Vikram Cement 2001 (132) ELT 662 (Tri)

XIV Catalyst Support Spring

XIV(a) The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) denying the modvat credit on the aforesaid items are as under:

"This is part of the MEG Plant. It performs the function of supporting the catalyst inside the vessel to ensure optimum reaction during manufacturing the final product.

This item fitted at MEG plant performs the function of supporting the catalyst inside the vessel is only a support and cannot be capital goods. Credit has been rightly denied."

XIV (b) Findings

Here also the Commissioner (Appeals) accepts that it is part of MEG plant. Hence, the item is squarely covered by Explanation 1 (b) to Rule 57Q.
