Levy of Purchase tax

10. 1[(1) Every dealer who in the course of his business purchases any goods specified in Schedule II from any person other than a registered dealer or 2[from a registered dealer who has opted for composition of tax under section 11 or from a registered dealer in the circumstances in which no tax u/s 9 is payable by the registered dealer on the sale price of such goods], shall be liable to pay tax on the purchase price of such goods if after their purchase,—

(a)

the goods other than those specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are not sold within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-State trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India but are sold or disposed of otherwise; or

4[(b)

the goods other than those specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are consumed or used,—

(i)

in the manufacture or processing of 5[goods declared tax free under section 16 other than the goods notified under sub-section (1B) of section 14] and the manufactured or processed goods are disposed of otherwise than by way of sale in the course of export out of the territory of India; or

(ii)

as plant, machinery, equipment and parts thereof in generation, transmission or distribution of electrical energy; or]

(c)

the goods other than those specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, after consumption or use in the manufacture or processing or mining of 6[any goods specified in Schedule II or the goods notified under sub-section (IB) of section 14], the manufactured or processed or mined goods are disposed off otherwise than by way of sale within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-State trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India; or

(d)

the goods specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are not sold within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-State trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India but are sold or disposed of otherwise; or

(e)

the goods specified in 3[Part III and Part IIIA] of the said Schedule, are consumed or used in the manufacture or processing or mining of goods,

and such tax shall be levied,—

(i)

in respect of goods referred to in clauses (a), (b) and (c), at 3a[the rate of 5 per cent] or the rate specified in column (3) of Schedule II, whichever is lower; and

(ii)

in respect of goods referred to in clauses (d) and (e), at the rate specified in column (3) of Schedule II.

Explanation : The rate specified in Schedule II shall be the rate at which tax would have been levied on the sales of such goods within the State of Madhya Pradesh on the date of such purchase 7[:]]

8 [Provided that in respect of the goods referred to in clause (b) consumed in manufacture or processing of goods specified in Schedule I notified under second proviso to clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 14 and the goods so manufactured or processed are disposed off otherwise than by way of sale in the course of export out of the territory of India, such tax shall be levied at the rate of 2 per cent :

Provided further that in respect of the goods referred to in clause (c) consumed in manufacture of goods specified in Schedule II notified under first proviso to clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 14 and the goods so manufactured are disposed off otherwise than by way of sale within the State of Madhya Pradesh or in the course of inter-state trade or commerce or in the course of export out of the territory of India, such tax shall be levied at the rate of 2 per cent. ]

(2) No tax under this section shall be levied in respect of any year on—

(a)

a dealer whose turnover in a year does not exceed the limit prescribed under sub-section 9[(2)] of section 5;

(b)

any other dealer who has no turnover, if his aggregate of purchase prices of all the goods does not exceed such amount as may be prescribed.

(3) Every dealer who has no turnover and is liable to pay tax under sub-section (1) shall, for the purpose of sections 18, 20,21,24,25 and 39, be deemed to be a registered dealer.

2.1. Consequences of not computing total income as per Section 115BAA

The Ordinance provided an option to the domestic companies to pay tax at lower rates by opting for section 115BAA regime provided its total income is computed without claiming additional depreciation, prescribed allowancesand deductions. Further, while computing the taxable income, no loss or unabsorbed depreciation shall be allowed to set-off if such loss or unabsorbed depreciation is attributable to any of the prescribed deduction or allowance.

The Ordinance did not contain any provisions as to the consequences for subsequently not fulfilling any of the prescribed conditions. VAT/CST - BOOK SALE AND RETENTION OF GOODS BY SELF FOR USE ON BEHALF OF OTHER PERSON - WHETHER LEVIABLE TO DUTY/TAX ?

4. A Plastic moulding company has developed a Mould for us and we have paid them for such mould. The mould will be used by the said company on our behalf for manufacture and supply of plastic parts exclusively for us. Please advise :

(1)

Since mould has not moved out of factory of the moulding company, would this be transaction of payment by us liable to excise and VAT ?

(2)

What will be treatment if after sometime we take back this mould ? Will duty or tax be leviable at that time ? If yes, on what value ?

In our view, the following shall be the consequences —

It is apparent that mould is being made/manufactured to be owned by your company. Hence, when charges for such mould are paid, it will have to be seen whether there is transfer of title of mould. As is apparent, mould becomes your property and accordingly, the same is a sale. Accordingly, the same is liable to excise duty and sales-tax. In our view, though there is no physical removal of goods from the factory of the moulding company; yet, since the title changes, it is a complete sale and would amount to 'removal' inasmuch as property belongs to you and any further use of moulds is only on your behalf. Viewed from another angle, when moulds are used inside the same factory for further manufacture, it amounts to 'captive use' and would be liable to duty in terms of the Explanation to rule 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The moulds must be shown as sold to you and received back on job-work basis under Rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Since both duty and tax stand paid at the time of sale of moulds to you, no further payment of duty or tax is warranted at the time when they are returned.

SERVICE TAX - TWO FOREIGN BRANCHES OF INDIA COMPANIES PROVIDED SERVICE TO EACH OTHER - TAXABILITY

5. A Ltd. and B Ltd. are two Indian companies (located in India). They have Branch X and Branch Y, respectively, outside India. Branch X provides services to Branch Y. Would this service be liable to service tax ? Please answer in light of applicability of rule 8 of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012.

Since Branch X of A Ltd. is located outside India, Branch X and A Ltd. would be deemed to be distinct persons under Explanations 3 and 4 to section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994. Similarly, Branch Y would also be a person separate person from B Ltd.

Since X and Y are separate persons and both are located outside India, Rule 8 of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012 would be inapplicable and furthermore, the service would be exempt under Entry 34(c) of the Notification No. 25/2012-ST.

The Lok Sabha passed the Finance Bill 2025 [hereinafter called 'Finance Bill (Lok Sabha)'] on March 25, 2025.While the Finance Bill,as passed by the Lok Sabha, largely retains the proposals made in the Finance Bill, certain noteworthy modifications have been made to the provisions relating to the block assessment, omission of equalisation levy and giving overriding powers to Section 44BBD over Section 115A and Section 44DA.

This article comprehensively analyses the changesmadeto the Finance Bill 2025 as passed by the Lok Sabha, highlighting their implications and the rationale behind these revisions.

1. The equalisation levy is withdrawn

Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 introduced the Equalisation Levy in respect of online advertisement services rendered to a specified person by a non-resident. The Finance Act 2020 expanded the scope of equalisation levy to the e-commerce supply of goods or services to a specified person by an e-commerce operator. However, the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 removed the equalisation levy on e-commerce supplies of goods or services with effect from 01-08-2024.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) amended Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 and the Income-tax Act ('ITA') to withdraw the equalisation levy from 01-04-2025 entirely. The following amendments have been made:

(a)

Amendments have been made to Sections 163 and 165 of the Finance Act 2016 to provide that the no equalisation levy shall apply to any consideration in respect of online advertisement services received or receivable by a non-resident on or after 01-04-2025.

(b)

A sunset date has been inserted in Section 10(50) of ITA to provide that this provision shall not apply from the assessment year 2026-27.

2. A Proviso has been inserted into Section 44BBD(2)

The Finance Bill 2025 proposed the insertion of Section 44BBD, which provides for the computation of income on a presumptive basis for non-residents engaged in the business of providing services or technology for setting up electronics manufacturing facilities in India. Section 44BBD(2) provides that a sum equal to 25% of the aggregate of the specified amounts shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of such business of the non-resident assessee.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) inserted a proviso to Section 44BBD(2), which provides that the provisions of Section 44DA or Section 115A shall not apply in respect of the amounts referred to in this subsection. This proviso will primarily impact the taxability of royalty and fees for technical services (FTS) earned by a non-resident.

The taxability of royalty and FTS depends upon the existence of the permanent establishment (PE) of a non-resident in India. If the PE exists in India and the royalty or FTS is connected to it, the income shall be taxable under the head "Business or Profession" as per Section 44DA. If the PE does not exist, the income shall be taxable under the head of other sources at the rate specified under Section 115A, subject to provisions of DTAA.

The impact of the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) is explained below.

2.1. No disallowance under Section 44DA

Section 44DA deals with the taxability of royalties and FTS connected to the PE in India. The first proviso to Section 44DA disallows the deduction in respect of the following:

(a)

Any expenditure or allowance that is not wholly or exclusively incurred for the business of such PE or fixed place of profession in India; or

(b)

Amount paid by the PE to its head office or to any of its other offices.

As the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 44DA, the above expenditure should not be disallowed if the royalty and FTS connected to the PE in India are taxable on a presumptive basis under Section 44BBD.

2.2. The concessional tax rate of Section 115A shall not be available

The proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 115A when the income is computed under Section 44BBD. Where the income is not computed under Section 44BBD, the tax rate under Section 115A will apply if the income is royalty or FTS. Therefore, the applicable tax rate for a non-resident providing services or technology in India shall be as follows:

(a)

Where the nature is business income, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income computed as per Section 44BBD shall be taxable at the applicable rate.

(b)

Polyset Corporation [2000] 115 ELT 41 (SC) : 3.3-1 Case Study - In this judgment the Supreme Court has ruled that the date of manufacture of goods is relevant for determining whether the goods are excisable and as to the rate of duty that the said goods must bear, what is relevant is the date of their clearance.

3.4 CCE v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 139 ELT 3 (SC) :

3.4-1 Case Study - While considering the eligibility of an exemption notification subject to the payment of appropriate duty on raw materials, the Supreme Court has held that "An exemption notification that uses the said phrase applies to goods which have been made from duty paid material. In the said phrase, due emphasis must be given to the words 'has already been paid'. For the purpose of getting the benefit of the exemption under the notification, the goods must be made from raw materials on which excise duty has, as a matter of fact, been paid, and has been paid at the 'appropriate' or correct rate. Unless the manufacturer has paid the correct amount of excise duty, he is not entitled to the benefit of the exemption notification" (paragraph six of the judgment). In paragraph seven, the Court observed, "Where the raw material is not liable to excise duty or such duty is nil, no excise duty is, as a matter of fact, paid upon it. To goods made out of such material the notification will not apply." Hence, the argument that "Nil rate of duty is also a rate of duty" is on a very fragile ground. A collective reading of the definition under section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, the Supreme Court's decision in Dhiren Chemical Industries (supra) and the decision of the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal in Amaravathi Co-operatives Sugar Mills v. CCE 2013 (291) ELT 126 (Trib. - Chennai) suggests that "the rate of duty being nil, the goods are not excisable goods".

3.5 H.M.M. v. UOI [2005] 192 ELT 63 (Delhi) :

3.5-1 Case Study - Where the Delhi High Court held that the duty being on manufacture and the goods having been exempted at the time of manufacture, the goods must be taken as exempted at the time of clearance, even though the exemption had been withdrawn by then.

The UOI had not been represented by anybody. So, nobody pointed out to the High Court that the issue has already seized to be res integra. That is to say, it had been a settled issue by the judgments in the cases of Wallace Flour Mills and Polyset discussed above.

This rule further provides that where integrated tax is paid on such goods, the amount of credit shall be allowed at the rates of 30% and 20%, respectively, of the said tax. The rule also specifies some conditions, inter alia, the scheme shall be available for six tax periods from the appointed date.

(d)

Using word only "inputs" in the above proviso unlike other sub-section using the word as "inputs held in stock and inputs contained in semi-finished or finished goods held in stock" indicates that the said proviso mainly relates to traders. The definition of 'inputs' covers all types of goods other than capital goods used or intended to be used in the business.

(e)

The aforesaid proviso to section 140(3) specifically excludes in its ambit a manufacturer' or a 'supplier of services'. It means that these are not allowed to take such credit at the prescribed rate even if they have the document for procurement of such goods but have not invoice or any other documents evidencing payment of duty or tax in respect of such inputs.

(f)

There is one condition mentioned in the said proviso regarding passing on of the benefit of such credit by way of reduced prices to the recipient required to be fulfilled to get the benefit of said proviso. It is clear that said condition is not applicable to a 'manufacturer' or a 'supplier of services' as they are specifically excluded from the said proviso and it is also seems justified as they are not getting any benefit of the said proviso. However, the language and words used by the last portion of the said proviso may create some ambiguity to interpret the correct meaning. The last portion of the proviso reads, as "including that the said taxable person shall pass on the benefit of such credit by way of reduced prices to the recipient, be allowed to take credit at such rate and in such manner as may be prescribed." The later part of the proviso and the words used "taxable person" instead of "registered person" in the said part may be interpreted in a different way.

(g)

However, it is a well-settled rule that a proviso is meant to be an exception to something within the main enactment or to qualify something enacted therein but the proviso would be within the purview of the enactment In other words, a proviso cannot be torn apart from the main enactment nor it can be used to nullify the real object of the main enactment.

Issues

The sections 115BAA and 115BAB start with a non-obstante clause and overrides the other provisions of the Act. However, the sections are subject to the provisions of Chapter XII.

Owing to manner in which the sections have been introduced in the Act, certain issues have emerged which would need clarification, which are briefly discussed here-in-below:

1. Applicable tax rate on Long-term capital gains, short-term capital gains on listed securities and income under other heads

The sections do not override the provisions of Chapter XII of the Act i.e. provisions contained in the said chapter would hold forte. Hence special rates mentioned in sections 111A, 112, 112A, etc. would continue to apply.

Having regard to the language used in the sections, in our view, companies having income from House Property, Short-term capitals gains (other than on listed securities) and Income from Other Sources viz. bank interest, etc. should be taxed at 17.16%/ 25.168% if the reduced tax rate regime is opted for. A new manufacturing company holding sizeable rent yielding real estate and fixed deposits would stand to benefit (on account of lower tax rate of 17.16%) as compared to any other company having similar sources of income. The tax authorities may however, seek to dispute the adoption of section 115BAB by such companies by contending that the intention is not to extend benefit of lower taxes to non-business income.

2. Whether past MAT credit would be allowed

Sub-section 5A of section 115JB has been amended stating that provisions of section 115JB would not apply to companies which have exercised option to be governed by the aforesaid regime. It may be noted that no amendment has been made in section 115JAA of the Act which deals with utilization of MAT credit on account of MAT paid in earlier years. A plain reading of the provisions, in our view, suggest that past MAT credit available to an existing company should be allowed as a set-off against the tax liability under section 115BAA. There is no express prohibition in section 115BAA to deny MAT credit unlike several other deductions and losses specifically mentioned.

In our view, the MAT credit to be allowed in a year should be limited to the difference between the tax liability under section 115BAA and that under section 115JB which would have been payable. The fact that provisions of section 115JB are not applicable should not impact the computation of the credit which is separately provided in section 115JAA(5) and is an independent exercise for the purpose of determining and granting MAT credit only.

However, considering that the section seeks to override all the provisions of the Act, there may be litigation on the issue.

3. Applicability of interest under section 234B, 234C, etc.

The new sections start as under:

"(1) notwithstanding anything contained in this Act……"

On account of the non-obstante clause in the sections which overrides the other provisions of the Act, there could be an argument that interest under section 234B and 234C cannot be levied.

Section 115JB of the Act has similar non-obstante clause but also has a sub-section (5) which states as under:

SHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and, therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

The Supreme Court held : The electricity is not an excisable item. In the instant civil appeal, the issue was with regard to the electricity which was generated inside the plant by heating of LSHS and which was captively consumed and used to manufacture cement/caustic soda. Rule 57A has an Explanatory clause (c) which states as to what inputs are included in Modvat credit. Explanation ( c) refers to ‘input used as fuel’. The said clause was introduced by Notification No. 4 of 1994. At that time, the Government made it clear that inputs used as fuel were entitled to MODVAT credit. That fuel, either utilized directly or for generating electricity, as an intermediary product, is integrally connected with several operations which result in the emergence of the final product, namely, cement/caustic soda. It is important to note that without utilization of LSHS, it is not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda. The electrolysis process is dependent on continuous flow of electricity. If there is disruption in the supply of electricity from the Electricity Board, then the entire plant of the assessee would fail and the manufacture of cement/caustic soda would not take place. Therefore, LSHS would come within the ambit of the expression ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product’. Electricity is one form of heat. It gets generated in several ways. LSHS is a fuel used in the generation of electricity. Since electricity is self-generated and since it comes into existence as an intermediary product, its utilization for production of final product is crucial. Hence, MODVAT credit on LSHS used in production of electricity could not be denied. Lastly, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced on behalf of the department, the expression ‘in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ was to be interpreted. The expression ‘in the manufacture of goods’ indicates the use of the input in the manufacture of the final product. The said expression normally covers the entire process of converting raw materials into finished goods such as caustic soda, cement, etc. However, the matter does not end with the said expression. The expression also covers inputs ‘used in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The said expression, namely, ‘in relation to’ also finds place in the extended definition of the word ‘manufacture’ in section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is for this reason that the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the expression ‘in relation to’ must be given a wide connotation. The Explanation to rule 57A shows an inclusive definition of the word ‘input’. Therefore, there is a dichotomy between inputs used in the manufacture of the final product and inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. The department gave a narrow meaning to the word ‘used’ in rule 57A. The department would have been right in saying that the input must be raw material consumed in the manufacture of final product. However, the expression ‘used’ in rule 57A uses the words ‘in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The words ‘in relation to’ which find place in section 2(f) of the 1944 Act have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover processes generating intermediate products and it is in this context that it has been repeatedly held by the Supreme Court that if manufacture of final product cannot take place without the process in question, then that process is an integral part of the activity of manufacture of the final product. Therefore, the words ‘in relation to the manufacture’ have been used to widen and expand the scope, meaning and content of the expression ‘inputs’ so as to attract goods which do not enter into finished goods. Where raw material is used in the manufacture of final product, it is an input used in the manufacture of final product. However, the doubt may arise only in regard to use of some articles not in the mainstream of manufacturing process, but something which is used for rendering final product marketable or something used otherwise in assisting the process of manufacture. This doubt is set at rest by use of the words ‘used in relation to manufacture’. In the instant case, the LSHS was used to generate electricity, which was captively consumed. Without continuous supply of such electricity generated in the plant, it was not possible to manufacture cement, caustic soda, etc. Without such supply, the process of electrolysis was not possible. Therefore, keeping in mind the expression ‘used in relation to the manufacture’ in rule 57A, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit on LSHS. The instant case fell in clause (c) and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) even before 16-3-1995

Background

Amidst the prolonged slowdown in the economy, the government brought in the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019, promulgated by the President of India, to provide impetus to the ailing corporate sector. The ordinance inter alia provides to reduce the corporate tax rate on certain classes of companies; rationalise the current Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rates and withdraw the enhanced surcharge from certain incomes arising from investment in capital markets etc.

The key amendments that find focus in this article relate to reduction in effective corporate tax rate for certain class of domestic companies. Due to such tax rate reduction, India's lowest bracket of corporate tax rate of 17.16 percent1 is now competitive with that of other emerging economies such as Vietnam (20 percent), Thailand (20 percent), Singapore (17 percent), Hong Kong (16.5 percent)2.

The reduction in corporate tax rates has been made effective through insertion of two new sections in the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) i.e. section 115BAA and section 115BAB (collectively referred to as 'Beneficial sections'). These sections are still subject to other provisions of Chapter XII of the Act, such as section 111/111A/112/113 etc. and hence any income in nature of long term/short term capital gains etc. covered under other sections of Chapter XII will continue to be taxed at existing rates.

The sections providing concessional tax rates have been made effective from the current Financial Year (FY) i.e. FY 2019-20 itself. Hence, companies considering to opt for the beneficial sections should take a timely call taking into account the impact of the change in effective tax rates on the advance tax computations for the next quarter/s, on tax provisioning etc.

The amendments also include reduction of tax rate on book profit u/s. 115JB of IT. Act known as Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate from the existing effective tax rates of 20.20 percent to 17.47 percent for all companies.

Newly inserted section 115BAA and section 115BAB:

1.

Relief to existing Companies – Section 115BAA: Under this section, a domestic company can opt for a lower effective tax rate of 25.17 percent(22 percent basic plus 10 percent surcharge plus 4 percent cess) subject to certain conditions. This provision is applicable to all domestic companies (irrespective of activities, turnover or year of incorporation). If a company opts for this option then it would not be eligible for certain expenses /deduction as discussed later in subsequent paragraphs.

2.

Relief to new manufacturing Companies – Section 115BAB: Under this section, new domestic manufacturing companies can opt for a lower rate of tax of 17.16 percent (15 percent basic plus 10 percent surcharge plus 4 percent cess), subject to fulfilment of following conditions:

Company should be set-up and registered on or after 1 October 2019;

Manufacturing to be commenced on or before 31 March 2023 and the company is not formed by splitting up/reconstruction, of a business already in existence;

Company should fulfil certain conditions regarding use of plant and machinery.

However, a company willing to opt for beneficial sections would not be entitled various tax exemption/deduction available under the sections 10AA (tax holiday for SEZ units), 32(1)(iia) (additional depreciation), 32AD (additional deduction for investment in machinery), 33AB (deduction for tea/coffee/rubber development account), 33ABA (site restoration fund), 35(1)(ii) or (iia) or (iii), 35(2AA), 35(2AB)(weighted deduction for expenditure on scientific research), 35AD (capital expenditure for specified business), 35CCC (expenditure on agriculture extension projects) or 35CCD (skill development project) or any under any provision of Chapter VI-A under the heading "C - deductions in respect of certain incomes" other than section 80JJAA of the Act (henceforth collectively mentioned as deduction/exemption provisions).

Further, the Company will not be allowed any set-off of losses carried forward from earlier years if such losses are attributable to any of the deduction/exemption provisions referred in above paragraph.

Further MAT provisions u/s 115JB shall not be applicable to companies opting for sections 115BAA/115BAB.

The option to avail concessional rate of tax as per the aforesaid sections is available from FY 2019-20 onwards and should be exercised before the due date of filing tax return of the year from which such option is exercised. A company not opting for the beneficial provisions due to its existing tax exemptions/deductions, can avail the option for beneficial provisions in the future; however, such option once exercised cannot be revoked in subsequent years.

M.F.(D.R.) CIRCULAR NO. B-42/1/96-TRU, DATED 27-9-1996

REVERSAL OF MODVAT CREDIT TAKEN ON INPUTS UNDER RULE 57CC

Kind attention is invited to the provisions of Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules for reversal of Modvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods or goods chargeable to 'nil' rate of excise duty. The provision has been made that where a manufacturer uses inputs which are common to both dutiable goods as well as exempted goods, the manufacturer is required to debit the amount equal to 8% of the value of the exempted goods when they are cleared from the factory.

2. In some cases, the exempted goods cleared by one manufacturer are used as inputs by another manufacturer. The manufacturer of exempted goods indicates the amount of Modvat credit reversed on the invoices issued by him for such exempted goods. In this context, some doubts have been raised whether the amount of Modvat credit so reversed is available as Modvat credit to the user of such exempted goods when he uses them as inputs in his factory.

3. In this context, it is clarified that the amount reversed is not by way of payment of excise duty. Accordingly, the amount of Modvat credit reversed and shown in the invoice by the manufacturer of exempted goods cannot be taken as credit by the user of exempted goods.

- In Modi Plastics v. CCE (2007) 216 ELT 112 (CESTAT SMB), final products entered in DSA (that time RG-1) were found defective. These were reused within the factory. Waste was also recycled. Final products after processing were cleared on payment of duty. It was held that assessee is eligible for duty exemption under Notification No. 67/1995-CE dated 16-3-1995 on finished goods reprocessed. Provisions not applicable to matches as final products - The provisions of notification No 67/1995 dated 16.3.95 is applicable to all final products except matches [This item was excluded from Cenvat provisions. Now it has been included. However, corresponding change has not been made in notification No. 67/1995-CE].

Flushing of gas in air is not captive consumption ? - In BOC India v. CCE 2004 (173) ELT 89 (CESTAT), assessee was flushing gas and was allowing it to escape in atmosphere for cleaning, before new gas was produced. This was technical necessity. It was held that the gas is not used in further manufacture and such gas cannot be said to have been captively consumed. Hence, exemption under notification No. 67/1995-CE is not available [May be it is not used 'in manufacture of final product', but certainly it is used 'in relation to manufacture of final product', and should be eligible].

In fact, in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE 2000 (124) ELT 323 (CEGAT), Naphtha used in flushing pipelines was held eligible as flushing is a process integrally connected with manufacturing process of final product.

No duty on intermediate products if duty on final product remitted - Remission of duty does not mean goods are exempt from duty or chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty. Hence, no duty is payable on intermediate products used in the final products on which duty has been remitted - Pepsico India Holding v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 222 (CESTAT).

Proportionate reversal of credit taken on molasses used in exempted products sufficient - Molasses is used to manufacture rectified spirit and denatured spirit. Rectified spirit is exempted. Denatured spirit is dutiable. First rectified spirit is manufactured. While manufacturing rectified spirit, Carbon dioxide is manufactured, which is sold on payment of duty. Part of rectified spirit is used to manufacture denatured spirit, which is dutiable. In Ugar Sugar Works v. CCE (2007) 214 ELT 337 (CESTAT), it is held that on reversal of credit on molasses used in manufacture of rectified spirit, balance Cenvat credit taken on molasses cannot be denied.

In Godavari Sugar Mills v. CCE (2007) 212 ELT 234 (CESTAT), it was held that if proportionate Cenvat credit taken on molasses is reversed, it is sufficient - same view in SCI India v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 565 (CESTAT), though order is not worded happily - same view in Sakthi Sugars v. CCE (2008) 12 STT 174 (CESTAT). - view confirmed in CCE v. Sakhi Sugars (2016) 53 GST 149 = 64 taxmann.com 316 (SC).

No duty payable if some waste final products get produced - In Matsushita Lakhanpal Battery v. CCE 2005 (186) ELT 445 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturing battery cells for which intermediate products were manufactured within the factory. Some of the battery cells got rejected during manufacture. These were not marketable and no duty was paid on them. Department contended that since final product is 'exempt' duty should be paid on 'intermediate products' which were used in such waste battery cells. It was held that even if some final product becomes scrap and is not dutiable, it does not mean that intermediate products have not been captively consumed in manufacture of final product. Hence, demand is not sustainable.

Intermediate product exempt even if manufactured by third party - Intermediate product/input/capital goods are exempt even if they are manufactured by third party, as long as the captive consumption is within the factory - Tambraparani Containers v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 276 (CESTAT) (similar decisions in respect of capital goods discussed in a later paragraph).

Exemption to intermediate product if final product cleared on payment of 'amount' - If final product is exempt from duty, normally duty is payable on intermediate product. However, if final product is cleared as per provisions of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules [i.e. after paying 'amount' or after reversing Cenvat credit], intermediate product will be exempt from duty - proviso (vi) to Notification No. 67/1995-CE - clarified and confirmed in CCE, Cochin TN 68/2001 dated 24.7.2001] - noted and followed in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 287 ELT 102 (CESTAT).

9.3

Exempted goods

As per Rule 2(d) of Cenvat Credit Rules, 'exempted goods' means goods which are exempt from whole of duty of excise leviable thereon and includes goods which are chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty and goods in respect of which the benefit of an exemption under Notification No. 1/2011-CE, dated the 1st March, 2011 or under entries at serial numbers 67 and 128 of Notification No. 12/2012-CE, dated the 17th March, 2012 is availed.

[In Notification No. 12/2012-CE, Sr. No. 67 is coal falling under heading 2701 and Sr. No. 128 is fertilizers. Duty on these articles is 1% subject to condition that Cenvat credit should not be availed]

Thus, 'exempted goods' for purpose of Cenvat cover (a) Goods chargeable to 'Nil' duty as per Tariff and (b) Goods which are exempt by a notification issued under section 5A (c) Goods on which 2% excise duty has been paid under exemption Notification No. 1/2011-CE dated 1-3-2011 or 1% under Notification No. 12/2012-CE dated 17-3-2012.

Exempted goods include non-excisable goods - For purpose of rule 6(1), 'exempted goods' or exempted final products shall include non-excisable goods - Explanation 1 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Value of such goods shall be invoice value. If such invoice value is not available, then it will be determined by reasonable means - Explanation 2 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2016.

Waste, by products are exempted goods w.e.f. 1-4-2016 - Bagasse, dross and skummings of non ferrous metals or any such by-product will be treated as 'exempted goods' w.e.f. 1-3-2015 for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules - CBE&C circular No. 1027/15/2016-CX dated 25-4-2016.

Exempted goods mean non-excisable goods also w.e.f. 1-3-2015 for purpose of rule 6 - As per explanation 1 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 'exempted goods' or 'final products' shall include non-excisable goods cleared for a consideration from the factory.

Gas which escapes in atmosphere - rule 6 does not apply - Oxygen gas which escapes in atmosphere during manufacture of Nitrogen is not 'manufactured product'. Hence, rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules does not apply - CCE v. Air Liquid India Holding (2009) 238 ELT 122 (CESTAT SMB).

Electricity is 'exempted goods' w.e.f. 1-3-2015- As per explanation 1 to rule 6(1) of Cenvat Credit Rules inserted w.e.f. 1-3-2015, for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules, 'exempted goods' or 'final products' shall include non-excisable goods cleared for a consideration from the factory.

This should cover electricity sold outside and rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules shall apply.

Packing material in which inputs were received can be exempted goods w.e.f. 1-3-2015 - If packing material in which inputs were received was sold for price, such sale can be considered as sale of 'exempted goods' for purpose of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules.

Pet Preform

The item in question, i.e., "pet preform", is moulded in such a way as to give it shape of containers of different sizes and styles. As the air is blown through it, it forms the shape of a container. Pet preforms cannot be used for any other purpose besides being used as a container. The fact that moulding is done to bring it in the shape does not take it away from the domain of plastic packing material. The fact that it is moulded into plastic containers would not take it outside the purview of the category of the materials intended for being used for the packing of plastic goods for sale. The process of moulding pet preform was required for putting it in shape with a view to adapt it for actual user. The process only facilitates the actual user for packing. Viewed from these aspects, the imposition of tax at 12.5 per cent is not justified. Being an item coming well under the purview of S1. No. 155 of Part III of Schedule C, tax is to be charged at four per cent. [Epitome Petrochemical Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, West Bengal and others, (2011) 41 VST 22; (2011) 58 S.T.A. 95, decided on 4.3.2011, by the Division Bench of West Bengal Taxation Tribunal; J.N.R.T. Commercial (P) Limited another v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, West Bengal Others, (2011) 58 S.T.A. 237, decided on 4.3.2011 by the Division Bench of West Bengal Taxation Tribunal]

However, SSI exemption will be available to packing material even if they bear brand name of other person. These provisions are discussed in paras 34.3-1 and 34.6.

Duty payable on goods manufactured for captive consumption, if not eligible for SSI concession - If goods which are not eligible for SSI concession are manufactured by SSI unit for captive consumption, duty will be payable, even if final product is eligible for SSI concession, as correctly held in Super Polyfabriks Ltd. v. CCE 1999(114) ELT 1019 (CEGAT).

Plaster of Paris (P.O.P.) – Whether it is same as Gypsum?

Entry 16 of Schedule – A which deals with tax free goods, reads as under:-"fertilizers including bio-fertilizers and organic fertilizers, gypsum, pesticides, weedicides, insecticides and fungicides"

As per the appellant, appellant is importing P.O.P. from outside Punjab and chemistry of P.O.P. and chemistry of gypsum was the same and therefore it fell in Entry 16 of Schedule A and was exempt from payment of tax. However, from bare perusal of Entry 16, it would come out that it relates to the fertilizers, pesticides, weedicides, fungicides relating to land and agriculture. The Gypsum in the entry will also relate to its use in reference to land and crops. Gypsum is stated to loosen soil structure and improve poor soil conditions. It is stated to be used when there is layer of hard soil in the field.

Appellant is dealing in P.O.P. which is used as a building material. It cannot be said to be relating to land or its use and cannot be an item covered in Entry 16 of Schedule A. I, therefore, agree with the order of the Commissioner dated 27.8.2008 where the Commissioner had determined the disputed question saying that P.O.P. was not gypsum covered in Entry 16 and not tax free. [*Prem Enterprises, Jalandhar v. State of Punjab, (2010) 35 PHT 67, decided on 14.9.2009 by Value Added Tax Tribunal, Punjab, Chandigarh]

*Note – The view taken in this case has been endorsed by the Division Bench of Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case reported as Prem Enterprises v. State of Punjab and another, (2013) 59 VST 237 (PH); VSTI 2013 (Delhi, Punjab and Haryana) …B-98; (2013) 44 PHT 62 (PH), decided on 9.1.2103 observing that-

"Though the chemical properties may be similar, but the fact remains that the uses of gypsum and POP are different. Entry 16 of Schedule A exempts fertilizers from tax. The definition is inclusive which includes gypsum as a fertilizer. Entry 16 exempts fertilizers from tax, whereas POP cannot remotely be used as fertilizer. Therefore, POP does not fall within entry 16 of Schedule A."

We have carefully considered the submissions from both the sides and perused the records. The Respondent manufactured PSF for which MEG is one of the inputs. Notification No. 225/86-CE dated 3/4/86 exempted PSF from Central excise duty chargeable thereon as it equivalent to the Central Excise Duty under Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty under Customs Tariff Act, 1975 paid on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF. This exemption notification provided similar duty concession in respect of other finished products mentioned in the table annexed to the notification and the duty concession was equal to the Central excise duty paid under Central Excise Act or additional Customs Duty paid under Customs Tariff Act, on the specified inputs used in the manufacture of the finished products. Though there is no explicit provision in this exemption notification regarding its applicability when the finished product is fully exempt from duty or is chargeable to nil rate of duty, it would be an obvious corollary that this exemption would not be applicable if the finished product is an exempted goods i.e. either fully exempt from duty by virtue of an exemption notification or chargeable to nil rate of duty. The point of dispute in this case is as to whether this exemption notification would be applicable when the finished goods - PSF in this case, have been cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export.

3.1 Rules 191BB permits removal of excisable goods from the place of manufacture or storage without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export, subject to the conditions prescribed in this Rule. The PSF, in question, in respect of which the set off of duty on MEG used in its manufacture is sought to be denied, had been cleared without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export in terms of the provisions of Rule 191BB. The Tribunal in the case of Orissa Synthetics Vs. CCE (supra) and CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. (supra), has with reference to exemption notification No. 225/96-CE, held that PSF cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of goods for export is not to be treated as exempted goods. It is not the contention of the Department that these judgments have been challenged before a higher court or have been set aside. Moreover when the Department has accepted the clearances of the PSF for export under bond without payment of duty, as eligible for the benefit of this exemption, there would be no justification in denying the same exemption to the goods cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of the finished goods for export.

3.2 The Notification No. 225/86-CE operates like Modvat scheme. Rule 57F (3) of Chapter V (AA) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 pertaining to Modvat scheme, provided that credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on any of the finished products in or in relation to manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used or for payment of duty on any waste arising in course of manufacture of finished products or for payment of duty on inputs themselves, if the same are allowed to be cleared as such. Proviso to this sub-Rule provided that the credit of the specified duty in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of final products cleared for export under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty and where for any reason such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations, as may be specified by the Central Government by notification in the official gazette. In the case of Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay (supra), the dispute arose as to whether the final products cleared under bond without payment of duty in terms of Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished product for export would be eligible for the benefit of the proviso to Rule 57F (3) and the Tribunal answered this question in the affirmative, holding that in respect of clearances of finished product without payment of duty under Rule 191BB, the benefit of proviso to Rule 57F (3) would be available. Same principle would apply in this case also and when the Department has accepted the applicability of the exemption in respect of the finished product exported under bond without payment of duty, the benefit of this exemption would also have to be extended in respect of the clearances without payment of duty under Rule 191B.

Per Rakesh Kumar :

The facts leading to filing of this appeal by Revenue are, in brief, as under.

1.1 The respondents are manufacturer of Polyester staple fiber (PSF) chargeable to Central Excise Duty under Chapter 55 of the Central Excise Tariff. One of the inputs used in the manufacture of PSF is Mono Ethlylene Glycol (MEG). The dispute in this case pertains to January 1987 to May 1991 period. During that period Notification No. 225/86-CE issued under the then Rule 8 (1) of Central Excise Rules, 1944 exempted "PSF including tops and polyester filament yarn (PFY)" from so much of duty of excise chargeable under the Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty chargeable under Customs Tariff Act, 1975, as the case may be, already paid on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF or PFY. During the period from May 1989 to August 1991, nine show cause notices were issued to the Respondent for recovery of allegedly wrongly availed input duty exemption amounting to Rs. 1,15,54,845/- on the following grounds :-

(a)

The Respondents are not eligible for set off of the duty paid on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF exported out of India without payment of duty;

(b)

set off of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for used in the manufacture of goods for export is not admissible;

(c)

set off of duty paid on MEG, which is contained in the bi-products or waste arisen in course of manufacture of PSF is not admissible;

(d)

set off of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared at nil rate of duty under Notification No. 191/85-CE is not admissible;

(e)

set off amounting to Rs. 6,50,090/-, which represents the duty on the quantity of MEG which was allegedly short received, is not admissible.

1.2 These show cause notices were adjudicated by the Assistant Commissioner by a common order dated 30th May 2003 by which the Assistant Commissioner while permitting the set off of duty on MEG contained in waste and by-products and also the set off of duty paid on MEG, used in the manufacture of PSF which was exported out of India under bond without payment of duty, disallowed -

(a)

set off of Rs. 15,63,263/- of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF which was cleared without payment of duty for manufacture under bond of finished goods for export under Rule 191BB;

(b)

the set off of Rs. 1,13,330/- of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared at nil rate of duty under Notification No. 191/85-CE dated 28/8/85, and

(c)

the set off of Rs. 6,50,090/- in respect of the quantity of MEG which was short received.

1.3 The Respondent filed the appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) challenging the Assistant Commissioner's order -

(a)

disallowing the set off of the duty of Rs. 15,63,263/- on MEG contained in the PSF cleared without payment of duty for manufacture in bond of finished goods for export under Rule 191BB; and

(b)

disallowing the set off of Rs. 6,50,090/- in respect of the quantity of the MEG held to have been short received. The Commissioner (Appeals) vide order-in-appeal No. 126-CE/LKO/04 dated 1/6/04 allowed the appeal on the following grounds :-

(i)

so far as set off of Rs. 15,63,263/- of the duty on the quantity of MEG used in the manufacture of PSF cleared without payment of duty for manufacture of finished goods for export under bond under Rule 191BB is concerned, this set off is admissible to the Respondent in view of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. Vs. CCE reported in 1989 (44) E.L.T. 794 (S.C.) and of the Tribunal in the cases of CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. reported in 1999 (107) E.L.T. 455 (Trib.) and Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay reported in 1995 (9) RLT 317 (CEGAT-WRB)=1995 (78) E.L.T. 595 (Trib.).

(ii)

BB which inter alia provided that a product can be cleared without payment of duty if it is meant to be used in the manufacture of final product which is to be exported. We note that this issue was examined at length in paras 7, 8 & 9 by this Tribunal (Final Order No. 477/97-NB dt. 15.4.97) in their own case of the appellants. For the sake of clarity, the same paras are reproduced as under:- "Heard the submissions of both sides. The facts of the case as narrated above are that the appellants are manufacturing POY. The appellants get a number of inputs for the manufacture of POY. Both polyester filament yarn and the inputs were specified under Rule 57A. The appellants filed a declaration under Rule 57G. During the month of May, June and July, 1992, the appellants cleared without payment of duty a particular quantity of POY under the provisions of Rule 191BB. The only dispute that arises is whether removal of the goods under the provisions of Rule 191BB can be treated as removal under an exemption notification. The notification covering the removal of the goods under Rule 191BB is the Notfn. No. 33/90-CE (NT). This notification inter alia provides that the goods can be removed without payment of duty under the provisions of Rule 191BB."

"We find that in the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited reported at page 599 of Reliance Industries Limited at para 6.2, this Tribunal held as under:-

"In the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited decided by the East Regional Bench, the man-made staple fibre was cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB of the Central Excise Rules and the department objected to the availing of Modvat Credit of duty on inputs used in these final products cleared under Rule 191BB of the Rules. The department's main contention was that such removals of final products without payment of duty under Rule 191BB were hit by Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules. The East Regional Bench, after considering all the arguments raised by the ld. SDR negatived the objection and allowed the appeal of Orissa Synthetics. For arriving at their conclusion, that Bench relied on the decision of the Delhi High Court in Hindustan Aluminium Corpn. reported in 1981 (8) ELT 642, wherein it was held by the Delhi High Court that the facility of removal without payment of duty under bond for export could not be equated with a general exemption from payment of duty of excise. That Bench also took note of the clarification issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs in consultation with the Ministry of Law about the scope of proviso (i) to sub-rule (2) of Rule 56A (analogous to the provisions of Rule 57C). In that clarification issued by the Board, the Board advised the field formations that the said proviso to Rule 56A (2) would not stand attracted, where the final products were exported under bond, since such removals could neither be construed to be exempted nor be regarded as goods charged to nil rate of duty. (Vide the extract of the advice of the Ministry of Law appearing in para 9 of the said order of the East Regional Bench). Thus we find that going by the allegation contained in the show cause notices involved in this appeal, the issue is identical in all respects and the ratio of that decision would apply to this case squarely."

"A careful reading of the above paragraph shows that the Tribunal had held that the goods manufactured from the inputs on which modvat credit has been taken which are cleared without payment of duty under Notfn. No. 33/90-CE (NT) does not mean that the goods are exempt from the whole of duty."

6. We find that the learned JDR has cited and relied upon the decision of this Tribunal in the case of East India Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. We have perused this decision. We find that this decision does not come under Rule 191BB but on the interpretation of Rule 57F (2) and 57F (3). Thus we find that this decision is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case. Following the ratio of the decision of this Tribunal in the case of the appellants themselves, we hold that the modvat credit is admissible to the appellants. In the result the appeals are allowed.

Per Shri G.R. Sharma :

The facts giving rise to the captioned appeal are that the appellants get PTA and convert it into polyester staple fibre (PSF). The PSF is sent to different parties who manufacture polyester fabrics from this and export it. The appellants for this purpose were following the procedure u/r 191-BB of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and transferring the PSF under Not. No. 33/90. The department alleged that PSF is being cleared at nil rate of duty under Not. No. 33/90. Rule 57C was attracted and the Asstt. Collector accordingly confirmed a demand of Rs. 1,54,472.26. In appeal, the ld. Collr. (Appeals) also agreed with the Asstt. Collr. observing that there is no denying the fact that particular clearance of PSF was at nil rate of duty vide Not. No. 33/90 dated 5.9.90. Therefore, such being the case, modvat claimed is not admissible and rejected the appeal of the appellants herein.

2. Shri Vinod Agarwal, ld. Advocate appearing for the appellants submits that the department has wrongly and erroneously interpreted the Not. No. 33/90 to hold that the goods were exempt and therefore, Rule 57C comes into play. The ld. Counsel submitted that Not. No. 33/90 dated 5.9.90 only allows the transfer of goods without payment of duty in terms of the procedure set out under Rule 191 BB. The ld. Counsel also submits that Rule 57C comes into play only when the goods are exempt. He submits that no exemption notification is issued either under sub-rule (1) of Rule 8 or Section 5A of the Central Excise Act, 1944. He submits that reading the notification along with the provisions of Rule 57C, there is nothing to show or to come to the conclusion that the goods were exempt. He submits that since the goods were not exempt, therefore, Rule 57C is not applicable to the facts of the present case. In support of his contention, he cited and relied upon the decision of this Tribunal in the case of J.K. Synthetics Limited Vs. C.C.E., Jaipur reported in 1996 (87) ELT 389 =1996 (15) RLT 462 (T). He submits that their case was squarely covered by the decision of the Tribunal in the above case and therefore, prays that the appeal may be allowed.

3. Shri Satnam Singh, ld. SDR appearing for the respondent Commr. submits that transfer of excisable goods are governed by the provisions of Rule 191 BB; that this Rule inter alia requires bond, permission etc. He submits that from the record, it is not evident whether such permission was taken. He also submits that the goods in actuality were transferred without payment of duty and therefore, they should be deemed to be cleared from the factory at nil rate of duty. He submitted that nil rate of date means an exemption, therefore, the provisions of Rule 57C shall be attracted, and therefore, justifies the decision of the lower authorities in view of his observation.

4. Heard the submissions of both sides. The first point that was made by the ld. Counsel regarding permission for change in cause title. It was submitted by the ld. Counsel that JCT Fibres Ltd. has since been changed to JCT Ltd. and therefore, prays for the change of cause title. The ld. SDR has no objection. The cause title is therefore, changed to M/s. JCT Limited.

5. The short point for determination in this appeal is whether the provisions of Rule 57C are attracted when PSFs were sent to manufacturers of polyester fabrics for export. For this purpose, we have to see what the provisions of Not. No. 33/90 are Not. No. 33/90 inter alia stipulates "Transfer of excisable goods without payment of duty." It does not say that the duty shall be chargeable at nil rate etc. This notification also does not speak of exemption of the goods. Now let us examine the provisions of Rule 57C. Rule 57C lays down that modvat credit shall not be available in cases where the final product is exempt. Admittedly, in the instant case when these two rules are read together, I find that under Not. No. 33/90, the word `exempt' is not used nor nil rate of duty is used. Therefore, the goods were not exempt so as to attract denial of modvat credit on inputs under Section 57C. I get support for this view from the decision of the Tribunal in the case of J.K. Synthetics Ltd. cited above. In para 6, the Tribunal had held as under :

utilised towards payment of duty of excise,-

(i)

on any of the final products in or, in relation to the manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used in accordance with the declaration filed under sub-rule (1) of rule 57G; or]

(ii)

on the waste, if any, arising in the course of manufacture of the final products; or

(iii)

on the inputs themselves if such inputs have been permitted to be cleared under sub-rule(l)]: [Provided that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared for export under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export in accordance with sub-rule (2), shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption [or for export] on payment of duty and, where for any reason, such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations as may be specified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette:

Provided further that no such refund of credit of duty shall be allowed if the manufacturer avails of drawback allowed under the Customs and Central Excise Duties (Drawback) Rules, 1971, or claims rebate of duty under rule 12A, in respect of such duty.]

[Provided also that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared either to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a hundred per cent Export-Oriented Unit under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty,]

It is seen that earlier under the first proviso MODVAT credit taken in respect of the inputs contained in the goods exported under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export could be utilised for payment of duty towards goods cleared for home consumption or for any reason if this adjustment was not possible the cash refund has been provided for. With effect from 1.3.92, the second proviso has been added. Under this even where the final products in which the inputs have been utilised are cleared to a unit in a free trade zone or to a l00% export oriented unit under bond, the same benefit as in the case of the export of the goods has been provided for. We observe that as such in Rule 57F (3) there is no specific provision in regard to the clearances made to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, We observe that when the clearances are made to a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit of any finished product without payment of duty from a unit which has taken MODVAT credit in respect of the inputs, the benefit is given as ultimately in terms of these schemes the goods allowed manufacture are exported. The units which are manufacturing goods under Rule 191B in terms of notification issued under this Rule are in our view similarly placed as the unit located in the free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. We see no reason as to why the same benefit as provided under Rule 57F for these units cannot be extended to this unit. Interest of revenue is safeguarded by the specific provision under the notification issued under Rule 191B for recovery of duty both in respect of the finished goods and the non-duty paid goods out of which the same are manufactured in bond in case the goods are not exported. We therefore hold that notwithstanding the absence of any specific mention in the proviso to Rule 57F(3) in regard to the finished goods in respect of which input credit is taken and which are cleared without payment of duty to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, the second proviso to Rule 57F(3) would cover such units also, as we do not find any reason to differentiate the operations in the unit functioning under Rule 191B from the operations carried out in the unit functioning under a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. In view of above, we hold that the appellants plea has to be allowed and we order accordingly.

(iii)

Since the Respondent's unit was under physical control and all the movement of the goods was under physical supervision of the Departmental Officers, the allegation of suppression of fact, and extended limitation period based on the same cannot be invoked.

1.4 It is against the above-mentioned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the Department has come in appeal before the Tribunal.

2. Heard both the sides.

2.1 Shri B.K. Singh, the learned Jt. CDR assailing the impugned order and reiterating the grounds of appeal pleaded that Notification No. 225/86-CE issued under Rule 8 (1) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 exempting the PSF from so much of the duty of excise leviable thereon as it is equivalent to Central Excise Duty paid under Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty paid under Customs Tariff Act, 1975, on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF, is just like any other exemption notification, that this exemption notification would not be applicable if no duty is payable on the finished product - PSF for any reason, that when PSF had been cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for manufacture of finished goods under bond for export out of India, the benefit of duty exemption under this notification would not be available, as when no duty is payable on the PSF, there is nothing to exempt, that the exemption notification No. 225/86-CE cannot be equated with Modvat scheme and the provisions of Modvat scheme cannot be extended to this notification, that in view of this, the impugned order permitting set off of duty on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF which had been cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished goods under bond for export is incorrect and that the judgments relied upon by the Commissioner (Appeals) in the impugned order, which pertain to the Modvat scheme, are not relevant.

2.2 Shri Sparsh Bhargava, Advocate, the learned Counsel for the respondent defending the impugned order pleaded that main issue involved in this case is as to whether the set off under Notification No. 225/86-CE of the duty paid on MEG used in the manufacture of PSF which was cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191B for use in the manufacture under bond of finished goods for export, is admissible or not, that the Tribunal in the case of Orissa Synthetics Vs. CCE reported in 1999 (111) E.L.T. 111 (Trib.) has held that the goods cleared for export under bond or cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB are not to be treated as the exempted goods and the benefit of Notification No. 225/86-CE would be admissible, that same view has been taken by the Tribunal in the case of CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. (supra), that in the case of Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay (supra), the Tribunal with regard to the Modvat provisions - Rule 57F (3) held that the inputs used in the manufacture of final products cleared under bond for export purposes in terms of Rule 191B/191BB of Central Excise Rules are eligible for the benefit of proviso to Rule 57F (3) and the goods cleared for export under bond without payment of duty are neither the goods exempt from whole of duty nor are the goods chargeable to nil rate of duty and hence, input duty credit in respect of such goods would be available, that the same principle would apply in this case, as Notification No. 225/86-CE operates like Modvat scheme and that in view of this, there is no merit in the Revenue's appeal.

Per Shri R. Jayaraman - This is an appeal against the Order-in-Appeal No. KVV 128/.92-B II dt. 16.7.92, rejecting the appeal of the appellants.

2.1 The facts alleged in the S.C.Ns issued to the appellants are briefly as below :-

The appellants have filed a declaration under Rule 57 G of the Central Excise Rules for the availment of Modvat credit of various inputs such as PTA, M.E.G used in the manufacture of their final product P.O. Y/P.S.F. Some of the final products have been cleared at 'Nil' rate under rule 191 Band Rule 191 BB. Hence they are not eligible to avail the Modvat Credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of final products so cleared at Nil rate of duty under Rule 191B/191BB, which should be reverted. It is alleged that Credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of POY/PSF cleared at 'Nil' rate of duty under Rule 191B/191 BB has been utilised for payment of duty on the above final products cleared for home consumption, which is in contravention of Rules 57A read with Rule 57C and Rule 57F of the Central Excise Rules. Accordingly S.C.N, proposes to recover the credit alleged to have been availed of illegally. The demands have been issued within the time limit prescribed under Rule 571 of the Central Excise Rules.

2.2 The Asstt. Collector under his order No. V (57A) 4.9/92 dt. 23.4.92 confirmed the demands raised in four S.C.Ns totally aggregating about Rs. 5.87 crores by ordering reversal of credit taken on POY/PSF cleared under Rule 191B/191 BB of the Central Excise Rules. He also imposed a penalty of Rs. 5000/- on the appellants. On appeal before the Collr. (A), penalty imposed was set aside. On the main issue relating to order of reversal of Modvat credit, the Collr. (A) agreed with the Asstt. Collector, but directed the Asstt. Collr. to rework the demand. The present appeal is against the said order.

Provided also that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared either to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a hundred per cent Export Oriented Unit under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty. It is seen that earlier under the first proviso Modvat credit taken in respect of the inputs contained in the goods exported under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export could be utilised for payment of duty towards goods cleared for home consumption or for any reason if this adjustment was not possible the cash refund has been provided for. With effect from 1-3-1992, the second proviso has been added under this even where the final products in which the inputs have been utilised are cleared to a unit in a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit under bond, the same benefit as in the case of the export of the goods has been provided for. We observe that as such in Rule 57F(3) there is no specific provision in regard to the clearances made to a unit functioning under Rule 191B. We observe that when the clearances are made to a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit of any finished product without payment of duty from a unit which has taken Modvat in respect of inputs, the benefit is given as ultimately in terms of the schemes the goods allowed manufacture are exported. The units which are manufacturing goods under Rule 191B in terms of notification issued under this Rule are in view similarly placed as the unit located in the free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. We see no reason as to why the same benefit as provided under Rule 57F for these units cannot be extended to this unit. Interest of revenue is safeguarded by the specific provision under the notification issued under Rule 191B for recovery of duty both in respect of the finished goods and the non-duty paid goods out of which the same are manufactured in bond in case the goods are not exported. We therefore hold that notwithstanding the absence of any specific mention in the proviso to Rule 57F (3) in regard to the finished goods in respect of which input credit is taken and which are cleared without payment of duty to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, the second proviso to Rule 57F (3) would cover such units also, as we do not find any reason to differentiate the operations in the unit functioning under Rule 191B from the operations carried out in the unit functioning under a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. In view of above, we hold that the appellants' plea has to be allowed and we order accordingly.

Respectfully following the decision of the Larger Bench in the matter of Hunsur Plywood Works (P) Ltd. Vs. CCE (supra), I, therefore, set aside the impugned order of the Commissioner and allow the appeal and I order accordingly.

Now coming to the objection that Modvat credit cannot be utilised in regard to duty payable on similar final products, where some of the final products are cleared under bond in terms of Rule 191 BB of the Central Excise Rules, the issue is squarely covered by the decision of the East Regional Bench in the case of Orissa Synthetics and also by our decision in the case of Reliance Industries. We have considered all the arguments from the revenue for coming to the conclusion that in the absence of specific legal provision either under Rule 57 C or under Rule 57 F (3) proviso, Modvat credit cannot be denied for utilisation in regard to clearance of similar final products. Rule 57 C seeks to deny Modvat credit, if the final products are either wholly exempted or are chargeable to Nil rate of duty. We have held that in the case of goods cleared under a Notification issued under Rule 191 BB for export purposes, such goods cannot be equated with goods exempted under an exemption Notification issued under Rule 8 (1) of the C.E. Rules or Section 5A of C.Ex. Act nor they can be construed as goods chargeable to Nil rate of duty. For arriving at this conclusion, we have taken note of the Board's own instructions issued in the context of identical provisions of Rule 56A of the C.E. Rules, after consulting the Ministry of Law. The argument of Shri Nair that irrespective of the fact that Rule 57C does not specifically provide for denying benefit in respect of clearances under Rule 191 BB, since Rule 57F (3) proviso can only cover direct exports from the factory and not removals under Rule 191 BB for further manufacture of export goods in another factory. We do not find any warrant to read such a restriction in Rule 57F (3) proviso; because proviso to Rule 57F (3) talks of "cleared for export under bond". In the absence of any specific restriction prescribed in that proviso, we are to go by what is meant by the term for export under bond' laid down in Rule 13 of the C.Ex. Rules. Under Rule 13, goods may be exported outside India without payment of duty from a warehouse or licensed factory, provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules and the owner enters into a bond for due performance. There is no dispute that Rule 191 BB is one of the relevant provision of Chapter IX of the Rules. Hence if the goods are cleared under Rule 191BB, they are goods cleared for export in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Viewed in this context, we could not persuade ourselves to agree that Rule 57F (3) proviso can he extended, only where the goods are cleared direct from the factory to the port of shipment. Hence, we find no reason to take any different view from the one we have already taken in the case of Reliance Industries. Hence we hold that objection from the Dept. on this ground is not sustainable and direct the authorities to allow the credit to be utilised in regard to clearance of similar final product.

Hundred per cent absorption or assimilation of the duty paid input in the final product is not a sine qua non of MODVAT credit, but to take benefit of MODVAT Scheme, the petitioner is required simply to establish that the input was used in the manufacture of final product. The sulphuric acid (duty paid input) can be said to have been used by the petitioner in the manufacture of final product when the entire relevant quantity thereof was applied or subjected to the manufacturing process". 6. The High Court in arriving at the above conclusion relied on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. Vs. C.C.E. - 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC). In this case, it is observed that the question for consideration was whether the appellants became ineligible to claim set-off of duty on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre to the extent it gave rise to methanol. In the premises, the Supreme Court held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ''The Supreme Court held that ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre, though methanol had arisen as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture, when ethylene glycol interacted with DMT to produce polyester fibre. Giving the reasoning, the Supreme Court says that it is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre and that the appellant was engaged in the production of polyester fibre and not methanol". (Emphasis supplied).

7. Accordingly, the High Court in its decision held that the entire quantity of sulphuric acid was necessary for manufacturing process and the modvat credit could not be denied simply because the entire input was not emerged in the final product in the manufacturing process.

8. The above ratio, in the judgments of the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court are applicable with the same force to the facts of the present case. It is therefore to be held that the entire quantity of pig iron is used in the manufacture of the exempted category of the P.D. Pumps and no quantity of the input is used in the manufacture of waste and scrap. In view of the provisions of Rule 57C, the modvat credit is not available to the appellants. Since in this case, I have relied on the ratio of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and that of the Allahabad High Court, specifically on the subject, there is no warrant to consider the other decisions cited before me by the appellants.

9. The appeal thus fails and the same is accordingly rejected.
