Sethna, the Id. counsel representing the Revenue, assiduously sought to urge that certain points of law were not considered in those decisions and hence the Bench should independently view the position, not being influenced by those decisions. In any case, if the Bench feels that these points of law are strong enough for acceptance, they should place the matter before the larger. Bench for a decision. 4.2 On factual position, he does not dispute that the appellants have filed a proper declaration for the inputs used in the final product P.O.Y/P.S.F and both the inputs and final products namely POY/PSF are covered by the Notification issued under Rule 57A. He also does not dispute that the issue relates to eligibility of Modvat credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of such POY/PSF cleared without payment of duty, under Rule 191B/191BB of the C-Ex.

5. The main thrust of his contentions can be summed up as below :-

(i)

Modvat is a scheme for averting the cascading effect of input taxation on the duty paid in regard to the final product. When the final product is cleared without payment of duty for whatever be the reason, there cannot be a cascading effect of input duty on the final product, so cleared without payment of duty.

(ii)

In this case, removals without payment of duty have been permitted to the exporters, who effected such removals in terms of the bond executed under Rule 191B/l91 BB of the Central Excise Rules. Reliance Industries are not exporting the goods. They take the credit of duty paid on inputs and use the inputs in the manufacture of POY/PSF, which are cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191B/191 BB. Such credit of duty paid on these inputs is utilised for payment of duty of POY/PSG cleared by them for home consumption. Viewed in this context, it would be apparent that the appellants avai1 of the benefit, which is not intended to them for clearing the goods for home consumption.

(iii)

The Modvat Scheme is an independent one, mainly formulated for averting the cascading effect of input taxation. The basic principle is "no credit - if no duty is paid on the final product cleared". This is clearly evident from a careful reading of Rule 57A, which is the substantive provision to determine the eligibility. Judged by what is prescribed in Rule 57A, credit cannot be given when the final product is cleared without payment of duty.

(iv)

Provisions of Rules 13,191B, 191BBenvisageadifferentschemepermitting removals of excisable goods without payment of duty for exports. Unless Modvat scheme contemplates by a specific provisions in Rule 57A envisaging eligibility of credit to such removals for exports, they cannot claim the credit and their claim is blocked right at the thresh hold of Rule 57A.

(v)

In this case, admittedly POY/PSF are not exported as such. They were used in manufacture of fabrics. Fabrics is the final product exported and it is not covered by Notification issued under Rule 57A. Hence credit cannot be made available.

(vi)

Proviso to sub rule (3) of Rule 57F does not make any exception in regard to removals under Rule 191B/191BB specifically as has been done in the case of removal of goods for export production in the Free trade zone or 100% E.O.U. Hence it is clear that unless the final products manufactured by the assessees themselves are exported under bond, credit accrued therefrom cannot be utilised for payment of duty on similar final products cleared for home consumption. Hence sub rule (5) of Rule 57F would be applicable, and accordingly such credit has to be reversed.

We, therefore, hold that inputs, in respect of which MODVAT credit has been taken, have not been used by the Appellants in the manufacture of a product which attracts nil rate of duty. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order and allow the Appeal.

Per Archana Wadhwa :

Modvat credit of Rs. 2,25,305.00 has been disallowed by the authorities below for the period of August, 1995 to June, 1996 on the ground that the various inputs used in the manufacture of their final product i.e. Refined Rice Bran Oil, cannot be considered as modvatable input inasmuch as the final product is cleared without payment of duty.

2. The appellants duly represented by Shri S.K. Roychowdhury submits that the appellants are engaged in the manufacture of Refined Rice Bran Oil which is chargeable to nil rate of duty as also the vegetable product which is a dutiable product. They availed the MODVAT Credit on the various inputs after declaring the same in their declaration under Rule 57G and all the inputs for Rice Bran Oil as also for vegetable product, were common inputs and as such, common RG-23A Part-I and II was being maintained by them. He submits that they are entitled to the MODVAT Credit even if a part of the inputs is used in the manufacture of Rice Bran Oil cleared by nil rate of duty in terms of proviso to Rule 57F(4) inserted by Notification No. 11/95 dated 16.3.95. He submitted that the said Rule permitted the assessee to utilise the MODVAT Credit towards the payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the fact whether such an iinput has actually been used in the manufacture of such a final product or not. In this view, he submits that the impugned Orders be set aside and Credit be allowed.

3. Shri T. Premkumar, learned S.D.R. appearing for the Revenue contends that the provisions of Rule 57F(4) are not applicable to the present situation inasmuch as the same are applicable when common inputs are being used in the manufacture of two different dutiable products, that is to say that one to one correlation is not required and Credit earned in respect of one final product can be utilised towards payment of duty on the other final product. As such he prays for rejection of the appeal.

4. I have considered the submission of both sides. The relevant proviso inserted in Notification No. 1/95-CE (NT) dated 16.3.95 is reproduced below for the sake of ready reference:-

"Provided also that, notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) of rule 57A and the notifications issued thereunder the credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty excise on any other final product, whether or not such inputs have actually been used in the manufacture of such other final product, if the said inputs have been received and used in the factory of production on or after the 16th day of March, 1995". (emphasis provided).

4.1 A reading of the above proviso shows that any credit of duty allowed in respect of any inputs can be utilised towards payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the input having been used in the said final product. As such, the first condition of the said proviso is that the credit of duty should have been allowed, i.e. the assessees are entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit of Duty on particular inputs and it is only after availing the said Credit that the manner of its utilisation has been laid down in the said proviso. In the instant case, the appellants were, at the first stage, not entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs used in the manufacture of Refind Rice Bran Oil because the said Oil was chargeable to nil rate of duty. As such the Rule 57C prohibited taking of Credit in such circumstances. When the availing of Credit is not permissible under the law, the question of its utilisation towards the payment of duty on any other final product does not arise. The proviso refers to a situation where the assessee manufacturer is entitled to availing the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs to be utilised in the manufacture of two different products and such accumulated availed Credit is allowed to be utilised towards the payment of the second final product, even though the input might not have been used in that final product. As such, I uphold the impugned orders passed by the authorities below in so far as the same relates to the denial of MODVAT Credit of Duty.

Brief facts of the case are that the appellants herein are engaged in the manufacture of man-made fabrics. One of the raw materials used in the manufacture of polyester fibre is Mono Ethylene Glycol (MEG). The appellants had taken credit of duty paid on MEG. Polyester fibre although attracting duty under CET sub heading 5501/20 was exempted under Notification No. 191/85 dated 28.8.85 when used in the manufacture of fibres. The appellants were working under Notification 191/85. They paid duty and afterwards the files refund claim which was rejected on the ground that Notification 225/86 under which set off was available on Mono Ethylene Glycol used in the manufacture of polyester staple fibre, did not provide for refund of duty paid on inputs. The rejection of the claim by the Assistant Collector was upheld by the Collector of Central Excise (Appeals) against whose order the assessees have preferred the above appeal.

2. None appears for the appellants inspite of notice and therefore, we have heard Shri R.S. Sangia, learned DR, perused the records and pass the following order.

3. The appellants had paid duty on MEG used in the manufacture of polyester fibre supplied to NTC units under Notification 191/85. The appellants claimed that they were entitled to the set off of duty on MEG under Notification 225/86. This notification exempts polyester staple fibre etc. from so much of excise duty leviable thereon which is paid on inputs and used in or in relation to the manufacture of final product. In this case, since the product in which MEG is used i.e. polyester staple fibre is fully exempt, the set off of duty is not available on MEG. The exemption is not for MEG used in the manufacture of staple fibre but to polyester staple fibre to the extent of duty paid on MEG. The Collector (Appeals)'s finding that Notification 225/86 is a specially concessional provision and it does not provide for any refund of duty paid on the inputs namely MEG is correct in the case of the clear language of Notification 225/86. We therefore, uphold the impugned order and reject the appeal.

The admitted position is that the final product has already been manufactured. The effluent containing traces of sodium cyanide are sought to be eliminated by using these inputs. In the circumstances, unless the Govt. by a policy decision based on environmental consideration, allows benefit of duty credit in respect of such inputs used for effluent treatment, extension of Modvat credit in respect of the inputs used in the effluent treatment is not permissible. They are also not used for recovery of sodium cyanide from the effluent to clear such recovered NACN on payment of duty. We therefore hold that the aforesaid three items used in the effluent treatment plant are not eligible for Modvat credit. It is reported that these inputs are also used in other uses in other sections of the plant. Since the dispute is not about those other usages, our findings above are confined only to their usage in the effluent treatment plant.

The time bar aspect is to be considered only in respect of demand relating to caustic soda, Hydrochloride acid and Ion exchange resins used in the effluent treatment plant. We have carefully looked in to this declaration. We find that there is a specific reference to effluent treatment plant against Hydrochloric acid in the declaration; In the case of caustic soda, usage is indicated as neutralisation of Sodium cyanide, which goes to indicate that it is for destroying the final product and goes with effluent treatment. It is reported that detailed process of manufacture has been filed along with the declaration, but no evidence in this regard is produced. All the same, going by the declaration filed and there is a scope for dispute on their eligibility for credit, we are inclined to accept the plea that there was no malafide in giving the declaration. (iii) Rule 57A is no doubt the Rule prescribing the applicability of the provisions of the Section relating to Modvat credit. But that rule cannot be read in isolation. It has to be read in conjunction with other rules contained in that Section. The Section as a whole envisages the availability of credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of final products, the manner of utilisation of inputs and of credit so earned. If one is to confine himself to read only Rule57 A for determining the quantum of credit to be availed of, the provisions of Rule 57 B allowing higher notional credit in some cases has to be kept in operative. We are to read the entire scheme as a whole as envisaged in Rules 57A to 57 J. The relevant Rule for denying credit is Rule 57 C, which stipulates that no credit shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to 'nil' rate of duty. We are to consider whether in the case of removals of goods under bond in terms of Rule 191 B/191 BB would be hit by the Rule. Likewise, we are to consider whether in the case of utilisation of inputs and credit earned thereon, if the inputs have gone into the goods cleared for export under Rules 191 B/191 BB, whether there is a bar in availment of credit. Thus we are of the view that Rule 57A cannot be considered in isolation. In so far as this case is concerned, it has to be considered in conjunction with Rules 57C and 57 F (3).

(iv)

Provisions of Rules 13, 191 B, 191 BB envisage the scheme relating to exports without payment of duty. But the scheme has been dovetailed with the Modvat scheme as is evident from the proviso to Rule 57F (3) which reads as below :-

Quote "Provided that credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared for export under bond for used in the intermediate products cleared for export in accordance with sub rule (2), shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty on similar rinal products cleared for home consumption or for export on payment of duty and where for any reason, such adjustment is not possible by refund to the manufacturer, subject to such safeguards, condition and limitations as may be prescribed by the Central Govt, in the Official Gazette". Unquote (emphasis supplied)

From the above, it looks apparent to us, that even if the declared inputs are used in the declared final product, when some of final products are cleared for export under bond, credit earned from such inputs can be utilised for clearance of similar final products for home consumption and for any reason such adjustment is not possible, even cash refund to the manufacturer of final products is permitted. Now, we are to consider the meaning of the words "final products cleared for export under bond" (emphasised in the above proviso). POY & PSF are the final products in so far as the appellant is concerned. They are removed under bond in terms of Rules 191 B and 191 BB of the Central Excise Rules. Now let us look at the provisions governing the export of excisable goods. Rules 12 and 12 A govern the grant of rebate of Central Excise duty paid on these goods exported, as also on the excisable materials used in the production of goods, which are exported.

Rule 13 indicates that in like manner. Excisable Goods may be exported without payment of duly provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the C.Ex Rules and the owner of the goods to be exported enters into a bond undertaking to export the goods. From Rule 13. it is clear, that wherever rebate is permitted under Rules 12 & 12 A, goods in like manner can be exported without payment of duty in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Rules 191 B& 191 BB are the rules prescribing the export of excisable goods under bond figuring in Chapter IX of the C.Ex. Rules. Hence, we cannot give any other meaning to the words "final products cleared for export under Bond" figuring in the proviso to Rule 57 F (3), other than that is contained in Rule 13, which is the general provision permitting export of excisable goods for export under-bond. Hence we are not impressed with the argument of the Id. counsel for the Revenue that Modvat scheme is to be considered dehors export under bond, which is a separate scheme for exports.

The Larger Bench has also observed that when the clearances are made to free trade zone or 100% EOU of final finished products without payment of duty from an unit which has taken Modvat credit in respect of the inputs, the benefit is given as ultimately in terms of the scheme, the goods allowed manufacture are exported. Para 5 of the Larger Bench in the matter of Hunsur Plywood Works (P) Ltd. Vs. CCE (supra) is extracted below. 5. We have given a careful thought to the pleas made by both the sides. The commercial plywoods manufactured by the appellants were cleared free of duty in terms of Rule 191B after following the procedures prescribed thereunder. Rule 191B figures in Chapter IX which carries a heading "Export under claim for rebate of duty or under bond" and the Rule carries the heading "Manufacture in bond of articles from excisable goods on which duty has not been paid". This Rule is applicable to manufacture in bond of such articles from such excisable goods and subject to such conditions and limitations as may be specified in the notification issued in this regard. Under this Rule, the Govt. of India has issued a notification under which decorative plywood is covered for in bond manufacture out of commercial plywood as one of the items for the purpose of export outside India. It was under this notification that the appellants cleared commercial plywoods manufactured by them to the manufacturer of the decorative plywoods under proper central excise prescribed documents. It is nobody's case that the manufacturer has not manufactured decorative plywood for export purpose out of commercial plywood in question under Rule 191B of the Central Excise Rules. In terms of the notification, the manufacturer of the decorative plywood, i.e. the buyer of the commercial plywood, the appellants customer, would have therefore executed a bond for twice the amount of duty payable beyond the non-duty excisable goods i.e. commercial plywood in this case, used for the manufacture of decorative plywood for export purpose. The excisable goods therefore received by the decorative plywood manufacturer were also required to be kept in terms of this notification in a separate room. A procedure is also prescribed under this notification for disposal of the waste arising during the manufacture either on payment of duty or for recycling in the same factory. This notification also has a provision for allowing the manufacturer of the finished goods who has manufactured under bond under Rule 191B for clearance for home consumption on payment of excise duty leviable by them on such article as also on the excisable goods used in the manufacture thereof in the same manner as excisable goods intended for home consumption are cleared from the place of their production or manufacture or storage. It is thus seen that Rule 191B is a very comprehensive procedure under which finished goods manufactured out of non-duty paid goods have to be properly accounted for and in the event of the goods not being exported the levy of duty is provided both in respect of the finished goods manufactured in bond as also the inputs contained thereunder which was received without payment of duty. In view of this procedure prescribed under Rule 191B the question that has to be considered is whether goods cleared by the appellants under Rule 191B free of duty to the other unit which manufactured decorative plywood for export purposes could be taken to be export for Modvat purposes in terms of Rule 57F (3). We observe that Rule 57F (3) during the relevant period i.e. 1-3-1993 to 31-7-1993 providing for the manner in which the credit taken in respect of the inputs could be utilised read as under :

2. Modvat credit allowed on Acetylene gas as it is not a tool. It is used in an essential process in the manufacture of the final product. Unless Oxygen is mixed with it, it cannot perform function of metal cutting. It can be construed as consumable for operation of the torch to produce high flame. "Since the process of removal of unwanted material from the castings is an essential process to the completion of the manufacture of final product, namely casting, we hold that acetylene gas has been used in relation to the manufacture of the final product. ... acetylene gas by itself cannot be said to perform the function of metal cutting, unless ...oxygen gas also gets mixed. ...Admittedly acetylene gas is stored in a cylinder from which the gas is drawn and passes through the torch and in that process it gets consumed. ...At the most, they can be construed as a consumable gas for operation of the fool...therefore,...Modvat credit is required to be extended in respect of acetylene gas."

3. Binders (Foundry Chemicals) are not eligible for Modvat credit as they are used in the preparation of sand moulds which are essential for the manufacture of castings and cannot be considered to have come into existence during the coarse of manufacture of the final product. "...we are convinced that the sand moulds are in the nature of equipment or apparatus used for the purpose of castings...they are produced independently and used for castings ...moulds cannot be considered to have come into existence during the course of manufacture of the final product. Hence the benefit of Rule 57P cannot also be extended. We, therefore, hold that binders and foundry chemicals are not eligible for Modvat credit."

4. Modvat credit not allowed on Sleeves, Graphite, Stopper head as these are used either in the mould or ladles which have also been denied Modvat credit. "...from the...nature of the inputs, we observe that ...they are used either in the mould or the ladle. We have held that moulds and ladles come under the category of equipment or apparatus. These sleeves and stopper heads could at the most be construed as fittings in those equipments, for a specific purpose required to be replaced after each heat. In this view of the matter, we hold that Modvat benefit is not admissible with regard to these two inputs."

5. Flourspar--is eligible for Modvat benefit as it is used directly in the manufacturing process in removing impurities. "The 'function of the flour spar is to remove impurities. ...flourspar is fed into the furnace after the scrap is melted.........In view of the aforesaid position, this item of input goes directly in the manufacturing process and cannot be denied Modvat benefit."

No. 95/79-CE does not contain a clause to the effect that proforma credit on inputs should be correlated to the duty payable on outputs, non-payment of duty on finished goods does not make the manufacturer ineligible to proforma credit. "Read by itself this notification does not have any condition that there should be any nexus between the inputs and outputs.... The Ld. JDR's argument that goods mentioned in column 5 (final products) are only those which pay duty is not supported by the wordings of the notification. No condition regarding payment of duty is contained any where in the notification. We are further supported in this view by a judgment of the Cegat (SRB) (CCE Bangalore v. Wipro Information Technology, Bangalore) reported in 1988(14) ECR 490 wherein it was held that proforma credit once allowed cannot be recovered subsequently even if finished goods are exempted later on, making proforma credit ineligible, since no interlinking account is provided for in rule."

Minority view:--Interpretation--as per proviso 2 of the Notfn. availability of proforma credit on inputs is directly proportional to the duty payable on the finished product and since tyres were cleared without payment of duty, set off cannot be allowed on the inputs used in the manufacture of tyres. No. 95/79-CE ".....the extent of the credit that could be taken in respect of the duty paid on the inputs shall be restricted to the duty payable on the end product if it happens to be less than the credit of duty taken on the inputs. On second appeal:

NC Sanding Sealer: Whether it fall within Sr. No. 174 of the list of industrial inputs under the Punjab Value Added Tax Act, 2005?

NC sanding Sealer is chemical filler. It smoothens the surface of wood. It is used for covering grains of wood and is used by both, domestic as well as industrial users. Entry 174 of industrial inputs in Schedule to the Punjab Value Added Tax Act, 2005 reads "Cellulose and its chemical derivatives, and cellulose others, not elsewhere specified or included in primary forms".

NC Sanding sealer is not covered under this entry, nor does this product fall in the category of industrial inputs. Since it is not covered in any of the entries of Schedules appended to the PVAT Act, it is exigible to VAT@12.5%. 8.6-5 Refund of input tax credit if goods were procured on payment of 0.1% GST or without GST under Adjudicating Authority or DFIA

Rule 89(4B) of CGST Rules amended w.e.f. 9-10-2018 states as follows.

Where the person claiming refund of unutilised input tax credit on account of zero rated supplies without payment of tax has -

(a) received supplies on which the supplier has availed the benefit of the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, notification No. 40/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated the 23rd October, 2017, published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Section 3, Sub-section (i), vide number G.S.R 1320(E), dated the 23rd October, 2017 (supply to merchant exporter on payment of 0.05% of SGST plus 0.05% of CGST) or notification No. 41/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate), dated the 23rd October, 2017, published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Section 3, Sub-section (i), vide number G.S.R 1321(E), dated the 23rd October, 2017(supply to merchant exporter on payment of 0.1% of IGST); or

(b)

availed the benefit of notification No. 78/2017-Customs, dated the 13th October, 2017, published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, section 3, sub-section (i), vide number G.S.R 1272(E), dated the 13th October, 2017 (Exempting goods imported by EOU from basic customs duty and IGST upto 31-3-2021) or notification No. 79/2017-Customs, dated the 13th October, 2017, published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, section 3, sub-section (i), vide number G.S.R 1299(E), dated the 13th October, 2017(Exempting goods imported under Advance Authorisation, DFIA or EPCG Authorisation from IGST upto 31-3-2021),

The refund of input tax credit, availed in respect of inputs received under the said notifications for export of goods and the input tax credit availed in respect of other inputs or input services to the extent used in making such export of goods, shall be granted [rule 89(4B) of CGST Rules as amended w.e.f. 9-10-2018].

Rule 89(4B) as existing upto 9-10-2018 - In the case of supplies received on which the supplier has availed the benefit of notification No. 40/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 23rd October, 2017 (supply to merchant exporter on payment of 0.05% of SGST plus 0.05% of CGST) or notification No. 41/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate) (supply to merchant exporter on payment of 0.1% of IGST) or dated 23rd October, 2017 or notification No. 78/2017-Customs dated the 13th October, 2017 (Exempting goods imported by EOU from basic customs duty and IGST upto 31-3-2019) or notification No. 79/2017-Customs dated the 13th October, 2017 (Exempting goods imported under Advance Authorisation, DFIA or EPCG Authorisation from IGST upto 31-3-2020), or all of them, refund of input tax credit, availed in respect of inputs received under the said notifications for export of goods and the input tax credit availed in respect of other inputs or input services to the extent used in making such export of goods, shall be granted - Rule 89(4B) of CGST Rules inserted on 23-1-2018 but with retrospective effect from 23-10-2017.

The supplier can import capital goods without payment of customs duty and IGST - The aforesaid restriction is not applicable to supplier who has imported capital goods under these provisions. Thus, even if supplier of goods to exporter had imported capital goods without payment of customs duty or IGST under EPCG scheme and used them to manufacturer goods supplied to exporter, the exporter can pay IGST on his goods exported and claim refund - CBI&C circular No. 45/19/2018-GST dated 30-5-2018].

Modvat - Phospheric acid added to cane juice to make up deficiency of phosphate is an input for quality sugar--Eligible. CE Rule 57A. "Modvat scheme does not restrict input duty relief only to essential raw materials or components. It is available to any item used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. The only restriction is that it is not to be an item of machinery/tool, appliance etc. Here the undisputed fact is that phosphoric acid is required to be added, where-ever P. 205 content is low in the cane juice for achieving whiteness of sugar. Hence, it is an input needed in the manufacture of the desired quality sugar......It is a chemical added to the product mix for achieving proper clarification of cane juice. Hence it goes as an input for the clarification of cane juice. Hence we cannot appreciate the stand taken by the Collector (Appeals) that the phosphoric acid is a tool or appliance. We also carefully considered the Boards' clarification......in a case where the cane juice does not have the desired level of P. 205 content and on account of that phosphoric acid is necessarily to be added for purpose of clarification, it cannot be dismissed as not an input.....Viewed in this context, the addition of phosphoric acid is a necessity and hence we could not agree with the clarification given by the Board."

"It is observed that the learned Collector (Appeals), while taking note of this has also taken note of the fact that in the same notification issued by the Govt. of India it has also been stated that no such credit shall be allowed if such inputs are clearly recognisable as being non-duty paid or charged to nil rate of duty or wholly exempt from duty. The learned Collector (Appeals) in his order has observed that since the Aluminium castings in respect of which input credit has been claimed were received without payment of duty, in view of the proviso to the Notification in F. No. 822/5/86-TRU dated 7.4.1986 the appellants were not eligible for the benefit of the input credit as claimed..........In the MODVAT Scheme since the benefit of credit is sought to be given for that quantum of duty which has been paid towards the goods or which is otherwise directed to be given in terms of the Rules, it has to be held the term "non-duty paid" refers to the goods where numerically no duty has been paid. As it is under Rule 57C no credit of duty is to be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of excise duty leviable thereon or if chargeable to Nil rate of duty. Thus if the inputs are used for the exempted goods, the inputs are not eligible for the benefit of MODVAT credit and the question of carrying forward the duty paid on the inputs, which resulted in the production of the exempted goods and which in turn are used in the manufacture of specified finished product, cannot arise."

Therefore, in 1986, the materials falling under Chapter XVII were not specified as input and they were therefore clearly outside the purview of MODVAT Scheme, ft was only in 1987 by virtue of Notification 83/87 dated 1.3.1987 materials like Lactose became eligible by being specified in the Notification as input for the purpose of MODVAT,.......in terms of Rule 57G they are eligible to take credit only from the date of obtaining the acknowledgement of the declaration and not prior to that date.....The contention that since they had already included the material in their declaration filed in 1986, and that therefore, they were eligible to take credit without any further declaration in 1987, does not have much force."

REVERSAL OF MODVAT CREDIT TAKEN ON INPUTS UNDER RULE 57CC

Kind attention is invited to the provisions of Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules for reversal of Modvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods or goods chargeable to 'nil' rate of excise duty. The provision has been made that where a manufacturer uses inputs which are common to both dutiable goods as well as exempted goods, the manufacturer is required to debit the amount equal to 8% of the value of the exempted goods when they are cleared from the factory.

2. In some cases, the exempted goods cleared by one manufacturer are used as inputs by another manufacturer. The manufacturer of exempted goods indicates the amount of Modvat credit reversed on the invoices issued by him for such exempted goods. In this context, some doubts have been raised whether the amount of Modvat credit so reversed is available as Modvat credit to the user of such exempted goods when he uses them as inputs in his factory.

3. In this context, it is clarified that the amount reversed is not by way of payment of excise duty. Accordingly, the amount of Modvat credit reversed and shown in the invoice by the manufacturer of exempted goods cannot be taken as credit by the user of exempted goods.

1. Modvat--Cleaning and degreasing have to be done on job pieces (wheels) before operations like electroplating, phosphating etc. are carried out. Materials required for cleaning and degreasing are therefore inputs used in or in relation to manufacture of the finished product and, as such, eligible for Modvat credit "In the present case the appellants have pleaded that cleaning and degreasing have to be done on the job pieces before operations like electroplating, phosphating, etc. are carried out. The use of these materials, therefore, in the absence of any rebuttal has to be accepted to be there. Such use has to be held in or in relation to the manufacture of the finished product in the context of the manufacturing process of the appellants. We, therefore, hold that the learned lower authority's orders denying the appellants the benefit of Modvat credit in respect of cleaning and degreasing chemicals is not maintainable in law."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Cenvat Credit - Modvat - EOUs--Credit not admissible for goods cleared to EOUs free of duty

FACT: Appellants manufacture Pumpable Slurry Explosives (PSE) and supply the same free of duty to a 100% Export Oriented Unit (EOU). The appellants want to be allowed to accumulate Modvat credit on inputs of PSE for utilisation later as and when they start clearing the goods on payment of duty.

HELD: Modvat--credit is not admissible as no duty leviable on the final product (PSE) cleared by the appellants. "A reading of the various Central Excise Rules and the Scheme of the MODVAT set out therein shows that the facility of MODVAT Credit is available in respect of duty paid on inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the specified final product and for utilizing the credit so allowed towards payment of duty of excise leviable on the final product. When, therefore, there is no duty leviable on the final products which have been cleared from the appellants' factory, the question of allowing them the MODVAT Credit on the inputs would not arise. Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules clearly envisages that no credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nit rate of duty. ...In view of above, we hold that there is no force in the appellants' plea......."

It was impossible to obtain the mother liquor or the resultant phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’ without the use of HCl. As long as HCl is used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, the applicability of provisions of rule 57CC cannot be ruled out. [Para 12] The appellant’s reference to the provisions of rule 57D in support of their contention that Modvat credit was not to be denied if a part of the same was contained in the by-product, was indicative of the legislative intent that reversal of 8 per cent amount of the value of the by-product in terms of provisions of rule 57CC would not apply. The expression ‘by-product’ occurring in rule 57D has to be examined and interpreted in the context of the said rule, which uses the other expression ‘waste’ or ‘refuse’, etc. It is in this scenario that the rule provides for non-reversal of Modvat credit, even if waste, refuse or by-product has emerged during the course of manufacture. The effect of the said rule would be that if waste product, which may not be excisable, e.g. , floor sweepings during the course of manufacture of biscuits, then the quantum of credit originally taken is not to be varied. Similarly, if iron and steel scrap arises during manufacture of iron products, the Modvat is not to be varied, but iron and scrap being excisable products, [the manufacturers] have to discharge duty burden. If the same are exempted, provisions of rule 57CC will apply. As such, it is to be concluded that rule 57D refers to waste scrap and by-product, which are not excisable at all. The said provision cannot be pressed into service in support of the plea that even if the by-product is excisable, but exempted, amount of 8 per cent is not required to be paid. The appellant was not being directed to reverse the credit amount equivalent to the inputs contained in the said exempted final products. Further, taking an hypothetical example of electrolysis of water, which an assessee may undertake to obtain oxygen, he cannot take the plea that hydrogen which also emerges during such electrolysis is an unintended product and even if the same is being sold as an exempted product, the same should be treated as a by-product and rule 57CC would not apply. [Para 13]

The issue in the instant case was not relatable to reversal of the credit originally taken by the appellant on the ground of emergence of any by-product. The issue was a straight and simple interpretation of rule 57CC, which as already held does not make any distinction between exempt final product or exempt by-product. As long as the excisable product cleared from an assessee’s factory enjoys exemption or attracts nil rate of duty, provisions of rule 57CC will come into play. The straight answer to the above question lies in the literal interpretation of the language employed in the said rule without straining to find out the legislative intent, especially when the language used is unambiguous. As already observed, the provisions of rule 57CC or rule 6 envisage common use of inputs in two final products, i.e., one dutiable and other exempted, for the applicability of the same. As such, as long as two final products emerging out of use of common inputs are excisable and one of them is exempted, the provisions of rule 57CC will apply. The exempted final product may be intended manufacture or unintended by-product. [Para 14]

2.1. Consequences of not computing total income as per Section 115BAA

The Ordinance provided an option to the domestic companies to pay tax at lower rates by opting for section 115BAA regime provided its total income is computed without claiming additional depreciation, prescribed allowancesand deductions. Further, while computing the taxable income, no loss or unabsorbed depreciation shall be allowed to set-off if such loss or unabsorbed depreciation is attributable to any of the prescribed deduction or allowance.

The Ordinance did not contain any provisions as to the consequences for subsequently not fulfilling any of the prescribed conditions. Thus, to remove the ambiguity, the Amendment Bill proposes that if a company, after opting for Section 115BAA, claims any of prescribed deduction or allowance in any previous year, then the option to pay tax at concessional rate shall become invalid for that year and for all subsequent assessment years.

2.2. Application of section 115BAA in case of amalgamation

It has been proposed in the Bill that in case of amalgamation, the successor co. shall not be allowed to set-off any loss or depreciation if such loss or depreciation is attributable to prohibited deduction or allowances as discussed earlier.

2.3. Allowability of deduction under section 80LA

One of the condition for opting for section 115BAA is that a domestic company shall not be allowed to claim any of the deduction as specified under Part-C of Chapter VI-A except deduction under section 80JJAA. In order to provide relief to the companies having a unit in the International Financial Services Centres (IFSCs), it has been proposed that deduction under 80LA shall be available even if such units opted for section 115BAA.

2.4. Adjustment of unabsorbed depreciation attributable to additional deprecation from block of asset

As companies opting for section 115BAA are not eligible to set-off the unabsorbed depreciation attributable to additional depreciation, a proviso has been proposed to be inserted in Section 115BAA(3) to clarify that if any unabsorbed depreciation, relating to additional depreciation, has not been given full effect, corresponding adjustment shall be made to WDV of the block of assets in prescribed manner. The CBDT may notify the mechanism for adjustment of unabsorbed depreciation (relating to additional depreciation) in situations relating to amalgamation, demerger, slump sale, etc.

HEADNOTE: Rule 56A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Proforma Credit - Inputs relief - proforma credit admissible even if end products (tyres) are exempts: U/Notfn. 95/79-CE, since no correlation is required. CE NOTFN. 95/79-CE

FACT: The issue is whether proforma credit can be availed of by the manufacturers in terms of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE on inputs even if the end product (tyres) listed is liable to nil rate of duly.

HELD: Set off Since Notfn. No. 95/79-CE does not contain a clause to the effect that proforma credit on inputs should be correlated to the duty payable on outputs, non-payment of duty on finished goods does not make the manufacturer ineligible to proforma credit. "Read by itself this notification does not have any condition that there should be any nexus between the inputs and outputs.... The Ld. JDR's argument that goods mentioned in column 5 (final products) are only those which pay duty is not supported by the wordings of the notification. No condition regarding payment of duty is contained any where in the notification. We are further supported in this view by a judgment of the Cegat (SRB) (CCE Bangalore v. Wipro Information Technology, Bangalore) reported in 1988(14) ECR 490 wherein it was held that proforma credit once allowed cannot be recovered subsequently even if finished goods are exempted later on, making proforma credit ineligible, since no interlinking account is provided for in rule."

Minority view:--Interpretation--as per proviso 2 of the Notfn. availability of proforma credit on inputs is directly proportional to the duty payable on the finished product and since tyres were cleared without payment of duty, set off cannot be allowed on the inputs used in the manufacture of tyres. Proviso 2 of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE ".....the extent of the credit that could be taken in respect of the duty paid on the inputs shall be restricted to the duty payable on the end product if it happens to be less than the credit of duty taken on the inputs. What follows from this therefore, is that if the duty payable on the end product is nil, then the extent of exemption that will be available will also be nil........In as much as, no duty in respect of these tyres has been paid, in terms of proviso 2 to the notification, the availability of the credit on the inputs in respect of these tyres will have therefore, to be nil."

Modvat--Benefit cannot be extended as the acid is not used for bringing into existence the final product, but to take care of environmental hazards created by the effluents. "The Notification envisages the benefit only if it is established that the use of the input is in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. Legally, going by the words of the Notification what it states is that the use should be such that it can be related to the emergence of the final end-product. In the present case the use of the acid is not for bringing into existence the final product but for taking care of the hazards involved by way of generation of effluents as a result of the process of manufacture of the final product. We observe that the treatment of effluent has to be taken to be a separate process where a totally different chemistry is involved."

2. Modvat--Input--Processes which are indispensible to the emergence of the end-product are to be held as used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. "With a view to draw line as to what constitutes the input in or in relation to the manufacture of a product, it can be safely held that the process which are indispensible to the emergence of the final product and which are inextricably linked up with the production stream of the end-product up to the stage of its emergence and the inputs which are so used in those processes without which the end-product may be difficult to be manufactured have to be held as used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. Inputs which are used after the emergence of the final product and which may be required to be used in the process at the post manufacturing stage of the end-product will have to be considered as a separate process for a different purpose."

Modvat - Inputs--Molybdenum sheets and Tungsten Nozzles are not inputs.--Molybdenum sheets act as electrodes to conduct electricity to generate heat, have a long life, and are thus a part of the furnace. Similarly, Tungsten nozzles are in the nature of a die or a tool/used for processing the materials--Credit inadmissible. CE Rule 57A. "In the present case the electrodes conduct the electricity to generate the heat. These stand on a different footing. The electrodes have a very long life and can be taken to be only as a part of the furnace rather than as an input used as an in-process material. ........ In view of the above we hold that so far as Molybdenum plates are concerned, the same are not eligible for the benefit of the Modvat Credit in regard to Tungsten nozzles we hold these help in giving shape to the end-product and have to be held to be an item in the nature of a die or a tool used for processing the materials. Since tools, etc. are ineligible for the benefit of the Modvat Credit in terms of the definition of 'input' under Rule 57A, we hold that the benefit of Modvat Credit will not be available in respect of the same."

Total set-off of duty paid on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre must be allowed even if some part of it is contained in the methanol which is a by-product of the chemical reaction during manufacture. Since the formation of methanol cannot be prevented by using less ethylene glycol, it is obvious that the final product is polyester fibre, not methanol. ".....it is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ......ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre. It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. It is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol from arising for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre. Thus, the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. It may be mentioned herein that it is not as if the appellants have used excess ethylene glycol wantonly to produce the methanol. It is clear that the appellants are not engaged in the production of methanol but in the production of polyester fibre. That position is undisputed. Therefore, it appears that the Tribunal erred when it held that the appellants were not entitled to a part of the credit of duty since ethylene glycol when it interacts with DMT also gives rise to methanol."

2. Set-off of duty paid on inputs can only be denied if the final product is totally exempt from duty. So credit of duty cannot be denied on non-excisable methanol which arose during the manufacture of dutiable polyester fibre. "....the only situation where the credit of the duty paid on the inputs could be denied was only where the final products were wholly exempt from the duty of excise or chargeable to nil rate of duty. In the present case, the excisable goods, namely, polyester fibre were not wholly exempt from duty nor chargeable to nil rate of duty. It cannot be read in the notification that the notification would not be available in case non-excisable good arise during the course of manufacture. In fact, the Tribunal seems to have erred in not bearing in mind that exemption notification was pressed in service in respect of polyester fibre which is excisable goods and not in respect of methanol which arises as a by-product as a part and parcel of chemical reaction."

3. Trade notice clarifying rule 56A must be considered in interpreting exemption Notfn. 201/79-CE since it is applicable to both. "On an analysis and comparison of aforesaid, it is clear that the clarification in the form of trade notice issued by the Pune Collect prate in respect of rule 56A was as much applicable to that rule as to notification No. 201/79. .....exemption notifications are meant to be implemented and trade notices in these matters clarify the stand of the Government for the trade. Admittedly, the scrubber liquor is to be added to adjust viscosity of the sodium silicate. Such addition was in the factory of the assessee and before sale of sodium silicate. Modvat Rules allow ‘Credit of any duty of excise paid on the goods used in the manufacture on said final products" (Rules 57A). Rule 57B further clarifies that "Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 57A, the manufacturer of final products shall be allowed to take credit of the specified duty paid... on inputs used in or relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not". It was not reasonable to argue that materials used for maintaining viscosity at the required level were not used in relation to manufacture, particularly, when the viscosity control was by the manufacturer before the sale of goods. It is also to be noted that Modvat follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not. Correctness of payment is not relevant; only the fact of payment is. A view to the contrary also goes against the broad definition of ‘manufacture’ in section 2 of the Central Excise Act in a manner as to include "any process - incidental or ancillary to the completion of manufacture". Thus, a finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to the given factual situation and relevant legal provisions. Hence, the assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit as claimed. Such price would have various components including Cost, Duties, Taxes, profits etc. The price is lump sum or composite price and cannot be divided into its components.

In CCE v. IPF Vikram India 2002(150) ELT 175 (CEGAT), it was held that Cenvat on inputs (now ITC) which have gone in waste is not deniable - Departmental appeal dismissed by SC on merits - 2003 (153) ELT A303.

Loss of input by evaporation during manufacturing processing is to be treated as ware or loss and Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such loss is not required to be reversed - CCE v. BOC (India) (2008) 223 ELT 33 (Guj HC DB).

Chlorine gas left in cylinder after use of gas in processing can be termed as 'process loss' and its Cenvat credit (now ITC) is available - CCE v. Andhra Paper Mill (2011) 269 ELT 79 (AP HC DB).

Even excess process loss is allowable if any evidence of clandestine removal is not available - Rollex Electro Products v. CCE (2016) 338 ELT 736 (CESTAT).

Loss of inputs during handling eligible - In or in relation to the manufacture covers the entire manufacturing process starting from initial stage of handling of inputs. Thus, if wastage of input at the initial handling from tank discharge due to various reasons like spillage, pipeline losses, handling losses etc., it is 'in or in relation to manufacture' and Cenvat (now ITC) cannot be denied. Deduction in case of business of waste collection and Processing [Section 80JJA]

6.9 Section 80JJA, effective assessment year 1999-2000 permits deduction :

◆ to any assessee from the profits of a business of waste collection and processing (as detailed therein); and

◆ to the extent of the lower of the income or Rs. 5 lacs.

The provision has been amended effective assessment year 2000-01 to the following effect :

(a) the scope of business is enlarged so as to include production of :

◆ bio-fertilizers;

◆ bio-pesticides; or

◆ other biological agents; and

(b) the extent of deduction is enlarged to the whole of profits without any ceiling as existed earlier, but, it is restricted to a period of five consecutive assessment years beginning from the year of commencement of business.

Accordingly, an assessee who has commenced the business in the previous year 1998-99, the effect would be :

◆ In assessment year 1999-2000, he would be entitled to a deduction of the lower of the profit from such business or Rs. 5 lacs.

◆ From assessment year 2000-2001, he would get deduction of the whole of the amount; and

◆ The period of five years would start from assessment year 1999-2000.

Pet Preform

The item in question, i.e., "pet preform", is moulded in such a way as to give it shape of containers of different sizes and styles. As the air is blown through it, it forms the shape of a container. Pet preforms cannot be used for any other purpose besides being used as a container. The fact that moulding is done to bring it in the shape does not take it away from the domain of plastic packing material. The fact that it is moulded into plastic containers would not take it outside the purview of the category of the materials intended for being used for the packing of plastic goods for sale. The process of moulding pet preform was required for putting it in shape with a view to adapt it for actual user. The process only facilitates the actual user for packing. Viewed from these aspects, the imposition of tax at 12.5 per cent is not justified. Being an item coming well under the purview of S1. No. 155 of Part III of Schedule C, tax is to be charged at four per cent. [Epitome Petrochemical Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, West Bengal and others, (2011) 41 VST 22; (2011) 58 S.T.A. 95, decided on 4.3.2011, by the Division Bench of West Bengal Taxation Tribunal; J.N.R.T. Commercial (P) Limited another v. Commissioner of Sales Tax, West Bengal Others, (2011) 58 S.T.A. 237, decided on 4.3.2011 by the Division Bench of West Bengal Taxation Tribunal]

In respect of the contention that in the Subsequent Guidance Note, the ICAI once again discussed the above two methods and, in the circumstances, the net method followed by the assessee was wrong because the assessee had followed the net method without making any adjustments as required under section 145A, it might be pointed out that section 145A was introduced by the Finance (No. 2) Bill 1998. Originally, the Bill contemplated the proposed amendment to apply from 1-4-1986 in relation to the assessment year 1986-87 and subsequent years. However, later on, when the said Bill was enacted into law, the provision was made applicable from 1-4-1999, i.e., assessment year 1999-2000. In this appeal, the assessment year involved was 1989-90. The Legislature clearly intended that the computation made by the assessee prior to the assessment year 1999-2000 should not be disturbed and, therefore, the Legislature had brought the said section 145A into force only from 1-4-1999. Accordingly, the appeal was to be dismissed.

The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

In this background, on 1-11-1997, a show cause notice was issued to the Appellant/Assessee raising a demand in the sum for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 2-5-1997, along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent to be calculated on the said amount for the period commencing from 12-8-1997 and ending on the date of payment. Furthermore, via the very SCN, a proposal was also made for imposing penalty.

In the reply, the assessee took stand that, for the period falling between 3-5-1997 and 19-6-1997, it had already 'expunged' MODVAT credit, in consonance with Notification No. 14/97 CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. In so far as the demand for interest was concerned, it was stated that it was premature, as under section 87(2)(c) of the Finance Act, interest would be payable, only, if, the amount demanded was not paid within ninety (90) days of the enactment of the Bill.

The stand, which, the Appellant /Assessee appeared to have taken with respect to penalty was that the alleged infraction was not an offence prior to the enactment of the Finance Act.

The Adjudicating authority sustained the demand in sum, equivalent to the excess credit availed of by the Appellant/Assessee for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 to 3-5-1997. Furthermore, the Appellant/Assessee was directed to pay interest at the rate of 18 per cent.

The Commissioner (Appeals), allowed the appeal of the Appellant/Assessee, albeit, partially. While the Commissioner (Appeals), confirmed the demand of duty for the period 23-7-1996 to 28-2-1997, along with interest, he set aside the demand of duty for the period spanning between 1-3-1997 and 3-5-1997.

The appellant-assessee, a private limited company engaged in manufacture and export of perfumery compounds and essential oils, had set up a 100% EOU at Nilakottai in FY 2002-03. For AY 2009-10, it claimed deduction under Section 10B on the EOU's profits of about Rs. 2.32 crores. It filed a return declaring income of about Rs. 7.13 lakhs, which was assessed at about Rs. 3.79 crores.

■

The AO disallowed the claim under Section 10B(7) read with Sections 80-IA(8) and 80-IA(10), alleging that profits were inflated through non-market factors. The AO recorded substantial purchases from related/group entities without establishing market value, large interest-free funding from partners/group entities without arm’s length interest, an abnormally high gross profit of about Rs. 2.33 crores on sales of about Rs. 5.84 crores, and no clear correlation between inputs and outputs, characterizing the activity as mere processing rather than manufacturing. On these bases, the AO concluded that the course of business was arranged to produce more than ordinary profits and denied the full deduction under Section 10B.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) partly allowed relief. It noted that the AO had not substantiated allegations regarding non-market purchases or related-party pricing, observed that interest-free loans may still attract Section 80-IA(10) if they lead to excess profits, held that invocation of Section 80-IA(10) was proper but that reasonable/ordinary profits must be determined using comparables, benchmarked the assessee against its sister concern Pragati Aroma Oil Distillers Pvt. Ltd. (engaged in the same activity), and restricted the Section 10B deduction to 19.06% of sales (the sister concern’s net profit rate), taxing the balance at normal rates.

■

On further appeal, the ITAT recorded that the AO’s conclusions based on low manufacturing expenses and high margins were largely presumptive and unsupported by proper evidence or comparables, yet noted that the assessee and the sister concern operated in the same line of business under common management and that the assessee had disclosed higher profits. The ITAT upheld the CIT(A)’s approach of using the sister concern as a benchmark and sustained the restriction of the eligible profits to about 19% for the purpose of Section 10B.

VAT/CST - BOOK SALE AND RETENTION OF GOODS BY SELF FOR USE ON BEHALF OF OTHER PERSON - WHETHER LEVIABLE TO DUTY/TAX ?

4. A Plastic moulding company has developed a Mould for us and we have paid them for such mould. The mould will be used by the said company on our behalf for manufacture and supply of plastic parts exclusively for us. Please advise :

(1)

Since mould has not moved out of factory of the moulding company, would this be transaction of payment by us liable to excise and VAT ?

(2)

What will be treatment if after sometime we take back this mould ? Will duty or tax be leviable at that time ? If yes, on what value ?

In our view, the following shall be the consequences —

It is apparent that mould is being made/manufactured to be owned by your company. Hence, when charges for such mould are paid, it will have to be seen whether there is transfer of title of mould. As is apparent, mould becomes your property and accordingly, the same is a sale. Accordingly, the same is liable to excise duty and sales-tax. In our view, though there is no physical removal of goods from the factory of the moulding company; yet, since the title changes, it is a complete sale and would amount to 'removal' inasmuch as property belongs to you and any further use of moulds is only on your behalf. Viewed from another angle, when moulds are used inside the same factory for further manufacture, it amounts to 'captive use' and would be liable to duty in terms of the Explanation to rule 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The moulds must be shown as sold to you and received back on job-work basis under Rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Since both duty and tax stand paid at the time of sale of moulds to you, no further payment of duty or tax is warranted at the time when they are returned.

SERVICE TAX - TWO FOREIGN BRANCHES OF INDIA COMPANIES PROVIDED SERVICE TO EACH OTHER - TAXABILITY

5. A Ltd. and B Ltd. are two Indian companies (located in India). They have Branch X and Branch Y, respectively, outside India. Branch X provides services to Branch Y. Would this service be liable to service tax ? Please answer in light of applicability of rule 8 of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012.

Since Branch X of A Ltd. is located outside India, Branch X and A Ltd. would be deemed to be distinct persons under Explanations 3 and 4 to section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994. Similarly, Branch Y would also be a person separate person from B Ltd.

Since X and Y are separate persons and both are located outside India, Rule 8 of the Place of Provision of Services Rules, 2012 would be inapplicable and furthermore, the service would be exempt under Entry 34(c) of the Notification No. 25/2012-ST.

Plaster of Paris (P.O.P.) – Whether it is same as Gypsum?

Entry 16 of Schedule – A which deals with tax free goods, reads as under:-"fertilizers including bio-fertilizers and organic fertilizers, gypsum, pesticides, weedicides, insecticides and fungicides"

As per the appellant, appellant is importing P.O.P. from outside Punjab and chemistry of P.O.P. and chemistry of gypsum was the same and therefore it fell in Entry 16 of Schedule A and was exempt from payment of tax. However, from bare perusal of Entry 16, it would come out that it relates to the fertilizers, pesticides, weedicides, fungicides relating to land and agriculture. The Gypsum in the entry will also relate to its use in reference to land and crops. Gypsum is stated to loosen soil structure and improve poor soil conditions. It is stated to be used when there is layer of hard soil in the field.

Appellant is dealing in P.O.P. which is used as a building material. It cannot be said to be relating to land or its use and cannot be an item covered in Entry 16 of Schedule A. I, therefore, agree with the order of the Commissioner dated 27.8.2008 where the Commissioner had determined the disputed question saying that P.O.P. was not gypsum covered in Entry 16 and not tax free. [*Prem Enterprises, Jalandhar v. State of Punjab, (2010) 35 PHT 67, decided on 14.9.2009 by Value Added Tax Tribunal, Punjab, Chandigarh]

*Note – The view taken in this case has been endorsed by the Division Bench of Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case reported as Prem Enterprises v. State of Punjab and another, (2013) 59 VST 237 (PH); VSTI 2013 (Delhi, Punjab and Haryana) …B-98; (2013) 44 PHT 62 (PH), decided on 9.1.2103 observing that-

"Though the chemical properties may be similar, but the fact remains that the uses of gypsum and POP are different. Entry 16 of Schedule A exempts fertilizers from tax. The definition is inclusive which includes gypsum as a fertilizer. Entry 16 exempts fertilizers from tax, whereas POP cannot remotely be used as fertilizer. Therefore, POP does not fall within entry 16 of Schedule A."

HEADNOTE: Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - Modvat credit - Inputs - Manufacturer took Modvat credit on polyester fibre used as inputs for manufacture of yarn - Process loss being abnormal, manufacturers were denied credit on certain parts of inputs - Manufacturer contended that process loss was more than normal because of poor quality of input - Further, Board’s Letter, dated 15-1-1988 clarified that credit of duty on input cannot be denied on ground that parts of inputs is contained in wastes and scraps, which may even be exempted from customs duty - Whether in view of this clarification and fact that revenue had not conducted any experiment to determine range of normal loss during processing of goods and further in view of lack of evidence of any malpractice by manufacturer, demand on manufacturer could not be sustained - Held, yes Circulars and Notifications : Board’s Letter, dated 15-1-1988

FACT: The appellants manufactured polyester viscose blended yarn and cotton polyester yarn. They took Cenvat credit on the polyester fibre which was the input. The revenue proceeded against the appellants on ground that in use of polyester in production the normal process loss can be limited only to 2 to 3 per cent. However, the actual loss in case of the appellants was much more. Therefore, the duty was demanded from the appellants on certain quantity of polyester fibres on which Modvat credit was taken. Besides that penalty was also imposed on the appellant. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside order of the original authority.

On appeal :

HELD: Revenue had not conducted any experiment to determine the range of normal loss, while processing the goods. Further in the Board’s Letter, dated 15-1-1988, it was clarified that credit to the duty on inputs cannot be denied on the ground that parts of the inputs is contained in the wastes and scraps, which may even be exempted from Customs duty. [Para 2]

No doubt, the loss of polyester fibre in this case was something more than the normal but the appellant attributes it to the poor quality of the fibre received. There was no evidence of any over malpractice by the respondents. In these circumstances, the order of the Commissioner appeared to be legal. Hence, the revenue’s appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 3]

HEADNOTE: MODVAT follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not Rule 57A, read with rule 57B, of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - CENVAT Credit - One H produced sulphuric acid - During manufacture of sulphuric acid, waste material arises which is called scrubber liquor - Scrubber liquor, though normally a polluting material, can safely substitute for water in case of production of sodium silicate - Assessee, a manufacturer of sodium silicate, entered into an agreement with H for supply of scrubber liquor to assessee on condition that scrubber liquor would be supplied to assessee free, except for central excise duty and sales tax paid by H on scrubber liquor - Assessee availed MODVAT Credit of duty paid by it on scrubber liquor - Adjudicating Authority denied MODVAT Credit on ground that scrubber liquor could not be considered as input - Whether finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to factual situation and relevant legal provisions - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee was eligible for MODVAT Credit as claimed - Held, yes

FACT: One H was producing, sulphuric acid. During the manufacture of the said acid, waste material arises which is called "Scrubber Liquor". The scrubber liquor is polluting and its disposal is expensive. However, it can be used in manufacturing sodium silicate. Water is required to be added to adjust the viscosity of sodium silicate. The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of sodium silicate. The assessee entered into an agreement with H for the supply of scrubber liquor to the assessee. H was paying central excise duty and sales tax on scrubber liquor. It was agreed that the scrubber liquor would be supplied to the assessee free, except for the central excise duty and sales tax. In the invoices, the price (at which duty was calculated) was being shown as rebate. The assessee availed MODVAT Credit of duty paid by it on scrubber liquor. The adjudicating authority denied the MODVAT Credit availed by the assessee on the ground that the scrubber liquor could not be considered as input. On appeal, the appellate authority upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

HELD: Admittedly, the scrubber liquor is to be added to adjust viscosity of the sodium silicate. Such addition was in the factory of the assessee and before sale of sodium silicate. Modvat Rules allow ‘Credit of any duty of excise paid on the goods used in the manufacture on said final products" (Rules 57A). Rule 57B further clarifies that "Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 57A, the manufacturer of final products shall be allowed to take credit of the specified duty paid... on inputs used in or relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not". It was not reasonable to argue that materials used for maintaining viscosity at the required level were not used in relation to manufacture, particularly, when the viscosity control was by the manufacturer before the sale of goods. It is also to be noted that Modvat follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not. Correctness of payment is not relevant; only the fact of payment is. A view to the contrary also goes against the broad definition of ‘manufacture’ in section 2 of the Central Excise Act in a manner as to include "any process - incidental or ancillary to the completion of manufacture". Thus, a finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to the given factual situation and relevant legal provisions. Hence, the assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit as claimed. [Para 9]

The petitioner company was engaged in the manufacture of fertilizers at its factory. These fertilizers were thereafter subsequently sold.

The first respondent was the State of Maharashtra, whereas the respondent Nos.2, 3 and 4 were the Officers and the Authorities exercising powers under the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 ('MVAT'). The respondent No.5, GAIL had been impleaded as a respondent simply because the petitioner stated that for the purposes of manufacture of fertilizers, the petitioner purchased natural gas from respondent No.5. This was an intra-state purchase. The purchase was under various gas purchase agreements. The purchase in natural gas was either utilized as fuel or as an input in the manufacture/processing of fertilizers/chemicals.

With effect from 01-07-2017, the GST regime had been implemented in India. As a matter of policy, the Central and the various State Governments chose to leave petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and alcoholic liquor for human consumption outside GST regime and continue to levy VAT/Central Sales Tax on the said commodities.

Various amendments were made to the MVAT Act vide Maharashtra Act No.XLII of 2017 to make the MVAT compatible with the GST regime. In and amongst the said amendments, was the insertion of section 16(6A) into the MVAT Act which provided that any person who was not involved in the sale of the six commodities, i.e., petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and alcoholic liquor for human consumption would no longer have a valid registration under the MVAT Act. However, the proviso to section 16(6A) provided that any person who was affected by section 16(6A), but wished to continue to do business in the aforementioned six commodities would have to apply to the respondents in the prescribed manner to have the cancellation of his registration revoked.

Prior to 1-7-2017, the sale of natural gas was governed by the residuary Entry of the MVAT Act, namely, Schedule-E and, hence, the applicable rate of tax on 30-6-2017 was 13.5 per cent. Furthermore, the petitioner was eligible to claim set off of the input MVAT paid by it subject to a reduction of 3 per cent on account of the provisions of Rule 53(1) and Rule 53(1A) of the MVAT Rules. In other words, the net effective rate of MVAT on natural gas was only 3 per cent prior to 1-7-2017 if the natural gas was consumed domestically as fuel or as an input for manufacture.

With effect from 1-7-2017, when any person purchased natural gas domestically, the seller would charge and collect full tax from him at the rate of 13.5 per cent. However, since the person was no longer a dealer under the MVAT Act due to section 16(6A), he could not claim set-off or refund of the input MVAT collected from him. Furthermore, he would be liable to pay GST on his outputs at the full rate since the GST Act only provided for adjustment of GST paid and not of VAT paid. Hence, such a person would be taxed at the full rate on his outputs without adjustment of the input tax paid by him. Whilst the effective rate of taxation on natural product prior to 1-7-2017 was 3 per cent, the effective rate after 1-7-2017 rose to 13.5 per cent.

Bharat Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. 1992 taxmann.com 38, assessee was eligible to set off on entire purchase of soya seeds - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]CST  VAT : Madhya Pradesh VAT - Where assessee purchased soya seeds after payment of VAT and consumed same in manufacture of edible oil and by-products de-oiled cake (DOC), sludge, etc. were also produced in manufacturing process, even though DOC was not taxable goods, assessee was entitled to benefit of set off, as provided under sections 14(1)(a), (2) and 26A(7), on entire purchase of soya seeds

FACT: The assessee was in the business of manufacture of edible oil. It purchased soya seeds from the registered dealers after payment of VAT and consumed the same in the manufacture of edible oil. In addition to the edible oil, by-products de-oiled cake (DOC), sludge, etc. were also produced in the course of manufacturing process. The by-product DOC was tax free.

The assessee claimed benefit of set off as provided under sections 14(1)(a),(2) and 26A(7).

The Assessing Authority opined that the assessee used soya seeds in the manufacture of edible oil. The DOC, a by-product, was not taxable. Hence, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of set off as provided under sections 14(1)(a), (2) and 26A(7) on entire purchase of soya seeds. He apportioned the tax liability after deducting the percentage of proportionate manufacture of DOC.

On writ:

HELD: The Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Bharat Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. 1992 taxmann.com 38 has considered the question of set off and applicability of principle of apportionment in the event of raw material purchased by dealer be used in manufacture of taxable goods and a by-product which is not taxable. It has held that a refinery would be entitled to set off to the entire tax paid by it on the purchase of raw material. [Para 11]

From a reading of the judgment of the Supreme Court, it is clear that manufacturer is eligible the benefit of set off on the entire amount of tax paid on purchase of raw material and principle of apportionment could not be invoked. The judgment of the Supreme Court is applicable to the instant case, because the DOC, a by-product, is tax free and another by-product sludge and main product oil are taxable. Hence, the authority cannot apportion the tax liability after deducting the percentage of proportionate manufacture of DOC. [Para 13]

In view of the aforesaid, the assessee was eligible to set off on entire purchase of soya seeds. [Para 19]
