FACT: The appellant-job-workers manufactured ‘Plastic half round rain water system’ using raw material supplied by the manufacturer. The appellants claimed benefit of notification No. 1 of 1993 which was denied because the goods manufactured were bearing brand name of manufacturer. Classification of goods manufactured as well as turnover limitation and valuation of goods were in dispute. The Tribunal held that goods manufactured were classifiable either under heading 39.25.99 or under heading 39.17.00 and remitted the matter back to redetermine the valuation and eligibility of Modvat after denying benefit of Notification as well as plea of limitation. On readjudication the Modvat credit was denied. The Commissioner determined demand and imposed penalty.

On appeal :

HELD: The limitation issue was settled by the earlier order of the Tribunal and it was not open to reopen that issue. However, the question of classification in the instant case was annexed issue. The imposition of penalty, therefore, was not called for. There was no cause for imposition of penalty in these appeals. More so when, section 11AC penalty for certain period, in this case could not be invoked, being period earlier to introduction of that section. As regards the plea made on interest under section 11AB, the application of Board Instruction No. 655/46/2002-CX, dated 26-6-2002 would govern and be applicable in this case to levy interest. The valuation was to be redetermined as per the formula prescribed by the Apex Court in the case of Ujjagar Print. The CA certificate had to be considered to determine the valuation and duty. As regards the plea of Modvat, there was no valid reasons to deny the same as arrived at in the order impugned. Since goods have been supplied by manufacturer to the job-workers, the Modvat credit would have to be granted and thereafter duty demand was to be reverted. [Para 4]

In view of the finding, these appeals were partly allowed after setting aside the penalty as imposed and the matter was remitted back to the Commissioner to re-determine the valuation of goods and quantum of duty and interest. [Para 5]

Therefore, there has to be a fulfilment of the pre-condition, namely, transposition, whether under section 17 or otherwise. Secondly, there ought to be no tax on any sale or purchase of the goods specified in that entry or part thereof. It is only upon such situation that there will be no deduction provided in clause (ii) or clause (iii) of section 8 and which provision deals with resale of the goods. The Lok Sabha passed the Finance Bill 2025 [hereinafter called 'Finance Bill (Lok Sabha)'] on March 25, 2025.While the Finance Bill,as passed by the Lok Sabha, largely retains the proposals made in the Finance Bill, certain noteworthy modifications have been made to the provisions relating to the block assessment, omission of equalisation levy and giving overriding powers to Section 44BBD over Section 115A and Section 44DA.

This article comprehensively analyses the changesmadeto the Finance Bill 2025 as passed by the Lok Sabha, highlighting their implications and the rationale behind these revisions.

1. The equalisation levy is withdrawn

Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 introduced the Equalisation Levy in respect of online advertisement services rendered to a specified person by a non-resident. The Finance Act 2020 expanded the scope of equalisation levy to the e-commerce supply of goods or services to a specified person by an e-commerce operator. However, the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 removed the equalisation levy on e-commerce supplies of goods or services with effect from 01-08-2024.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) amended Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 and the Income-tax Act ('ITA') to withdraw the equalisation levy from 01-04-2025 entirely. The following amendments have been made:

(a)

Amendments have been made to Sections 163 and 165 of the Finance Act 2016 to provide that the no equalisation levy shall apply to any consideration in respect of online advertisement services received or receivable by a non-resident on or after 01-04-2025.

(b)

A sunset date has been inserted in Section 10(50) of ITA to provide that this provision shall not apply from the assessment year 2026-27.

2. A Proviso has been inserted into Section 44BBD(2)

The Finance Bill 2025 proposed the insertion of Section 44BBD, which provides for the computation of income on a presumptive basis for non-residents engaged in the business of providing services or technology for setting up electronics manufacturing facilities in India. Section 44BBD(2) provides that a sum equal to 25% of the aggregate of the specified amounts shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of such business of the non-resident assessee.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) inserted a proviso to Section 44BBD(2), which provides that the provisions of Section 44DA or Section 115A shall not apply in respect of the amounts referred to in this subsection. This proviso will primarily impact the taxability of royalty and fees for technical services (FTS) earned by a non-resident.

The taxability of royalty and FTS depends upon the existence of the permanent establishment (PE) of a non-resident in India. If the PE exists in India and the royalty or FTS is connected to it, the income shall be taxable under the head "Business or Profession" as per Section 44DA. If the PE does not exist, the income shall be taxable under the head of other sources at the rate specified under Section 115A, subject to provisions of DTAA.

The impact of the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) is explained below.

2.1. No disallowance under Section 44DA

Section 44DA deals with the taxability of royalties and FTS connected to the PE in India. The first proviso to Section 44DA disallows the deduction in respect of the following:

(a)

Any expenditure or allowance that is not wholly or exclusively incurred for the business of such PE or fixed place of profession in India; or

(b)

Amount paid by the PE to its head office or to any of its other offices.

As the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 44DA, the above expenditure should not be disallowed if the royalty and FTS connected to the PE in India are taxable on a presumptive basis under Section 44BBD.

2.2. The concessional tax rate of Section 115A shall not be available

The proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 115A when the income is computed under Section 44BBD. Where the income is not computed under Section 44BBD, the tax rate under Section 115A will apply if the income is royalty or FTS. Therefore, the applicable tax rate for a non-resident providing services or technology in India shall be as follows:

(a)

Where the nature is business income, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income computed as per Section 44BBD shall be taxable at the applicable rate.

(b)

The appellant’s reference to the provisions of rule 57D in support of their contention that Modvat credit was not to be denied if a part of the same was contained in the by-product, was indicative of the legislative intent that reversal of 8 per cent amount of the value of the by-product in terms of provisions of rule 57CC would not apply. The expression ‘by-product’ occurring in rule 57D has to be examined and interpreted in the context of the said rule, which uses the other expression ‘waste’ or ‘refuse’, etc. It is in this scenario that the rule provides for non-reversal of Modvat credit, even if waste, refuse or by-product has emerged during the course of manufacture. The effect of the said rule would be that if waste product, which may not be excisable, e.g. , floor sweepings during the course of manufacture of biscuits, then the quantum of credit originally taken is not to be varied. Similarly, if iron and steel scrap arises during manufacture of iron products, the Modvat is not to be varied, but iron and scrap being excisable products, [the manufacturers] have to discharge duty burden. If the same are exempted, provisions of rule 57CC will apply. As such, it is to be concluded that rule 57D refers to waste scrap and by-product, which are not excisable at all. The said provision cannot be pressed into service in support of the plea that even if the by-product is excisable, but exempted, amount of 8 per cent is not required to be paid. The appellant was not being directed to reverse the credit amount equivalent to the inputs contained in the said exempted final products. Further, taking an hypothetical example of electrolysis of water, which an assessee may undertake to obtain oxygen, he cannot take the plea that hydrogen which also emerges during such electrolysis is an unintended product and even if the same is being sold as an exempted product, the same should be treated as a by-product and rule 57CC would not apply. [Para 13]

The issue in the instant case was not relatable to reversal of the credit originally taken by the appellant on the ground of emergence of any by-product. The issue was a straight and simple interpretation of rule 57CC, which as already held does not make any distinction between exempt final product or exempt by-product. As long as the excisable product cleared from an assessee’s factory enjoys exemption or attracts nil rate of duty, provisions of rule 57CC will come into play. The straight answer to the above question lies in the literal interpretation of the language employed in the said rule without straining to find out the legislative intent, especially when the language used is unambiguous. As already observed, the provisions of rule 57CC or rule 6 envisage common use of inputs in two final products, i.e., one dutiable and other exempted, for the applicability of the same. As such, as long as two final products emerging out of use of common inputs are excisable and one of them is exempted, the provisions of rule 57CC will apply. The exempted final product may be intended manufacture or unintended by-product. [Para 14]

However, the proviso to section 16(6A) provided that any person who was affected by section 16(6A), but wished to continue to do business in the aforementioned six commodities would have to apply to the respondents in the prescribed manner to have the cancellation of his registration revoked. Prior to 1-7-2017, the sale of natural gas was governed by the residuary Entry of the MVAT Act, namely, Schedule-E and, hence, the applicable rate of tax on 30-6-2017 was 13.5 per cent. Furthermore, the petitioner was eligible to claim set off of the input MVAT paid by it subject to a reduction of 3 per cent on account of the provisions of Rule 53(1) and Rule 53(1A) of the MVAT Rules. In other words, the net effective rate of MVAT on natural gas was only 3 per cent prior to 1-7-2017 if the natural gas was consumed domestically as fuel or as an input for manufacture.

With effect from 1-7-2017, when any person purchased natural gas domestically, the seller would charge and collect full tax from him at the rate of 13.5 per cent. However, since the person was no longer a dealer under the MVAT Act due to section 16(6A), he could not claim set-off or refund of the input MVAT collected from him. Furthermore, he would be liable to pay GST on his outputs at the full rate since the GST Act only provided for adjustment of GST paid and not of VAT paid. Hence, such a person would be taxed at the full rate on his outputs without adjustment of the input tax paid by him. Whilst the effective rate of taxation on natural product prior to 1-7-2017 was 3 per cent, the effective rate after 1-7-2017 rose to 13.5 per cent.

Realizing the above, the respondents sought to provide relief to the taxpayers. The net effective rate of tax on natural gas prior to 30-6-2017 was 3 per cent. Hence, vide Notification No.VAT1517/ CR136( A)/Taxation1 dated 24-8-2017, with effect from 24-8-2017, Entry 16 was inserted into Schedule-B of the MVAT Act which made provisions for a concessional rate of 3 per cent on the sale of natural gas. In other words, the Notification dated 24-8-2017 sought to maintain quo ante.

The Notification dated 24-8-2017 also provided that for a seller to be eligible to avail the 3 per cent concessional rate, the purchasing dealer must be certified by the Respondents in Proforma-A. The petitioners duly applied and received from the respondents Proforma with effect from 24-8-2017.

However, unfortunately, there existed anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017. While sub-clause (i) of Entry 16 used the phrase 'dealer', the main body of the entry uses the phrase 'registered dealer'. The word 'dealer' continued to be defined under the MVAT Act as a person who is involved in buying or selling goods. Hence, a person who was involved in purchase of natural gas, but not in the sale of natural gas would still be considered as a dealer. However, such a person would not be a 'registered dealer' on account of the provisions of section 16(6A). It was submitted that it was never the intention of the respondents at the time of the enactment of the Notification dated 24-8-2017 to restrict the benefits to only registered dealers. That was clear from the fact that no goods as defined in the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, ('MGST Act') can be manufactured from natural gas as well as the usage of the phrase 'of any other goods whatsoever.'

It was further supported by the issuance of Notification No.VAT-1517/ CR-136 (a)/Taxation 1 dated 13-10-2017 by the respondents. This Notification dated 13.10.2017 sought to cure the anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017 and amended Entry 16 of Schedule B to do so. Explanations (b) and (c) as inserted by the Notification dated 13-10-2017 expanded the scope of terms 'goods' and 'registered dealers' to include goods covered by the MGST Act and persons registered under the MGST Act respectively. This effectively cured the anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017.

Polyset Corporation [2000] 115 ELT 41 (SC) : 3.3-1 Case Study - In this judgment the Supreme Court has ruled that the date of manufacture of goods is relevant for determining whether the goods are excisable and as to the rate of duty that the said goods must bear, what is relevant is the date of their clearance.

3.4 CCE v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 139 ELT 3 (SC) :

3.4-1 Case Study - While considering the eligibility of an exemption notification subject to the payment of appropriate duty on raw materials, the Supreme Court has held that "An exemption notification that uses the said phrase applies to goods which have been made from duty paid material. In the said phrase, due emphasis must be given to the words 'has already been paid'. For the purpose of getting the benefit of the exemption under the notification, the goods must be made from raw materials on which excise duty has, as a matter of fact, been paid, and has been paid at the 'appropriate' or correct rate. Unless the manufacturer has paid the correct amount of excise duty, he is not entitled to the benefit of the exemption notification" (paragraph six of the judgment). In paragraph seven, the Court observed, "Where the raw material is not liable to excise duty or such duty is nil, no excise duty is, as a matter of fact, paid upon it. To goods made out of such material the notification will not apply." Hence, the argument that "Nil rate of duty is also a rate of duty" is on a very fragile ground. A collective reading of the definition under section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, the Supreme Court's decision in Dhiren Chemical Industries (supra) and the decision of the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal in Amaravathi Co-operatives Sugar Mills v. CCE 2013 (291) ELT 126 (Trib. - Chennai) suggests that "the rate of duty being nil, the goods are not excisable goods".

3.5 H.M.M. v. UOI [2005] 192 ELT 63 (Delhi) :

3.5-1 Case Study - Where the Delhi High Court held that the duty being on manufacture and the goods having been exempted at the time of manufacture, the goods must be taken as exempted at the time of clearance, even though the exemption had been withdrawn by then.

The UOI had not been represented by anybody. So, nobody pointed out to the High Court that the issue has already seized to be res integra. That is to say, it had been a settled issue by the judgments in the cases of Wallace Flour Mills and Polyset discussed above.

(a)

One important point related to section 140(3) is that said section does not provide any benefit in respect of eligible duties contained in capital goods held in stock as on the appointed day, as the said section 140(3) uses the word "inputs" which does not includes Capital Goods.

(b) Clause (v) of above sub-section specifies a condition that the supplier of services should not be eligible for any abatement under this Act. Here it is important to know the meaning of word "this Act". Section 1(1) of the CGST Act reads as "This act may be called as the Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017". So, the restriction is only against that abatement which provides under the Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 not in cases where supplier of services are eligible for abatement under other GST Law, i.e., under SGST Act, UTGST Act or IGST Act.

(c)

The proviso to above sub-section also allows to take credit at prescribed rate without having possession of an invoice or any other documents evidencing payment of duty in respect of inputs, subject to fulfillment of certain specified conditions as prescribed. Rule 117(4)(a)(ii) provides that the input tax credit under the said proviso shall be allowed at the rate of 60% on such goods which attract central tax at the rate of 9% or more and 40% for other goods of the central tax applicable on supply of such goods after the appointed date and shall be credited after the central tax payable on such supply has been paid. This rule further provides that where integrated tax is paid on such goods, the amount of credit shall be allowed at the rates of 30% and 20%, respectively, of the said tax. The rule also specifies some conditions, inter alia, the scheme shall be available for six tax periods from the appointed date.

(d)

Using word only "inputs" in the above proviso unlike other sub-section using the word as "inputs held in stock and inputs contained in semi-finished or finished goods held in stock" indicates that the said proviso mainly relates to traders. The definition of 'inputs' covers all types of goods other than capital goods used or intended to be used in the business.

(e)

The aforesaid proviso to section 140(3) specifically excludes in its ambit a manufacturer' or a 'supplier of services'. It means that these are not allowed to take such credit at the prescribed rate even if they have the document for procurement of such goods but have not invoice or any other documents evidencing payment of duty or tax in respect of such inputs.

(f)

There is one condition mentioned in the said proviso regarding passing on of the benefit of such credit by way of reduced prices to the recipient required to be fulfilled to get the benefit of said proviso. It is clear that said condition is not applicable to a 'manufacturer' or a 'supplier of services' as they are specifically excluded from the said proviso and it is also seems justified as they are not getting any benefit of the said proviso. However, the language and words used by the last portion of the said proviso may create some ambiguity to interpret the correct meaning. The last portion of the proviso reads, as "including that the said taxable person shall pass on the benefit of such credit by way of reduced prices to the recipient, be allowed to take credit at such rate and in such manner as may be prescribed." The later part of the proviso and the words used "taxable person" instead of "registered person" in the said part may be interpreted in a different way.

(g)

However, it is a well-settled rule that a proviso is meant to be an exception to something within the main enactment or to qualify something enacted therein but the proviso would be within the purview of the enactment In other words, a proviso cannot be torn apart from the main enactment nor it can be used to nullify the real object of the main enactment.

Excise duty on chassis fitted with engines for such vehicles is also being reduced from 16 per cent plus 10,000 per chassis to 12 per cent plus 10,000 per chassis. Excise duty on battery-powered cars (electric cars) is being reduced from 8 per cent to nil. The battery powered car means a car which runs soley on electrical energy derived from one or more electrical batteries fitted to such car. Excise duty on hybrid motor vehicles is being reduced from 24 per cent to 14 per cent. Excise duty on small cars (motor vehicles of length not exceeding 4000mm and engine capacity not exceeding 1200cc for petrol, LPG and CNG and 1500CC for diesel falling under chapter heading Nos. 8702 and 8703), is being reduced from 16 per cent to 12 per cent. Issues

The sections 115BAA and 115BAB start with a non-obstante clause and overrides the other provisions of the Act. However, the sections are subject to the provisions of Chapter XII.

Owing to manner in which the sections have been introduced in the Act, certain issues have emerged which would need clarification, which are briefly discussed here-in-below:

1. Applicable tax rate on Long-term capital gains, short-term capital gains on listed securities and income under other heads

The sections do not override the provisions of Chapter XII of the Act i.e. provisions contained in the said chapter would hold forte. Hence special rates mentioned in sections 111A, 112, 112A, etc. would continue to apply.

Having regard to the language used in the sections, in our view, companies having income from House Property, Short-term capitals gains (other than on listed securities) and Income from Other Sources viz. bank interest, etc. should be taxed at 17.16%/ 25.168% if the reduced tax rate regime is opted for. A new manufacturing company holding sizeable rent yielding real estate and fixed deposits would stand to benefit (on account of lower tax rate of 17.16%) as compared to any other company having similar sources of income. The tax authorities may however, seek to dispute the adoption of section 115BAB by such companies by contending that the intention is not to extend benefit of lower taxes to non-business income.

2. Whether past MAT credit would be allowed

Sub-section 5A of section 115JB has been amended stating that provisions of section 115JB would not apply to companies which have exercised option to be governed by the aforesaid regime. It may be noted that no amendment has been made in section 115JAA of the Act which deals with utilization of MAT credit on account of MAT paid in earlier years. A plain reading of the provisions, in our view, suggest that past MAT credit available to an existing company should be allowed as a set-off against the tax liability under section 115BAA. There is no express prohibition in section 115BAA to deny MAT credit unlike several other deductions and losses specifically mentioned.

In our view, the MAT credit to be allowed in a year should be limited to the difference between the tax liability under section 115BAA and that under section 115JB which would have been payable. The fact that provisions of section 115JB are not applicable should not impact the computation of the credit which is separately provided in section 115JAA(5) and is an independent exercise for the purpose of determining and granting MAT credit only.

However, considering that the section seeks to override all the provisions of the Act, there may be litigation on the issue.

3. Applicability of interest under section 234B, 234C, etc.

The new sections start as under:

"(1) notwithstanding anything contained in this Act……"

On account of the non-obstante clause in the sections which overrides the other provisions of the Act, there could be an argument that interest under section 234B and 234C cannot be levied.

Section 115JB of the Act has similar non-obstante clause but also has a sub-section (5) which states as under:

Special provision for payment of tax by certain companies.

115JB. (1) Not withstanding anything contained in any other provision of this Act, where in the case of an assessee, being a company,

(5) Save as otherwise provided in this section, all other provisions of this Act shall apply to every assessee, being a company, mentioned in this section……"

It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and, therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

The Supreme Court held : The electricity is not an excisable item. In the instant civil appeal, the issue was with regard to the electricity which was generated inside the plant by heating of LSHS and which was captively consumed and used to manufacture cement/caustic soda. Rule 57A has an Explanatory clause (c) which states as to what inputs are included in Modvat credit. Explanation ( c) refers to ‘input used as fuel’. The said clause was introduced by Notification No. 4 of 1994. At that time, the Government made it clear that inputs used as fuel were entitled to MODVAT credit. That fuel, either utilized directly or for generating electricity, as an intermediary product, is integrally connected with several operations which result in the emergence of the final product, namely, cement/caustic soda. It is important to note that without utilization of LSHS, it is not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda. The electrolysis process is dependent on continuous flow of electricity. If there is disruption in the supply of electricity from the Electricity Board, then the entire plant of the assessee would fail and the manufacture of cement/caustic soda would not take place. Therefore, LSHS would come within the ambit of the expression ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product’. Electricity is one form of heat. It gets generated in several ways. LSHS is a fuel used in the generation of electricity. Since electricity is self-generated and since it comes into existence as an intermediary product, its utilization for production of final product is crucial. Hence, MODVAT credit on LSHS used in production of electricity could not be denied. Lastly, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced on behalf of the department, the expression ‘in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ was to be interpreted. The expression ‘in the manufacture of goods’ indicates the use of the input in the manufacture of the final product. The said expression normally covers the entire process of converting raw materials into finished goods such as caustic soda, cement, etc. However, the matter does not end with the said expression. The expression also covers inputs ‘used in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The said expression, namely, ‘in relation to’ also finds place in the extended definition of the word ‘manufacture’ in section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is for this reason that the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the expression ‘in relation to’ must be given a wide connotation. The Explanation to rule 57A shows an inclusive definition of the word ‘input’. Therefore, there is a dichotomy between inputs used in the manufacture of the final product and inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. The department gave a narrow meaning to the word ‘used’ in rule 57A. The department would have been right in saying that the input must be raw material consumed in the manufacture of final product. However, the expression ‘used’ in rule 57A uses the words ‘in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The words ‘in relation to’ which find place in section 2(f) of the 1944 Act have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover processes generating intermediate products and it is in this context that it has been repeatedly held by the Supreme Court that if manufacture of final product cannot take place without the process in question, then that process is an integral part of the activity of manufacture of the final product. Therefore, the words ‘in relation to the manufacture’ have been used to widen and expand the scope, meaning and content of the expression ‘inputs’ so as to attract goods which do not enter into finished goods. Where raw material is used in the manufacture of final product, it is an input used in the manufacture of final product. However, the doubt may arise only in regard to use of some articles not in the mainstream of manufacturing process, but something which is used for rendering final product marketable or something used otherwise in assisting the process of manufacture. This doubt is set at rest by use of the words ‘used in relation to manufacture’. In the instant case, the LSHS was used to generate electricity, which was captively consumed. Without continuous supply of such electricity generated in the plant, it was not possible to manufacture cement, caustic soda, etc. Without such supply, the process of electrolysis was not possible. Therefore, keeping in mind the expression ‘used in relation to the manufacture’ in rule 57A, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit on LSHS. The instant case fell in clause (c) and, therefore, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit under Explanatory clause (c) even before 16-3-1995

iii.

The section provides for taxation with reference to preordained criteria which are mentioned in provision itself-amounts received or payable to an assessee non-resident, whether in India or outside India, had to be included for purpose of calculating income under section 44 BB.

iv. There is no compelling reason to assign a narrow and restricted meaning to the expression 'services' in section 44BB and confine it to services other than technical, consultancy or managerial services. In the absence of any words of limitation or exclusion, the word 'services' shall be understood in its plain and ordinary sense. If the legislature wanted to give a restricted meaning to the expression 'services', explicit words to that effect would have been deployed. The contextual setting and the company in which the expression 'services' is found is suggestive of inference that far from excluding technical/consultancy services, they were also intended to be brought within the ambit of section 44BB.The word 'services' followed by an expansive phrase 'in connection with' are relatable to prospecting for and exploration of mineral oil. That means, all services associated with prospecting for and exploration activities are brought within the scope and reach of section 44BB.

v.

Another category of assessees governed by section 44BB are those supplying plant and machinery on hire. Both these two categories of assessees covered by section 44BB engage themselves in core activities pertaining to prospecting and exploration of oil and gas and the Parliament thought it fit to accord a special treatment to the income derived by these two categories of non-residents in India.

vi.

Between the competing provisions, namely section 9(1)(vii) read with sections 44DA and 44BB,section 44BB being a more specific provision, will prevail for the purposes of computation. Section 44DA provides for method of computation of income by way of fees for technical services received by a non-resident or a foreign company carrying on business through a PE in India. If the non-resident is engaged in the business of providing services in connection with the prospecting etc. of mineral oils, the computation provisions relating to fees for technical services will have to yield to section 44BB. In a case of business governed by section 44BB, normally, the enterprise concerned would be having a PE in India. It is difficult to envisage a situation of a person being engaged in providing services or facilities in connection with prospecting and extraction of mineral oils not having a fixed place of business from where the operations are carried on. Thus, the existence of PE is a common feature in both the sections, though there is an explicit reference to PE under section 44DA. Rendering of technical services through PE may be a common feature of both the sections, although in the case of section 44DA,it is explicitly mentioned. But, what is important is the nature of business and it is that factor which serves as an indicator to apply one of the two sections. If the business is of the specific nature envisaged by section 44BB, the computation provisions therein would prevail over the computation provisions in section 44DA.In other words, the income received by a non-resident entity for the technical services provided in relation to prospecting and extraction of mineral oil, will be wholly governed by section 44BB for the purposes of computation.

vii.

Explanation appended to section 44BB provides that for the purpose of this section, plant includes ships, aircrafts, apparatus and equipments used for the purpose of said business and mineral oils include petroleum and natural gas. Thus, the amount received by the assessee on account of supply of spare parts of ships, aircrafts, apparatus and equipments used for the purpose of the business is squarely covered under section 44BB.

viii.

If an assessee does not claim benefit of section 44BB(3),it cannot claim that amount, which it receives by way of mobilisation advance outside India, should not be included for purpose of calculating income under section 44BB.

ix.

Services provided by non-resident in connection with movement of offshore rigs set up by assessee on high seas for exploration, prospecting and production of mineral oil from the seabed is assessable under section 44BB and not as fees for technical services under section 9(1)(vii).

x.

The Hon'ble Calcutta High Court in the case of Schlumberger Sea Co. Inc. [157 CTR 538] has held that once a non-resident supplier of machinery comes within the purview of section 44BB,then it cannot come again under the purview of the other parts of the Act, dealing with profits and gains of business or profession.

xi.

Section 195A is not applicable to it and concept of multiple-stage grossing up of income is also not applicable to deemed profits to be computed under section 44BB.

xii.

It is open to an assessee to claim lower profits and gains, if he kept and maintained books of account and other documents as required under section 44AA(2) and get accounts audited and furnish report.

Background

Amidst the prolonged slowdown in the economy, the government brought in the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019, promulgated by the President of India, to provide impetus to the ailing corporate sector. The ordinance inter alia provides to reduce the corporate tax rate on certain classes of companies; rationalise the current Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rates and withdraw the enhanced surcharge from certain incomes arising from investment in capital markets etc.

The key amendments that find focus in this article relate to reduction in effective corporate tax rate for certain class of domestic companies. Due to such tax rate reduction, India's lowest bracket of corporate tax rate of 17.16 percent1 is now competitive with that of other emerging economies such as Vietnam (20 percent), Thailand (20 percent), Singapore (17 percent), Hong Kong (16.5 percent)2.

The reduction in corporate tax rates has been made effective through insertion of two new sections in the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) i.e. section 115BAA and section 115BAB (collectively referred to as 'Beneficial sections'). These sections are still subject to other provisions of Chapter XII of the Act, such as section 111/111A/112/113 etc. and hence any income in nature of long term/short term capital gains etc. covered under other sections of Chapter XII will continue to be taxed at existing rates.

The sections providing concessional tax rates have been made effective from the current Financial Year (FY) i.e. FY 2019-20 itself. Hence, companies considering to opt for the beneficial sections should take a timely call taking into account the impact of the change in effective tax rates on the advance tax computations for the next quarter/s, on tax provisioning etc.

The amendments also include reduction of tax rate on book profit u/s. 115JB of IT. Act known as Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate from the existing effective tax rates of 20.20 percent to 17.47 percent for all companies.

are paid is effectively connected with the permanent establishment or fixed place of profession. Such income would be computed and assessed under the head "business" in accordance with the provisions of the Act, subject to the condition that no deduction would be allowed in respect of any expenditure or allowance which is not wholly or exclusively incurred for the business of such permanent establishment or fixed place of profession or in respect of amounts, if any, paid by the permanent establishment to its head office or to any of its other offices.

• Under section 44BB one does not find any reference to a permanent establishment in India. The type of services contemplated by the provision is more specific than what is contemplated by section 44DA. Section 44BB refers specifically to "services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire, used or to be used in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of mineral oils". Revenues earned by the non-resident from rendering such specific services are covered by section 44BB.

•

If as contended by the Revenue, section 44DA covers all types of services rendered by the non-resident, that would reduce section 44BB to a useless lumber or dead letter and such a result would be opposed to the very essence of the rule of harmonious construction. [Para 11]

Effect of amendment w.e.f. 1-4-2011

•

The second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44DA inserted by the Finance Act, 2010 w.e.f. 01.04.2011 makes the position clear. Simultaneously, a reference to section 44DA was inserted in the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44BB.

•

It should be remembered that section 44DA also requires that the non-resident or the foreign company should carry on business in India through a permanent establishment situated therein and the right, property or contract in respect of which the royalty or fees for technical services is paid should be effectively connected with the permanent establishment. Such a requirement has not been spelt out in section 44BB; moreover, a flat rate of 10 per cent of the revenues received by the non-resident for the specific services rendered by it are deemed to be profits from the business chargeable to tax in India under section 44BB, whereas under section 44DA, deduction of expenditure or allowance wholly and exclusively incurred by the non-resident for the business of the permanent establishment in India and for expenditure towards reimbursement of actual expense by the permanent establishment to its head office or to any of its other offices is allowed from the revenues received by the non-resident.

•

Because of the different modes or methods prescribed in the two sections for computing the profits, it apparently became necessary to clarify the position by making necessary amendments. That perhaps is the reason for inserting the second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44DA and a reference to section 44DA in the proviso below sub-section (1) of section 44BB.

•

A careful perusal of both the provisos shows that they refer only to computation of the profits under the sections. If both the sections have to be read harmoniously and in such a manner that neither of them becomes a useless lumber then the only way in which the provisos can be given effect to is to understand them as referring only to the computation of profits, and to understand the amendments as having been inserted only to clarify the position.

•

So understood, the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44BB can only mean that the flat rate of 10 per cent of the revenues cannot be deemed to be the profits of the non-resident where the services are of the type which do not fall under that section, but are more general in nature so as to fall under section 44DA. Similarly, the second proviso to sub-section (1) of section 44DA can only be interpreted to mean that where the services are general in nature and fall under the sub-section read with Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vii), then an assessee rendering such services as provided in section 44BB cannot claim the benefit of being assessed on the basis that 10 per cent of the revenues will be deemed to be the profits as provided in section 44BB [Para 12].

Conclusion

•

In other words, the amendment made by the Finance Act, 2010 with effect from 1-4-2011 in both the sections, cannot have the effect of altering or effacing the fundamental nature of both the provisions or their respective spheres of operation or to take away the separate identity of section 44BB.

•

Therefore, these amendments would not assist the Revenue's contention in the present case. Therefore, in the present case the profits shall be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 44BB and not section 44DA. [Para 12]

Counsel that JCT Fibres Ltd. has since been changed to JCT Ltd. and therefore, prays for the change of cause title. The ld. SDR has no objection. The cause title is therefore, changed to M/s. 5. The short point for determination in this appeal is whether the provisions of Rule 57C are attracted when PSFs were sent to manufacturers of polyester fabrics for export. For this purpose, we have to see what the provisions of Not. No. 33/90 are Not. No. 33/90 inter alia stipulates "Transfer of excisable goods without payment of duty." It does not say that the duty shall be chargeable at nil rate etc. This notification also does not speak of exemption of the goods. Now let us examine the provisions of Rule 57C. Rule 57C lays down that modvat credit shall not be available in cases where the final product is exempt. Admittedly, in the instant case when these two rules are read together, I find that under Not. No. 33/90, the word `exempt' is not used nor nil rate of duty is used. Therefore, the goods were not exempt so as to attract denial of modvat credit on inputs under Section 57C. I get support for this view from the decision of the Tribunal in the case of J.K. Synthetics Ltd. cited above. In para 6, the Tribunal had held as under :

We have carefully considered the submissions from both the sides and perused the records. The Respondent manufactured PSF for which MEG is one of the inputs. Notification No. 225/86-CE dated 3/4/86 exempted PSF from Central excise duty chargeable thereon as it equivalent to the Central Excise Duty under Central Excise Act, 1944 or additional Customs Duty under Customs Tariff Act, 1975 paid on the MEG used in the manufacture of such PSF. This exemption notification provided similar duty concession in respect of other finished products mentioned in the table annexed to the notification and the duty concession was equal to the Central excise duty paid under Central Excise Act or additional Customs Duty paid under Customs Tariff Act, on the specified inputs used in the manufacture of the finished products. Though there is no explicit provision in this exemption notification regarding its applicability when the finished product is fully exempt from duty or is chargeable to nil rate of duty, it would be an obvious corollary that this exemption would not be applicable if the finished product is an exempted goods i.e. either fully exempt from duty by virtue of an exemption notification or chargeable to nil rate of duty. The point of dispute in this case is as to whether this exemption notification would be applicable when the finished goods - PSF in this case, have been cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export.

3.1 Rules 191BB permits removal of excisable goods from the place of manufacture or storage without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export, subject to the conditions prescribed in this Rule. The PSF, in question, in respect of which the set off of duty on MEG used in its manufacture is sought to be denied, had been cleared without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of finished goods for export in terms of the provisions of Rule 191BB. The Tribunal in the case of Orissa Synthetics Vs. CCE (supra) and CCE, Chandigarh Vs. JCT Ltd. (supra), has with reference to exemption notification No. 225/96-CE, held that PSF cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of goods for export is not to be treated as exempted goods. It is not the contention of the Department that these judgments have been challenged before a higher court or have been set aside. Moreover when the Department has accepted the clearances of the PSF for export under bond without payment of duty, as eligible for the benefit of this exemption, there would be no justification in denying the same exemption to the goods cleared under Rule 191BB without payment of duty for use in the manufacture of the finished goods for export.

3.2 The Notification No. 225/86-CE operates like Modvat scheme. Rule 57F (3) of Chapter V (AA) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 pertaining to Modvat scheme, provided that credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on any of the finished products in or in relation to manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used or for payment of duty on any waste arising in course of manufacture of finished products or for payment of duty on inputs themselves, if the same are allowed to be cleared as such. Proviso to this sub-Rule provided that the credit of the specified duty in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of final products cleared for export under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty and where for any reason such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations, as may be specified by the Central Government by notification in the official gazette. In the case of Reliance Industries Ltd. Vs. CCE, Bombay (supra), the dispute arose as to whether the final products cleared under bond without payment of duty in terms of Rule 191BB for use in the manufacture of finished product for export would be eligible for the benefit of the proviso to Rule 57F (3) and the Tribunal answered this question in the affirmative, holding that in respect of clearances of finished product without payment of duty under Rule 191BB, the benefit of proviso to Rule 57F (3) would be available. Same principle would apply in this case also and when the Department has accepted the applicability of the exemption in respect of the finished product exported under bond without payment of duty, the benefit of this exemption would also have to be extended in respect of the clearances without payment of duty under Rule 191B.

5. The main thrust of his contentions can be summed up as below :-

(i)

Modvat is a scheme for averting the cascading effect of input taxation on the duty paid in regard to the final product. When the final product is cleared without payment of duty for whatever be the reason, there cannot be a cascading effect of input duty on the final product, so cleared without payment of duty.

(ii)

In this case, removals without payment of duty have been permitted to the exporters, who effected such removals in terms of the bond executed under Rule 191B/l91 BB of the Central Excise Rules. Reliance Industries are not exporting the goods. They take the credit of duty paid on inputs and use the inputs in the manufacture of POY/PSF, which are cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191B/191 BB. Such credit of duty paid on these inputs is utilised for payment of duty of POY/PSG cleared by them for home consumption. Viewed in this context, it would be apparent that the appellants avai1 of the benefit, which is not intended to them for clearing the goods for home consumption.

(iii)

The Modvat Scheme is an independent one, mainly formulated for averting the cascading effect of input taxation. The basic principle is "no credit - if no duty is paid on the final product cleared". This is clearly evident from a careful reading of Rule 57A, which is the substantive provision to determine the eligibility. Judged by what is prescribed in Rule 57A, credit cannot be given when the final product is cleared without payment of duty.

(iv)

Provisions of Rules 13,191B, 191BBenvisageadifferentschemepermitting removals of excisable goods without payment of duty for exports. Unless Modvat scheme contemplates by a specific provisions in Rule 57A envisaging eligibility of credit to such removals for exports, they cannot claim the credit and their claim is blocked right at the thresh hold of Rule 57A.

(v)

In this case, admittedly POY/PSF are not exported as such. They were used in manufacture of fabrics. Fabrics is the final product exported and it is not covered by Notification issued under Rule 57A. Hence credit cannot be made available.

(vi)

Proviso to sub rule (3) of Rule 57F does not make any exception in regard to removals under Rule 191B/191BB specifically as has been done in the case of removal of goods for export production in the Free trade zone or 100% E.O.U. Hence it is clear that unless the final products manufactured by the assessees themselves are exported under bond, credit accrued therefrom cannot be utilised for payment of duty on similar final products cleared for home consumption. Hence sub rule (5) of Rule 57F would be applicable, and accordingly such credit has to be reversed.

(vii)

"We find that in the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited reported at page 599 of Reliance Industries Limited at para 6.2, this Tribunal held as under:-

"In the case of Orissa Synthetic Limited decided by the East Regional Bench, the man-made staple fibre was cleared without payment of duty under Rule 191BB of the Central Excise Rules and the department objected to the availing of Modvat Credit of duty on inputs used in these final products cleared under Rule 191BB of the Rules. The department's main contention was that such removals of final products without payment of duty under Rule 191BB were hit by Rule 57C of the Central Excise Rules. The East Regional Bench, after considering all the arguments raised by the ld. SDR negatived the objection and allowed the appeal of Orissa Synthetics. For arriving at their conclusion, that Bench relied on the decision of the Delhi High Court in Hindustan Aluminium Corpn. reported in 1981 (8) ELT 642, wherein it was held by the Delhi High Court that the facility of removal without payment of duty under bond for export could not be equated with a general exemption from payment of duty of excise. That Bench also took note of the clarification issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs in consultation with the Ministry of Law about the scope of proviso (i) to sub-rule (2) of Rule 56A (analogous to the provisions of Rule 57C). In that clarification issued by the Board, the Board advised the field formations that the said proviso to Rule 56A (2) would not stand attracted, where the final products were exported under bond, since such removals could neither be construed to be exempted nor be regarded as goods charged to nil rate of duty. (Vide the extract of the advice of the Ministry of Law appearing in para 9 of the said order of the East Regional Bench). Thus we find that going by the allegation contained in the show cause notices involved in this appeal, the issue is identical in all respects and the ratio of that decision would apply to this case squarely."

"A careful reading of the above paragraph shows that the Tribunal had held that the goods manufactured from the inputs on which modvat credit has been taken which are cleared without payment of duty under Notfn. No. 33/90-CE (NT) does not mean that the goods are exempt from the whole of duty."

Moreover, proviso to Rule 57F (3) specifically confers the benefit only on the manufacturer and not on the exporter of goods.

(iii) Rule 57A is no doubt the Rule prescribing the applicability of the provisions of the Section relating to Modvat credit. But that rule cannot be read in isolation. It has to be read in conjunction with other rules contained in that Section. The Section as a whole envisages the availability of credit of duty paid on inputs used in the manufacture of final products, the manner of utilisation of inputs and of credit so earned. If one is to confine himself to read only Rule57 A for determining the quantum of credit to be availed of, the provisions of Rule 57 B allowing higher notional credit in some cases has to be kept in operative. We are to read the entire scheme as a whole as envisaged in Rules 57A to 57 J. The relevant Rule for denying credit is Rule 57 C, which stipulates that no credit shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to 'nil' rate of duty. We are to consider whether in the case of removals of goods under bond in terms of Rule 191 B/191 BB would be hit by the Rule. Likewise, we are to consider whether in the case of utilisation of inputs and credit earned thereon, if the inputs have gone into the goods cleared for export under Rules 191 B/191 BB, whether there is a bar in availment of credit. Thus we are of the view that Rule 57A cannot be considered in isolation. In so far as this case is concerned, it has to be considered in conjunction with Rules 57C and 57 F (3).

Provisions of Rules 13, 191 B, 191 BB envisage the scheme relating to exports without payment of duty. But the scheme has been dovetailed with the Modvat scheme as is evident from the proviso to Rule 57F (3) which reads as below :-

Quote "Provided that credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared for export under bond for used in the intermediate products cleared for export in accordance with sub rule (2), shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty on similar rinal products cleared for home consumption or for export on payment of duty and where for any reason, such adjustment is not possible by refund to the manufacturer, subject to such safeguards, condition and limitations as may be prescribed by the Central Govt, in the Official Gazette". Unquote (emphasis supplied)

From the above, it looks apparent to us, that even if the declared inputs are used in the declared final product, when some of final products are cleared for export under bond, credit earned from such inputs can be utilised for clearance of similar final products for home consumption and for any reason such adjustment is not possible, even cash refund to the manufacturer of final products is permitted. Now, we are to consider the meaning of the words "final products cleared for export under bond" (emphasised in the above proviso). POY & PSF are the final products in so far as the appellant is concerned. They are removed under bond in terms of Rules 191 B and 191 BB of the Central Excise Rules. Now let us look at the provisions governing the export of excisable goods. Rules 12 and 12 A govern the grant of rebate of Central Excise duty paid on these goods exported, as also on the excisable materials used in the production of goods, which are exported.

Rule 13 indicates that in like manner. Excisable Goods may be exported without payment of duly provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the C.Ex Rules and the owner of the goods to be exported enters into a bond undertaking to export the goods. From Rule 13. it is clear, that wherever rebate is permitted under Rules 12 & 12 A, goods in like manner can be exported without payment of duty in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Rules 191 B& 191 BB are the rules prescribing the export of excisable goods under bond figuring in Chapter IX of the C.Ex. Rules. Hence, we cannot give any other meaning to the words "final products cleared for export under Bond" figuring in the proviso to Rule 57 F (3), other than that is contained in Rule 13, which is the general provision permitting export of excisable goods for export under-bond. Hence we are not impressed with the argument of the Id. counsel for the Revenue that Modvat scheme is to be considered dehors export under bond, which is a separate scheme for exports.

3. The appellants had paid duty on MEG used in the manufacture of polyester fibre supplied to NTC units under Notification 191/85. The appellants claimed that they were entitled to the set off of duty on MEG under Notification 225/86. This notification exempts polyester staple fibre etc. from so much of excise duty leviable thereon which is paid on inputs and used in or in relation to the manufacture of final product. In this case, since the product in which MEG is used i.e. polyester staple fibre is fully exempt, the set off of duty is not available on MEG. The exemption is not for MEG used in the manufacture of staple fibre but to polyester staple fibre to the extent of duty paid on MEG. Per Archana Wadhwa :

Modvat credit of Rs. 2,25,305.00 has been disallowed by the authorities below for the period of August, 1995 to June, 1996 on the ground that the various inputs used in the manufacture of their final product i.e. Refined Rice Bran Oil, cannot be considered as modvatable input inasmuch as the final product is cleared without payment of duty.

2. The appellants duly represented by Shri S.K. Roychowdhury submits that the appellants are engaged in the manufacture of Refined Rice Bran Oil which is chargeable to nil rate of duty as also the vegetable product which is a dutiable product. They availed the MODVAT Credit on the various inputs after declaring the same in their declaration under Rule 57G and all the inputs for Rice Bran Oil as also for vegetable product, were common inputs and as such, common RG-23A Part-I and II was being maintained by them. He submits that they are entitled to the MODVAT Credit even if a part of the inputs is used in the manufacture of Rice Bran Oil cleared by nil rate of duty in terms of proviso to Rule 57F(4) inserted by Notification No. 11/95 dated 16.3.95. He submitted that the said Rule permitted the assessee to utilise the MODVAT Credit towards the payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the fact whether such an iinput has actually been used in the manufacture of such a final product or not. In this view, he submits that the impugned Orders be set aside and Credit be allowed.

3. Shri T. Premkumar, learned S.D.R. appearing for the Revenue contends that the provisions of Rule 57F(4) are not applicable to the present situation inasmuch as the same are applicable when common inputs are being used in the manufacture of two different dutiable products, that is to say that one to one correlation is not required and Credit earned in respect of one final product can be utilised towards payment of duty on the other final product. As such he prays for rejection of the appeal.

4. I have considered the submission of both sides. The relevant proviso inserted in Notification No. 1/95-CE (NT) dated 16.3.95 is reproduced below for the sake of ready reference:-

"Provided also that, notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (1) of rule 57A and the notifications issued thereunder the credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty excise on any other final product, whether or not such inputs have actually been used in the manufacture of such other final product, if the said inputs have been received and used in the factory of production on or after the 16th day of March, 1995". (emphasis provided).

4.1 A reading of the above proviso shows that any credit of duty allowed in respect of any inputs can be utilised towards payment of duty on any other final product irrespective of the input having been used in the said final product. As such, the first condition of the said proviso is that the credit of duty should have been allowed, i.e. the assessees are entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit of Duty on particular inputs and it is only after availing the said Credit that the manner of its utilisation has been laid down in the said proviso. In the instant case, the appellants were, at the first stage, not entitled to avail the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs used in the manufacture of Refind Rice Bran Oil because the said Oil was chargeable to nil rate of duty. As such the Rule 57C prohibited taking of Credit in such circumstances. When the availing of Credit is not permissible under the law, the question of its utilisation towards the payment of duty on any other final product does not arise. The proviso refers to a situation where the assessee manufacturer is entitled to availing the MODVAT Credit in respect of the inputs to be utilised in the manufacture of two different products and such accumulated availed Credit is allowed to be utilised towards the payment of the second final product, even though the input might not have been used in that final product. As such, I uphold the impugned orders passed by the authorities below in so far as the same relates to the denial of MODVAT Credit of Duty.

The latter then manufacture the final product which is exported. The clearance of MMSF is without payment of duty on the strength of a suitable bond to ensure the utilisation of the said material for the manufacture of the final product which is exported. Ruie57C lays down that no credit to duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty. The Collector has held in his impugned order that they had made a very thin distinction between exemption and clearance without payment of duty, which is basically same. Shri Gopal Prasad submitted that this conclusion of the Collector is not correct. Notification 33/90, in terms of which they had cleared their product MMSF, permits goods to be removed without payment of duty for supply to manufacturers of final products which are exported. The expression (removal) without payment of duty is distinct and different from exempt from whole of the duty or chargeable to nil rate of duty. The Collector had referred to the amendment of Rule 57C by Notification 4/92 dated 1.3.92 and concluded that since by this amendment the final products cleared to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a 100 per cent Export oriented unit have been exempted from the effect of Rule 5 7C removal without payment of duty for supply to the ultimate exporter for manufacture of the resultant product will not get such a benefit in the absence of such exemption from the scope of Rule 57C being specifically extended to such non-duty paid removals. The learned Consultant contended that this interpretation of the Col lector is wrong. In the case of clearances of final products to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a 100 per cent Export Oriented Unit, these are exempt from the whole of the duty leviable and hence it was necessary to specifically provide for them as otherwise they would be hit by Rule 57C. Such is not the case with clearances without payment of duty under Notification 33/90 dated 5.9.90 issued under Rule 191 BB (1). That is not an exemption Notification. Such exemption Notifications were issued under Rule 8 of the Central Rules, 1944 earlier (now under Section 5A of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944). This vital difference has not been accepted by the Collector.

In this connection, he referred to the judgement of the Honourable Delhi High Court in Hindustan Aluminium Corporation Limited. Vs. Collector of Central Excise, reported in 1987 (8) ELT 642 where the facility of export under bond without payment of duty was held to be not the same as a general exemption from payment of any excise duty at all. Shri Gopal Prasad submitted that the ratio of this decision is equally applicable for clearance of goods in terms of Rule 191 BB and accordingly Rule 57C is not applicable to such cases.

3. The learned Counsel then referred to the clarification issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs in consultation with the Ministry of Law about the scope of provisonal, to sub-Rule (2) of Rule 56A which is similar to Rule 57 C. There also, the crucial expression was exempted from the whole of duty of excise leviable thereon or are chargeable to nil rate of duty. It was advised by the Law Ministry that exemption has a definite connotation and such exemption will have to be attributable to a Notification issued under Rule 8 and that exports under bond are duty free not by virtue of any exemption issued under Rule 8 and hence the first prohibition contained in clause (i) of the proviso to sub-Rule (2) of Rule 56A did not come into play. The learned consultant submitted that the same position will apply to Rule 57 (c) also.

It is seen that earlier under the first proviso MODVAT credit taken in respect of the inputs contained in the goods exported under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export could be utilised for payment of duty towards goods cleared for home consumption or for any reason if this adjustment was not possible the cash refund has been provided for. With effect from 1.3.92, the second proviso has been added. Under this even where the final products in which the inputs have been utilised are cleared to a unit in a free trade zone or to a l00% export oriented unit under bond, the same benefit as in the case of the export of the goods has been provided for. We observe that as such in Rule 57F (3) there is no specific provision in regard to the clearances made to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, We observe that when the clearances are made to a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit of any finished product without payment of duty from a unit which has taken MODVAT credit in respect of the inputs, the benefit is given as ultimately in terms of these schemes the goods allowed manufacture are exported. The units which are manufacturing goods under Rule 191B in terms of notification issued under this Rule are in our view similarly placed as the unit located in the free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. We see no reason as to why the same benefit as provided under Rule 57F for these units cannot be extended to this unit. Interest of revenue is safeguarded by the specific provision under the notification issued under Rule 191B for recovery of duty both in respect of the finished goods and the non-duty paid goods out of which the same are manufactured in bond in case the goods are not exported. We therefore hold that notwithstanding the absence of any specific mention in the proviso to Rule 57F(3) in regard to the finished goods in respect of which input credit is taken and which are cleared without payment of duty to a unit functioning under Rule 191B, the second proviso to Rule 57F(3) would cover such units also, as we do not find any reason to differentiate the operations in the unit functioning under Rule 191B from the operations carried out in the unit functioning under a free trade zone or to a 100% export oriented unit. In view of above, we hold that the appellants plea has to be allowed and we order accordingly.

Para 5 of the Larger Bench in the matter of Hunsur Plywood Works (P) Ltd. Vs. CCE (supra) is extracted below. 5. We have given a careful thought to the pleas made by both the sides. The commercial plywoods manufactured by the appellants were cleared free of duty in terms of Rule 191B after following the procedures prescribed thereunder. Rule 191B figures in Chapter IX which carries a heading "Export under claim for rebate of duty or under bond" and the Rule carries the heading "Manufacture in bond of articles from excisable goods on which duty has not been paid". This Rule is applicable to manufacture in bond of such articles from such excisable goods and subject to such conditions and limitations as may be specified in the notification issued in this regard. Under this Rule, the Govt. of India has issued a notification under which decorative plywood is covered for in bond manufacture out of commercial plywood as one of the items for the purpose of export outside India. It was under this notification that the appellants cleared commercial plywoods manufactured by them to the manufacturer of the decorative plywoods under proper central excise prescribed documents. It is nobody's case that the manufacturer has not manufactured decorative plywood for export purpose out of commercial plywood in question under Rule 191B of the Central Excise Rules. In terms of the notification, the manufacturer of the decorative plywood, i.e. the buyer of the commercial plywood, the appellants customer, would have therefore executed a bond for twice the amount of duty payable beyond the non-duty excisable goods i.e. commercial plywood in this case, used for the manufacture of decorative plywood for export purpose. The excisable goods therefore received by the decorative plywood manufacturer were also required to be kept in terms of this notification in a separate room. A procedure is also prescribed under this notification for disposal of the waste arising during the manufacture either on payment of duty or for recycling in the same factory. This notification also has a provision for allowing the manufacturer of the finished goods who has manufactured under bond under Rule 191B for clearance for home consumption on payment of excise duty leviable by them on such article as also on the excisable goods used in the manufacture thereof in the same manner as excisable goods intended for home consumption are cleared from the place of their production or manufacture or storage. It is thus seen that Rule 191B is a very comprehensive procedure under which finished goods manufactured out of non-duty paid goods have to be properly accounted for and in the event of the goods not being exported the levy of duty is provided both in respect of the finished goods manufactured in bond as also the inputs contained thereunder which was received without payment of duty. In view of this procedure prescribed under Rule 191B the question that has to be considered is whether goods cleared by the appellants under Rule 191B free of duty to the other unit which manufactured decorative plywood for export purposes could be taken to be export for Modvat purposes in terms of Rule 57F (3). We observe that Rule 57F (3) during the relevant period i.e. 1-3-1993 to 31-7-1993 providing for the manner in which the credit taken in respect of the inputs could be utilised read as under :

(3) Credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs may be utilised towards payment of duty of excise,-

on any of the final products in or in relation to the manufacture of which such inputs are intended to be used in accordance with the declaration filed under sub-rule (1) of Rule 57G; or

(ii)

on the waste, if any, arising in the course of manufacture of the final products; or

(iii)

on the inputs themselves if such inputs have been permitted to be cleared under sub-rule (1):

Provided that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared for export under bond or used in the intermediate products cleared for export in accordance with sub-rule (2), shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption or for export on payment of duty and, where for any reason, such adjustment is not possible, by refund to the manufacturer subject to such safeguards, conditions and limitations as may be specified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette:

Provided further that no such refund of credit of duty shall be allowed if the manufacturer avails of drawback; allowed under the Customs and Central Excise Duties (Drawback) Rules, 1971, or claims rebate of duty under Rule 12A, in respect of such duty.

Provided also that the credit of specified duty in respect of inputs used in the final products cleared either to a unit in a Free Trade Zone or to a hundred per cent Export Oriented Unit under bond shall be allowed to be utilised towards payment of duty of excise on similar final products cleared for home consumption on payment of duty.

Per Shri R. Jayaraman : This is an appeal against the Order in Appeal No. PCJ/ 3/B,III/93 dt. 5.3.93. The following are the issues to be considered in this appeal before the Tribunal. Five items were declared as inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product butare hold to be not eligible to avail of Modvat credit in terms of Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules. The disputed inputs are liquid nitrogen, tri-ethylene glocol, (TEG), thermex, finor and KEM Watreat. The other issue is whether Modvat credit of duty paid on inputs can be availed of and utilised in regard to the clearance of similar final products, if some of the final products are cleared for export under bond in terms of Rule 191 -BB of the Central Excise Rules.

2. The appellants are engaged in the manufacture of Polyester Staple fibre and the aforesaid inputs were declared as inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. However, the dept. objected to their eligibility on the ground that they are not utilised in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product and hence they are not eligible to take credit. Thus, credit amounting to Rs. 4,22,405/ - was sought to be reversed.

3. Shri Habbu the Id. adv. submits that though there were other issues covered by the impugned order, they have already been settled and only the aforesaid two issues are outstanding for consideration by the Tribunal. As regards the individual inputs, he refers to the writ up filed in the paper book pointing out that in the case of liquid nitrogen, thermex, Finor and -KEM Watreat, they are going into the manufacturing stream and hence they are inputs used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. As regards the input TEG for want of sufficient data, he is not pressing the issue for decision on merits in so far as this appeal is concerned. As regards the denial of Modvat credit in respect of duty on inputs used in the final products which were cleared under Rule 191 BB of the C.E. Rules, he seeks to rely on the decision of the East Regional Bench in the case of Orissa Synthetics and also this Bench decision contained in 2128/94WRB dt. 1.12.94 in the case of Reliance Industries Ltd.

4. Shri Nair the Id. SDR points out that liquid nitrogen is only giving of blanket cover in the reactor vessel and it also acts as a conveying material and hence it cannot be said to be an input used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. In the case of Thermex, it is only a hearing medium and being in nature of an equipment, it cannot be allowed Modvat benefit. In the case of floor, he pleads that it is only made for increasing (he efficiency of the boiler and goes along with the equipment. Likewise, in the case of KEM Watreat, it is a chemical used for treating water for cooling purposes. Hence it does not go into the manufacturing process.

5. As regards the denial of Modvat credit in respect of inputs used in the final product cleared for export under Rule 191 BB, he pleads that a reference Application has been moved against the decision of this Bench in the case of Reliance Industries. He would plead that export under bond referred to in Rule 57F (3)can only mean exports directly from the factory to a place outside India in terms of the bond executed under Rule 13 of the Central Excise Rules. It cannot seek to cover transfer of materials from one factory to another in terms of Rule 191 B B of the Central Excise Rules. Hence in such cases Rule 57F (3) proviso cannot be applied, irrespective of the fact that Rule 57-C seeks to cover only goods exempted or are chargeable to Nil rate of duty.
