is an integral part of the manufacturing process, chemicals added to water for achieving the required degree of efficiency in cooling system are eligible inputs.

6.6. In the result, in so far as the disputed five inputs are concerned, Modvat credit is admissible in respect of the following inputs namely, liquid nitrogen, thermex, finor and KEM Watreat. As regards TEG, Modvat credit should be reversed, since the appeal in regard to the input was not pressed on merits. 7. Now coming to the objection that Modvat credit cannot be utilised in regard to duty payable on similar final products, where some of the final products are cleared under bond in terms of Rule 191 BB of the Central Excise Rules, the issue is squarely covered by the decision of the East Regional Bench in the case of Orissa Synthetics and also by our decision in the case of Reliance Industries. We have considered all the arguments from the revenue for coming to the conclusion that in the absence of specific legal provision either under Rule 57 C or under Rule 57 F (3) proviso, Modvat credit cannot be denied for utilisation in regard to clearance of similar final products. Rule 57 C seeks to deny Modvat credit, if the final products are either wholly exempted or are chargeable to Nil rate of duty. We have held that in the case of goods cleared under a Notification issued under Rule 191 BB for export purposes, such goods cannot be equated with goods exempted under an exemption Notification issued under Rule 8 (1) of the C.E. Rules or Section 5A of C.Ex. Act nor they can be construed as goods chargeable to Nil rate of duty. For arriving at this conclusion, we have taken note of the Board's own instructions issued in the context of identical provisions of Rule 56A of the C.E. Rules, after consulting the Ministry of Law. The argument of Shri Nair that irrespective of the fact that Rule 57C does not specifically provide for denying benefit in respect of clearances under Rule 191 BB, since Rule 57F (3) proviso can only cover direct exports from the factory and not removals under Rule 191 BB for further manufacture of export goods in another factory. We do not find any warrant to read such a restriction in Rule 57F (3) proviso; because proviso to Rule 57F (3) talks of "cleared for export under bond". In the absence of any specific restriction prescribed in that proviso, we are to go by what is meant by the term for export under bond' laid down in Rule 13 of the C.Ex. Rules. Under Rule 13, goods may be exported outside India without payment of duty from a warehouse or licensed factory, provided the export is made in accordance with the procedure set out in the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules and the owner enters into a bond for due performance. There is no dispute that Rule 191 BB is one of the relevant provision of Chapter IX of the Rules. Hence if the goods are cleared under Rule 191BB, they are goods cleared for export in accordance with the relevant provisions of Chapter IX of the Rules. Viewed in this context, we could not persuade ourselves to agree that Rule 57F (3) proviso can he extended, only where the goods are cleared direct from the factory to the port of shipment. Hence, we find no reason to take any different view from the one we have already taken in the case of Reliance Industries. Hence we hold that objection from the Dept. on this ground is not sustainable and direct the authorities to allow the credit to be utilised in regard to clearance of similar final product.

8. In the result, we hold that inputs namely liquid Nitrogen, Thermex, Finor and KEM Watreat are eligible to avail Modvat credit. As regards TEG, appeal is dismissed, since issue is not pressed on merits. We also direct that Modvat credit of duty paid on inputs used in the final products, which were so farcleared for export in terms of Rule 191 BB; should be allowed to be utilised in regard to clearance of similar products for home consumption.

HEADNOTE: MODVAT follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not Rule 57A, read with rule 57B, of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 - CENVAT Credit - One H produced sulphuric acid - During manufacture of sulphuric acid, waste material arises which is called scrubber liquor - Scrubber liquor, though normally a polluting material, can safely substitute for water in case of production of sodium silicate - Assessee, a manufacturer of sodium silicate, entered into an agreement with H for supply of scrubber liquor to assessee on condition that scrubber liquor would be supplied to assessee free, except for central excise duty and sales tax paid by H on scrubber liquor - Assessee availed MODVAT Credit of duty paid by it on scrubber liquor - Adjudicating Authority denied MODVAT Credit on ground that scrubber liquor could not be considered as input - Whether finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to factual situation and relevant legal provisions - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee was eligible for MODVAT Credit as claimed - Held, yes

FACT: One H was producing, sulphuric acid. During the manufacture of the said acid, waste material arises which is called "Scrubber Liquor". The scrubber liquor is polluting and its disposal is expensive. However, it can be used in manufacturing sodium silicate. Water is required to be added to adjust the viscosity of sodium silicate. The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of sodium silicate. The assessee entered into an agreement with H for the supply of scrubber liquor to the assessee. H was paying central excise duty and sales tax on scrubber liquor. It was agreed that the scrubber liquor would be supplied to the assessee free, except for the central excise duty and sales tax. In the invoices, the price (at which duty was calculated) was being shown as rebate. The assessee availed MODVAT Credit of duty paid by it on scrubber liquor. The adjudicating authority denied the MODVAT Credit availed by the assessee on the ground that the scrubber liquor could not be considered as input. On appeal, the appellate authority upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal:

HELD: Admittedly, the scrubber liquor is to be added to adjust viscosity of the sodium silicate. Such addition was in the factory of the assessee and before sale of sodium silicate. Modvat Rules allow ‘Credit of any duty of excise paid on the goods used in the manufacture on said final products" (Rules 57A). Rule 57B further clarifies that "Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 57A, the manufacturer of final products shall be allowed to take credit of the specified duty paid... on inputs used in or relation to the manufacture of final products, whether directly or indirectly and whether contained in the final products or not". It was not reasonable to argue that materials used for maintaining viscosity at the required level were not used in relation to manufacture, particularly, when the viscosity control was by the manufacturer before the sale of goods. It is also to be noted that Modvat follows payment of duty on inputs, whether such payment of duty was correctly made or not. Correctness of payment is not relevant; only the fact of payment is. A view to the contrary also goes against the broad definition of ‘manufacture’ in section 2 of the Central Excise Act in a manner as to include "any process - incidental or ancillary to the completion of manufacture". Thus, a finding that scrubber liquor was not an input was contrary to the given factual situation and relevant legal provisions. Hence, the assessee was eligible for MODVAT credit as claimed. [Para 9]

As long as HCl is used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, the applicability of provisions of rule 57CC cannot be ruled out. [Para 12] The appellant’s reference to the provisions of rule 57D in support of their contention that Modvat credit was not to be denied if a part of the same was contained in the by-product, was indicative of the legislative intent that reversal of 8 per cent amount of the value of the by-product in terms of provisions of rule 57CC would not apply. The expression ‘by-product’ occurring in rule 57D has to be examined and interpreted in the context of the said rule, which uses the other expression ‘waste’ or ‘refuse’, etc. It is in this scenario that the rule provides for non-reversal of Modvat credit, even if waste, refuse or by-product has emerged during the course of manufacture. The effect of the said rule would be that if waste product, which may not be excisable, e.g. , floor sweepings during the course of manufacture of biscuits, then the quantum of credit originally taken is not to be varied. Similarly, if iron and steel scrap arises during manufacture of iron products, the Modvat is not to be varied, but iron and scrap being excisable products, [the manufacturers] have to discharge duty burden. If the same are exempted, provisions of rule 57CC will apply. As such, it is to be concluded that rule 57D refers to waste scrap and by-product, which are not excisable at all. The said provision cannot be pressed into service in support of the plea that even if the by-product is excisable, but exempted, amount of 8 per cent is not required to be paid. The appellant was not being directed to reverse the credit amount equivalent to the inputs contained in the said exempted final products. Further, taking an hypothetical example of electrolysis of water, which an assessee may undertake to obtain oxygen, he cannot take the plea that hydrogen which also emerges during such electrolysis is an unintended product and even if the same is being sold as an exempted product, the same should be treated as a by-product and rule 57CC would not apply. [Para 13]

The issue in the instant case was not relatable to reversal of the credit originally taken by the appellant on the ground of emergence of any by-product. The issue was a straight and simple interpretation of rule 57CC, which as already held does not make any distinction between exempt final product or exempt by-product. As long as the excisable product cleared from an assessee’s factory enjoys exemption or attracts nil rate of duty, provisions of rule 57CC will come into play. The straight answer to the above question lies in the literal interpretation of the language employed in the said rule without straining to find out the legislative intent, especially when the language used is unambiguous. As already observed, the provisions of rule 57CC or rule 6 envisage common use of inputs in two final products, i.e., one dutiable and other exempted, for the applicability of the same. As such, as long as two final products emerging out of use of common inputs are excisable and one of them is exempted, the provisions of rule 57CC will apply. The exempted final product may be intended manufacture or unintended by-product. [Para 14]

Kind attention is invited to the provisions of Rule 57CC of the Central Excise Rules for reversal of Modvat credit in respect of inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods or goods chargeable to 'nil' rate of excise duty. The provision has been made that where a manufacturer uses inputs which are common to both dutiable goods as well as exempted goods, the manufacturer is required to debit the amount equal to 8% of the value of the exempted goods when they are cleared from the factory.

2. In some cases, the exempted goods cleared by one manufacturer are used as inputs by another manufacturer. The manufacturer of exempted goods indicates the amount of Modvat credit reversed on the invoices issued by him for such exempted goods. In this context, some doubts have been raised whether the amount of Modvat credit so reversed is available as Modvat credit to the user of such exempted goods when he uses them as inputs in his factory.

3. In this context, it is clarified that the amount reversed is not by way of payment of excise duty. Accordingly, the amount of Modvat credit reversed and shown in the invoice by the manufacturer of exempted goods cannot be taken as credit by the user of exempted goods.

Hundred per cent absorption or assimilation of the duty paid input in the final product is not a sine qua non of MODVAT credit, but to take benefit of MODVAT Scheme, the petitioner is required simply to establish that the input was used in the manufacture of final product. The sulphuric acid (duty paid input) can be said to have been used by the petitioner in the manufacture of final product when the entire relevant quantity thereof was applied or subjected to the manufacturing process". 6. The High Court in arriving at the above conclusion relied on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. Vs. C.C.E. - 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC). In this case, it is observed that the question for consideration was whether the appellants became ineligible to claim set-off of duty on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre to the extent it gave rise to methanol. In the premises, the Supreme Court held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ''The Supreme Court held that ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre, though methanol had arisen as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture, when ethylene glycol interacted with DMT to produce polyester fibre. Giving the reasoning, the Supreme Court says that it is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre and that the appellant was engaged in the production of polyester fibre and not methanol". (Emphasis supplied).

7. Accordingly, the High Court in its decision held that the entire quantity of sulphuric acid was necessary for manufacturing process and the modvat credit could not be denied simply because the entire input was not emerged in the final product in the manufacturing process.

8. The above ratio, in the judgments of the Supreme Court and the Allahabad High Court are applicable with the same force to the facts of the present case. It is therefore to be held that the entire quantity of pig iron is used in the manufacture of the exempted category of the P.D. Pumps and no quantity of the input is used in the manufacture of waste and scrap. In view of the provisions of Rule 57C, the modvat credit is not available to the appellants. Since in this case, I have relied on the ratio of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and that of the Allahabad High Court, specifically on the subject, there is no warrant to consider the other decisions cited before me by the appellants.

The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

The Supreme Court in its landmark judgment in the case of Swadeshi Polytex Limited vs. Collector of Central Excise 1989 (44) ELT 794 (SC) was pleased to hold as follows :

This was a decision rendered under the proforma regime (set off duty on inputs) wherein provision similar to Rule 57D which permits retention of modvat credit on inputs even if the same is used in the manufacture of dutiable final products and emergence of by-products, waste or refuse is not to be denied.

Para 20

"It is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible.

It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. Thus the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. 2. SCENARIO UNDER THE MODVAT REGIME BETWEEN 01/03/86 TO 03/09/94

Bearing the spirit of the decision of the Supreme Court in Swadeshi Polytex the lawmakers when they introduced Modvat Scheme, brought into force a specific provision in the form of Rule 57D(1) of the Central Excise Rules which reads as under :

Credit of specified duty allowed in respect of any inputs shall not be denied or varied on the ground that part of the inputs is contained in any waste, refuse or by product arising during the manufacture of the final product, whether or not such waste, refuse or by product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty or is not specified as a final product under Rule 57A.

Credit to duty not to be allowed if final products are exempt. No credit of the specified duty paid on the inputs used in the manufacture of a final product shall be allowed if the final product is exempt from the whole of the duty of excise leviable thereon or is chargeable to nil rate of duty.

SHS, the department contended that LSHS had been basically used in the generation of electricity which was not specified as final product and, hence, no MODVAT credit of duty paid on LSHS was admissible. It was further contended that LSHS generated electricity but that process did not result in manufacture of cement and caustic soda, and, therefore, MODVAT credit was not admissible for the duty paid on LSHS.

The Supreme Court held : The electricity is not an excisable item. In the instant civil appeal, the issue was with regard to the electricity which was generated inside the plant by heating of LSHS and which was captively consumed and used to manufacture cement/caustic soda. Rule 57A has an Explanatory clause (c) which states as to what inputs are included in Modvat credit. Explanation ( c) refers to ‘input used as fuel’. The said clause was introduced by Notification No. 4 of 1994. At that time, the Government made it clear that inputs used as fuel were entitled to MODVAT credit. That fuel, either utilized directly or for generating electricity, as an intermediary product, is integrally connected with several operations which result in the emergence of the final product, namely, cement/caustic soda. It is important to note that without utilization of LSHS, it is not possible to manufacture cement/caustic soda. The electrolysis process is dependent on continuous flow of electricity. If there is disruption in the supply of electricity from the Electricity Board, then the entire plant of the assessee would fail and the manufacture of cement/caustic soda would not take place. Therefore, LSHS would come within the ambit of the expression ‘used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product’. Electricity is one form of heat. It gets generated in several ways. LSHS is a fuel used in the generation of electricity. Since electricity is self-generated and since it comes into existence as an intermediary product, its utilization for production of final product is crucial. Hence, MODVAT credit on LSHS used in production of electricity could not be denied. Lastly, in order to appreciate the arguments advanced on behalf of the department, the expression ‘in or in relation to the manufacture of final products’ was to be interpreted. The expression ‘in the manufacture of goods’ indicates the use of the input in the manufacture of the final product. The said expression normally covers the entire process of converting raw materials into finished goods such as caustic soda, cement, etc. However, the matter does not end with the said expression. The expression also covers inputs ‘used in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The said expression, namely, ‘in relation to’ also finds place in the extended definition of the word ‘manufacture’ in section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. It is for this reason that the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the expression ‘in relation to’ must be given a wide connotation. The Explanation to rule 57A shows an inclusive definition of the word ‘input’. Therefore, there is a dichotomy between inputs used in the manufacture of the final product and inputs used in relation to the manufacture of final products. The department gave a narrow meaning to the word ‘used’ in rule 57A. The department would have been right in saying that the input must be raw material consumed in the manufacture of final product. However, the expression ‘used’ in rule 57A uses the words ‘in relation to the manufacture of final products’. The words ‘in relation to’ which find place in section 2(f) of the 1944 Act have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover processes generating intermediate products and it is in this context that it has been repeatedly held by the Supreme Court that if manufacture of final product cannot take place without the process in question, then that process is an integral part of the activity of manufacture of the final product. Therefore, the words ‘in relation to the manufacture’ have been used to widen and expand the scope, meaning and content of the expression ‘inputs’ so as to attract goods which do not enter into finished goods. Where raw material is used in the manufacture of final product, it is an input used in the manufacture of final product. However, the doubt may arise only in regard to use of some articles not in the mainstream of manufacturing process, but something which is used for rendering final product marketable or something used otherwise in assisting the process of manufacture. This doubt is set at rest by use of the words ‘used in relation to manufacture’. In the instant case, the LSHS was used to generate electricity, which was captively consumed. Without continuous supply of such electricity generated in the plant, it was not possible to manufacture cement, caustic soda, etc. Without such supply, the process of electrolysis was not possible. Therefore, keeping in mind the expression ‘used in relation to the manufacture’ in rule 57A, the assessee was entitled to MODVAT credit on LSHS. 18. We have considered the pleas made by both the sides. We observe that MODVAT scheme has been introduced with a view to mitigate and obviate the cascading effect from the duty. This would mean that duty in respect of inputs which were used in or in relation to the manufacture of the finished product should get added on into the cost of the finished goods manufactured. To effectuate the purposes and the objects of this scheme, various rules have been incorporated in the statute. The relevant rules for consideration before us are Rule 57A, Rule 57D, Rule 57F. it was to be held that phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’ were the intentionally manufactured products. If the entire process from start to end is examined, undoubtedly HCl had to be held as having been used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’. [Para 9] Rule 57CC (rule 6) applies to the final product, dutiable or exempted and makes no distinction between an intended final product or unintended emergence of by-product. The said rule in simple terms requires the assessee to pay an amount equal to 8 per cent of the value of the goods cleared at nil rate of duty, even where the inputs have been used directly or indirectly in the manufacture of such final product. As HCl had been used in the instant case in the manufacture of final product phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, which attract nil rate of duty, the provisions of rule 57CC would apply. It was impossible to obtain the mother liquor or the resultant phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’ without the use of HCl. As long as HCl is used in the manufacture of phosphoryl ‘A’ and ‘B’, the applicability of provisions of rule 57CC cannot be ruled out. [Para 12]

The appellant’s reference to the provisions of rule 57D in support of their contention that Modvat credit was not to be denied if a part of the same was contained in the by-product, was indicative of the legislative intent that reversal of 8 per cent amount of the value of the by-product in terms of provisions of rule 57CC would not apply. The expression ‘by-product’ occurring in rule 57D has to be examined and interpreted in the context of the said rule, which uses the other expression ‘waste’ or ‘refuse’, etc. It is in this scenario that the rule provides for non-reversal of Modvat credit, even if waste, refuse or by-product has emerged during the course of manufacture. The effect of the said rule would be that if waste product, which may not be excisable, e.g. , floor sweepings during the course of manufacture of biscuits, then the quantum of credit originally taken is not to be varied. Similarly, if iron and steel scrap arises during manufacture of iron products, the Modvat is not to be varied, but iron and scrap being excisable products, [the manufacturers] have to discharge duty burden. If the same are exempted, provisions of rule 57CC will apply. As such, it is to be concluded that rule 57D refers to waste scrap and by-product, which are not excisable at all. The said provision cannot be pressed into service in support of the plea that even if the by-product is excisable, but exempted, amount of 8 per cent is not required to be paid. The appellant was not being directed to reverse the credit amount equivalent to the inputs contained in the said exempted final products. Further, taking an hypothetical example of electrolysis of water, which an assessee may undertake to obtain oxygen, he cannot take the plea that hydrogen which also emerges during such electrolysis is an unintended product and even if the same is being sold as an exempted product, the same should be treated as a by-product and rule 57CC would not apply. [Para 13]

The issue in the instant case was not relatable to reversal of the credit originally taken by the appellant on the ground of emergence of any by-product. The issue was a straight and simple interpretation of rule 57CC, which as already held does not make any distinction between exempt final product or exempt by-product. As long as the excisable product cleared from an assessee’s factory enjoys exemption or attracts nil rate of duty, provisions of rule 57CC will come into play. The straight answer to the above question lies in the literal interpretation of the language employed in the said rule without straining to find out the legislative intent, especially when the language used is unambiguous. As already observed, the provisions of rule 57CC or rule 6 envisage common use of inputs in two final products, i.e., one dutiable and other exempted, for the applicability of the same. As such, as long as two final products emerging out of use of common inputs are excisable and one of them is exempted, the provisions of rule 57CC will apply. The exempted final product may be intended manufacture or unintended by-product. [Para 14]

Polyset Corporation [2000] 115 ELT 41 (SC) : 3.3-1 Case Study - In this judgment the Supreme Court has ruled that the date of manufacture of goods is relevant for determining whether the goods are excisable and as to the rate of duty that the said goods must bear, what is relevant is the date of their clearance.

3.4 CCE v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 139 ELT 3 (SC) :

3.4-1 Case Study - While considering the eligibility of an exemption notification subject to the payment of appropriate duty on raw materials, the Supreme Court has held that "An exemption notification that uses the said phrase applies to goods which have been made from duty paid material. In the said phrase, due emphasis must be given to the words 'has already been paid'. For the purpose of getting the benefit of the exemption under the notification, the goods must be made from raw materials on which excise duty has, as a matter of fact, been paid, and has been paid at the 'appropriate' or correct rate. Unless the manufacturer has paid the correct amount of excise duty, he is not entitled to the benefit of the exemption notification" (paragraph six of the judgment). In paragraph seven, the Court observed, "Where the raw material is not liable to excise duty or such duty is nil, no excise duty is, as a matter of fact, paid upon it. To goods made out of such material the notification will not apply." Hence, the argument that "Nil rate of duty is also a rate of duty" is on a very fragile ground. A collective reading of the definition under section 2(d) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, the Supreme Court's decision in Dhiren Chemical Industries (supra) and the decision of the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal in Amaravathi Co-operatives Sugar Mills v. CCE 2013 (291) ELT 126 (Trib. - Chennai) suggests that "the rate of duty being nil, the goods are not excisable goods".

3.5 H.M.M. v. UOI [2005] 192 ELT 63 (Delhi) :

3.5-1 Case Study - Where the Delhi High Court held that the duty being on manufacture and the goods having been exempted at the time of manufacture, the goods must be taken as exempted at the time of clearance, even though the exemption had been withdrawn by then.

The UOI had not been represented by anybody. So, nobody pointed out to the High Court that the issue has already seized to be res integra. That is to say, it had been a settled issue by the judgments in the cases of Wallace Flour Mills and Polyset discussed above.

3.6-1 Case Study - In this case CESTAT held that "press mud and sludge are specified in the First Schedule of the Central Excise Tariff against headings 23032000 and 23033000, but they are not subject to a duty of excise, as under the rate column the duty of excise is indicated as nil. The judgment, therefore, says that the rate of duty being nil, the goods are not excisable.

2. Modvat--Input--Processes which are indispensible to the emergence of the end-product are to be held as used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. "With a view to draw line as to what constitutes the input in or in relation to the manufacture of a product, it can be safely held that the process which are indispensible to the emergence of the final product and which are inextricably linked up with the production stream of the end-product up to the stage of its emergence and the inputs which are so used in those processes without which the end-product may be difficult to be manufactured have to be held as used in or in relation to the manufacture of the final product. Inputs which are used after the emergence of the final product and which may be required to be used in the process at the post manufacturing stage of the end-product will have to be considered as a separate process for a different purpose."

It should also be noted that there is no correlation of the raw material and the final product, that is to say, it is not as if credit can be taken only on a final product, that is, manufactured out of the particular raw material to which the credit is related. The credit may be taken against the excise duty on a final product manufactured on the very day it becomes available. The High Court of Rajasthan in Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. Union of India 2008 (223) ELT 149 has held that in case inputs are received in factory and used in manufacture of end product, no excise duty becomes payable on end product. The relevant date for considering exemption from duty of the end product in or in relation to which inputs are used is the date of its receipt in factory and condition is its actual use in or in relation to manufacture of end product by the manufacturer. The chargeability to duty or non-chargeability due to exemption or notified nil rate is to be considered at the stage before goods are actually produced, but on receipt of inputs intended to be used in manufacture of such goods. That being so ultimate clearance of goods at nil rate due to contingency existing at the time of removal does not affect the entitlement that legally arises long before that date.

13. The assessee’s unit at Daman imported goods under a bill of entry. On strength of said bill of entry, assessee’s head office at Mumbai availed of credit. The Appellant/Assessee was a manufacturer of Glass Bottles, which fell under sub-heading No. 7007.90 of the Schedule appended to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.

For the purpose of manufacturing Glass Bottles, the Appellant/Assessee used several inputs, including Furnace Oil. Furnace oil, was used by the Appellant/Assessee, as fuel.

The Appellant /Assessee availed of MODVAT credit in respect of 'specified duty', by relying upon Notification No. 5/94-CE (NT), dated 1-3-1994. The said notification was issued under Rule 57A of the Central Excise Rules, 1944, as prevalent at the relevant point in time.

The Notification dated 1-3-1994 was, however, amended, by Notification No. 14/97-CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. The net effect of the said amendment was that the credit on inputs, which, inter alia, included Furnace oil was restricted to '10 per cent ad valorem'. This impacted the Appellant/Assessee, in as much as, it was seeking MODVAT credit on Furnace oil uptil that date at the rate of '15 per cent ad valorem'.

The notification dated 3-5-1997, would, ordinarily, have operated prospectively, but for the legislative intervention made in the matter, via section 87 of the Finance Act, 1997 (Act No. 26 of 1997). The Finance Act, which was given effect from 14-5-1997, amended the notification dated 3-5-1997, in a manner that the restriction imposed on the rate, at which MODVAT credit could be availed of on specified inputs, which included furnace oil, was made operable, albeit, retrospectively, that is, even for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 3-5-1997. Thus, a perusal of section 87 of the Finance Act, would show that it provides in no uncertain terms, amongst other aspects that the restriction provided in Notification dated 3-5-1997, shall (a) be deemed to have, and to have always had, effect on and from the 23-7-1996; and (b) is deemed to prevail, and to have always prevailed, over all notifications issued on or after the 23-7-1996, but before the 3-5-1997, under rule 57A in relation to specified petroleum products. The Explanation to Sub section (1) of section 87, clearly, brings Furnace oil within the realm of the said provision.

In this background, on 1-11-1997, a show cause notice was issued to the Appellant/Assessee raising a demand in the sum for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 and 2-5-1997, along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent to be calculated on the said amount for the period commencing from 12-8-1997 and ending on the date of payment. Furthermore, via the very SCN, a proposal was also made for imposing penalty.

In the reply, the assessee took stand that, for the period falling between 3-5-1997 and 19-6-1997, it had already 'expunged' MODVAT credit, in consonance with Notification No. 14/97 CE (NT), dated 3-5-1997. In so far as the demand for interest was concerned, it was stated that it was premature, as under section 87(2)(c) of the Finance Act, interest would be payable, only, if, the amount demanded was not paid within ninety (90) days of the enactment of the Bill.

The stand, which, the Appellant /Assessee appeared to have taken with respect to penalty was that the alleged infraction was not an offence prior to the enactment of the Finance Act.

The Adjudicating authority sustained the demand in sum, equivalent to the excess credit availed of by the Appellant/Assessee for the period spanning between 23-7-1996 to 3-5-1997. Furthermore, the Appellant/Assessee was directed to pay interest at the rate of 18 per cent.

The Commissioner (Appeals), allowed the appeal of the Appellant/Assessee, albeit, partially. While the Commissioner (Appeals), confirmed the demand of duty for the period 23-7-1996 to 28-2-1997, along with interest, he set aside the demand of duty for the period spanning between 1-3-1997 and 3-5-1997.

commodities, i.e., petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and alcoholic liquor for human consumption would no longer have a valid registration under the MVAT Act. However, the proviso to section 16(6A) provided that any person who was affected by section 16(6A), but wished to continue to do business in the aforementioned six commodities would have to apply to the respondents in the prescribed manner to have the cancellation of his registration revoked. Prior to 1-7-2017, the sale of natural gas was governed by the residuary Entry of the MVAT Act, namely, Schedule-E and, hence, the applicable rate of tax on 30-6-2017 was 13.5 per cent. Furthermore, the petitioner was eligible to claim set off of the input MVAT paid by it subject to a reduction of 3 per cent on account of the provisions of Rule 53(1) and Rule 53(1A) of the MVAT Rules. In other words, the net effective rate of MVAT on natural gas was only 3 per cent prior to 1-7-2017 if the natural gas was consumed domestically as fuel or as an input for manufacture.

With effect from 1-7-2017, when any person purchased natural gas domestically, the seller would charge and collect full tax from him at the rate of 13.5 per cent. However, since the person was no longer a dealer under the MVAT Act due to section 16(6A), he could not claim set-off or refund of the input MVAT collected from him. Furthermore, he would be liable to pay GST on his outputs at the full rate since the GST Act only provided for adjustment of GST paid and not of VAT paid. Hence, such a person would be taxed at the full rate on his outputs without adjustment of the input tax paid by him. Whilst the effective rate of taxation on natural product prior to 1-7-2017 was 3 per cent, the effective rate after 1-7-2017 rose to 13.5 per cent.

Realizing the above, the respondents sought to provide relief to the taxpayers. The net effective rate of tax on natural gas prior to 30-6-2017 was 3 per cent. Hence, vide Notification No.VAT1517/ CR136( A)/Taxation1 dated 24-8-2017, with effect from 24-8-2017, Entry 16 was inserted into Schedule-B of the MVAT Act which made provisions for a concessional rate of 3 per cent on the sale of natural gas. In other words, the Notification dated 24-8-2017 sought to maintain quo ante.

The Notification dated 24-8-2017 also provided that for a seller to be eligible to avail the 3 per cent concessional rate, the purchasing dealer must be certified by the Respondents in Proforma-A. The petitioners duly applied and received from the respondents Proforma with effect from 24-8-2017.

However, unfortunately, there existed anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017. While sub-clause (i) of Entry 16 used the phrase 'dealer', the main body of the entry uses the phrase 'registered dealer'. The word 'dealer' continued to be defined under the MVAT Act as a person who is involved in buying or selling goods. Hence, a person who was involved in purchase of natural gas, but not in the sale of natural gas would still be considered as a dealer. However, such a person would not be a 'registered dealer' on account of the provisions of section 16(6A). It was submitted that it was never the intention of the respondents at the time of the enactment of the Notification dated 24-8-2017 to restrict the benefits to only registered dealers. That was clear from the fact that no goods as defined in the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, ('MGST Act') can be manufactured from natural gas as well as the usage of the phrase 'of any other goods whatsoever.'

It was further supported by the issuance of Notification No.VAT-1517/ CR-136 (a)/Taxation 1 dated 13-10-2017 by the respondents. This Notification dated 13.10.2017 sought to cure the anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017 and amended Entry 16 of Schedule B to do so. Explanations (b) and (c) as inserted by the Notification dated 13-10-2017 expanded the scope of terms 'goods' and 'registered dealers' to include goods covered by the MGST Act and persons registered under the MGST Act respectively. This effectively cured the anomaly in the Notification dated 24-8-2017.

FACT: The issue is whether proforma credit can be availed of by the manufacturers in terms of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE on inputs even if the end product (tyres) listed is liable to nil rate of duly.

HELD: Set off Since Notfn. No. 95/79-CE does not contain a clause to the effect that proforma credit on inputs should be correlated to the duty payable on outputs, non-payment of duty on finished goods does not make the manufacturer ineligible to proforma credit. "Read by itself this notification does not have any condition that there should be any nexus between the inputs and outputs.... The Ld. JDR's argument that goods mentioned in column 5 (final products) are only those which pay duty is not supported by the wordings of the notification. No condition regarding payment of duty is contained any where in the notification. We are further supported in this view by a judgment of the Cegat (SRB) (CCE Bangalore v. Wipro Information Technology, Bangalore) reported in 1988(14) ECR 490 wherein it was held that proforma credit once allowed cannot be recovered subsequently even if finished goods are exempted later on, making proforma credit ineligible, since no interlinking account is provided for in rule."

Minority view:--Interpretation--as per proviso 2 of the Notfn. availability of proforma credit on inputs is directly proportional to the duty payable on the finished product and since tyres were cleared without payment of duty, set off cannot be allowed on the inputs used in the manufacture of tyres. Proviso 2 of Notfn. No. 95/79-CE ".....the extent of the credit that could be taken in respect of the duty paid on the inputs shall be restricted to the duty payable on the end product if it happens to be less than the credit of duty taken on the inputs. What follows from this therefore, is that if the duty payable on the end product is nil, then the extent of exemption that will be available will also be nil........In as much as, no duty in respect of these tyres has been paid, in terms of proviso 2 to the notification, the availability of the credit on the inputs in respect of these tyres will have therefore, to be nil."

Background

Amidst the prolonged slowdown in the economy, the government brought in the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019, promulgated by the President of India, to provide impetus to the ailing corporate sector. The ordinance inter alia provides to reduce the corporate tax rate on certain classes of companies; rationalise the current Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rates and withdraw the enhanced surcharge from certain incomes arising from investment in capital markets etc.

The key amendments that find focus in this article relate to reduction in effective corporate tax rate for certain class of domestic companies. Due to such tax rate reduction, India's lowest bracket of corporate tax rate of 17.16 percent1 is now competitive with that of other emerging economies such as Vietnam (20 percent), Thailand (20 percent), Singapore (17 percent), Hong Kong (16.5 percent)2.

The reduction in corporate tax rates has been made effective through insertion of two new sections in the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) i.e. section 115BAA and section 115BAB (collectively referred to as 'Beneficial sections'). These sections are still subject to other provisions of Chapter XII of the Act, such as section 111/111A/112/113 etc. and hence any income in nature of long term/short term capital gains etc. covered under other sections of Chapter XII will continue to be taxed at existing rates.

The sections providing concessional tax rates have been made effective from the current Financial Year (FY) i.e. FY 2019-20 itself. Hence, companies considering to opt for the beneficial sections should take a timely call taking into account the impact of the change in effective tax rates on the advance tax computations for the next quarter/s, on tax provisioning etc.

The amendments also include reduction of tax rate on book profit u/s. 115JB of IT. Act known as Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate from the existing effective tax rates of 20.20 percent to 17.47 percent for all companies.

Newly inserted section 115BAA and section 115BAB:

1.

Relief to existing Companies – Section 115BAA: Under this section, a domestic company can opt for a lower effective tax rate of 25.17 percent(22 percent basic plus 10 percent surcharge plus 4 percent cess) subject to certain conditions. This provision is applicable to all domestic companies (irrespective of activities, turnover or year of incorporation). If a company opts for this option then it would not be eligible for certain expenses /deduction as discussed later in subsequent paragraphs.

2.

Relief to new manufacturing Companies – Section 115BAB: Under this section, new domestic manufacturing companies can opt for a lower rate of tax of 17.16 percent (15 percent basic plus 10 percent surcharge plus 4 percent cess), subject to fulfilment of following conditions:

Company should be set-up and registered on or after 1 October 2019;

Manufacturing to be commenced on or before 31 March 2023 and the company is not formed by splitting up/reconstruction, of a business already in existence;

Company should fulfil certain conditions regarding use of plant and machinery.

However, a company willing to opt for beneficial sections would not be entitled various tax exemption/deduction available under the sections 10AA (tax holiday for SEZ units), 32(1)(iia) (additional depreciation), 32AD (additional deduction for investment in machinery), 33AB (deduction for tea/coffee/rubber development account), 33ABA (site restoration fund), 35(1)(ii) or (iia) or (iii), 35(2AA), 35(2AB)(weighted deduction for expenditure on scientific research), 35AD (capital expenditure for specified business), 35CCC (expenditure on agriculture extension projects) or 35CCD (skill development project) or any under any provision of Chapter VI-A under the heading "C - deductions in respect of certain incomes" other than section 80JJAA of the Act (henceforth collectively mentioned as deduction/exemption provisions).

Further, the Company will not be allowed any set-off of losses carried forward from earlier years if such losses are attributable to any of the deduction/exemption provisions referred in above paragraph.

Further MAT provisions u/s 115JB shall not be applicable to companies opting for sections 115BAA/115BAB.

The option to avail concessional rate of tax as per the aforesaid sections is available from FY 2019-20 onwards and should be exercised before the due date of filing tax return of the year from which such option is exercised. A company not opting for the beneficial provisions due to its existing tax exemptions/deductions, can avail the option for beneficial provisions in the future; however, such option once exercised cannot be revoked in subsequent years.

FACT: The assessee was in the business of manufacture of edible oil. It purchased soya seeds from the registered dealers after payment of VAT and consumed the same in the manufacture of edible oil. In addition to the edible oil, by-products de-oiled cake (DOC), sludge, etc. were also produced in the course of manufacturing process. The by-product DOC was tax free.

The assessee claimed benefit of set off as provided under sections 14(1)(a),(2) and 26A(7).

The Assessing Authority opined that the assessee used soya seeds in the manufacture of edible oil. The DOC, a by-product, was not taxable. Hence, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of set off as provided under sections 14(1)(a), (2) and 26A(7) on entire purchase of soya seeds. He apportioned the tax liability after deducting the percentage of proportionate manufacture of DOC.

On writ:

HELD: The Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Bharat Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. 1992 taxmann.com 38 has considered the question of set off and applicability of principle of apportionment in the event of raw material purchased by dealer be used in manufacture of taxable goods and a by-product which is not taxable. It has held that a refinery would be entitled to set off to the entire tax paid by it on the purchase of raw material. [Para 11]

From a reading of the judgment of the Supreme Court, it is clear that manufacturer is eligible the benefit of set off on the entire amount of tax paid on purchase of raw material and principle of apportionment could not be invoked. The judgment of the Supreme Court is applicable to the instant case, because the DOC, a by-product, is tax free and another by-product sludge and main product oil are taxable. Hence, the authority cannot apportion the tax liability after deducting the percentage of proportionate manufacture of DOC. [Para 13]

In view of the aforesaid, the assessee was eligible to set off on entire purchase of soya seeds. [Para 19]

Battery Operated Vehicles: Whether they fall within "Renewable energy devices"?

Certain States have specifically reduced the rates and certain other States have exempted the battery operated vehicles but there is no such exemption available under the PVAT Act. Memos issued by the Transport Commissioner, Punjab are also of no help as through these memos the company was allowed to operate battery operated vehicles in the Punjab State. The depreciation chart issued by the Income Tax Department is also not relevant to the case. The departmental representative has clearly brought out that in the case decided by VAT Tribunal, Gujarat wherein GEDA has recognized battery operated vehicles as renewable energy devices whereas PEDA has recognized only six forms of renewable energy devices i.e. solar energy, wind energy, bio energy, hydro energy, geothermal energy and the device of these energies do not include battery operated vehicles.

Therefore, it is determined that battery operated vehicles do not fall under entry no. 94 of Schedule B and are taxable under Schedule F to the PVAT Act @12.5%. Rule 117(4)(a)(ii) provides that the input tax credit under the said proviso shall be allowed at the rate of 60% on such goods which attract central tax at the rate of 9% or more and 40% for other goods of the central tax applicable on supply of such goods after the appointed date and shall be credited after the central tax payable on such supply has been paid. This rule further provides that where integrated tax is paid on such goods, the amount of credit shall be allowed at the rates of 30% and 20%, respectively, of the said tax. The rule also specifies some conditions, inter alia, the scheme shall be available for six tax periods from the appointed date.

(d)

Using word only "inputs" in the above proviso unlike other sub-section using the word as "inputs held in stock and inputs contained in semi-finished or finished goods held in stock" indicates that the said proviso mainly relates to traders. The definition of 'inputs' covers all types of goods other than capital goods used or intended to be used in the business.

(e)

The aforesaid proviso to section 140(3) specifically excludes in its ambit a manufacturer' or a 'supplier of services'. It means that these are not allowed to take such credit at the prescribed rate even if they have the document for procurement of such goods but have not invoice or any other documents evidencing payment of duty or tax in respect of such inputs.

(f)

There is one condition mentioned in the said proviso regarding passing on of the benefit of such credit by way of reduced prices to the recipient required to be fulfilled to get the benefit of said proviso. It is clear that said condition is not applicable to a 'manufacturer' or a 'supplier of services' as they are specifically excluded from the said proviso and it is also seems justified as they are not getting any benefit of the said proviso. However, the language and words used by the last portion of the said proviso may create some ambiguity to interpret the correct meaning. The last portion of the proviso reads, as "including that the said taxable person shall pass on the benefit of such credit by way of reduced prices to the recipient, be allowed to take credit at such rate and in such manner as may be prescribed." The later part of the proviso and the words used "taxable person" instead of "registered person" in the said part may be interpreted in a different way.

(g)

However, it is a well-settled rule that a proviso is meant to be an exception to something within the main enactment or to qualify something enacted therein but the proviso would be within the purview of the enactment In other words, a proviso cannot be torn apart from the main enactment nor it can be used to nullify the real object of the main enactment.

Flushing of gas in air is not captive consumption ? - In BOC India v. CCE 2004 (173) ELT 89 (CESTAT), assessee was flushing gas and was allowing it to escape in atmosphere for cleaning, before new gas was produced. This was technical necessity. It was held that the gas is not used in further manufacture and such gas cannot be said to have been captively consumed. Hence, exemption under notification No. 67/1995-CE is not available [May be it is not used 'in manufacture of final product', but certainly it is used 'in relation to manufacture of final product', and should be eligible].

In fact, in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE 2000 (124) ELT 323 (CEGAT), Naphtha used in flushing pipelines was held eligible as flushing is a process integrally connected with manufacturing process of final product.

No duty on intermediate products if duty on final product remitted - Remission of duty does not mean goods are exempt from duty or chargeable to 'Nil' rate of duty. Hence, no duty is payable on intermediate products used in the final products on which duty has been remitted - Pepsico India Holding v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 222 (CESTAT).

Proportionate reversal of credit taken on molasses used in exempted products sufficient - Molasses is used to manufacture rectified spirit and denatured spirit. Rectified spirit is exempted. Denatured spirit is dutiable. First rectified spirit is manufactured. While manufacturing rectified spirit, Carbon dioxide is manufactured, which is sold on payment of duty. Part of rectified spirit is used to manufacture denatured spirit, which is dutiable. In Ugar Sugar Works v. CCE (2007) 214 ELT 337 (CESTAT), it is held that on reversal of credit on molasses used in manufacture of rectified spirit, balance Cenvat credit taken on molasses cannot be denied.

In Godavari Sugar Mills v. CCE (2007) 212 ELT 234 (CESTAT), it was held that if proportionate Cenvat credit taken on molasses is reversed, it is sufficient - same view in SCI India v. CCE (2008) 221 ELT 565 (CESTAT), though order is not worded happily - same view in Sakthi Sugars v. CCE (2008) 12 STT 174 (CESTAT). - view confirmed in CCE v. Sakhi Sugars (2016) 53 GST 149 = 64 taxmann.com 316 (SC).

No duty payable if some waste final products get produced - In Matsushita Lakhanpal Battery v. CCE 2005 (186) ELT 445 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturing battery cells for which intermediate products were manufactured within the factory. Some of the battery cells got rejected during manufacture. These were not marketable and no duty was paid on them. Department contended that since final product is 'exempt' duty should be paid on 'intermediate products' which were used in such waste battery cells. It was held that even if some final product becomes scrap and is not dutiable, it does not mean that intermediate products have not been captively consumed in manufacture of final product. Hence, demand is not sustainable.

Intermediate product exempt even if manufactured by third party - Intermediate product/input/capital goods are exempt even if they are manufactured by third party, as long as the captive consumption is within the factory - Tambraparani Containers v. CCE 2005 (187) ELT 276 (CESTAT) (similar decisions in respect of capital goods discussed in a later paragraph).

Exemption to intermediate product if final product cleared on payment of 'amount' - If final product is exempt from duty, normally duty is payable on intermediate product. However, if final product is cleared as per provisions of rule 6 of Cenvat Credit Rules [i.e. after paying 'amount' or after reversing Cenvat credit], intermediate product will be exempt from duty - proviso (vi) to Notification No. 67/1995-CE - clarified and confirmed in CCE, Cochin TN 68/2001 dated 24.7.2001] - noted and followed in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 287 ELT 102 (CESTAT).

3. The mean rate of Central Excise duty has been brought down to 14 per cent from the current level of 16 per cent. This is a very welcome measure, provided the industries pass on the benefit to the consumers. At the same time, the service tax rate has been retained at 12 per cent. The probable GST rate which is likely to be introduced from 2010 onwards should fall between 12 per cent-14 per cent.

Duty cut on Motor Vehicles 4. In a major fillip to the Automobile industry, excise duty on variety of motor vehicles has been reduced. Excise duty on motor vehicles for transport of more than 13 persons including driver is being reduced from 16 per cent to 12 per cent. Excise duty on chassis fitted with engines for such vehicles is also being reduced from 16 per cent plus 10,000 per chassis to 12 per cent plus 10,000 per chassis. Excise duty on battery-powered cars (electric cars) is being reduced from 8 per cent to nil. The battery powered car means a car which runs soley on electrical energy derived from one or more electrical batteries fitted to such car. Specified parts for such cars (for use in manufacture of such cars) are being fully exempt from excise duty, provided the procedure laid down in Central Excise (Removal of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty for Manufacture of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2001, is followed. Excise duty on hybrid motor vehicles is being reduced from 24 per cent to 14 per cent. Excise duty on small cars (motor vehicles of length not exceeding 4000mm and engine capacity not exceeding 1200cc for petrol, LPG and CNG and 1500CC for diesel falling under chapter heading Nos. 8702 and 8703), is being reduced from 16 per cent to 12 per cent. Excise duty on three wheelers (for transport of not more than 7 persons including the driver) is being reduced from 16 per cent to 12 per cent. Excise duty on motor cycles (including mopeds and scooters) is being reduced from 16 per cent to 12 per cent.

Excise duty has been exempted on anti AIDs and bulk drugs; packaged tender coconut water; tea and coffee mixes; composting machines; methanol/methanol crystals; milk containing edible nuts with sugar or other ingredients; specified refrigeration equipments and wireless data modem cards. Excise duty has been reduced from 12 per cent to 8 per cent on writing paper, printing paper and packing paper. Reduction is in duty from 16 per cent to 8 per cent on drugs and pharmaceuticals; water filtration and purification devices; breakfast cereals; sherbets; pan masala not containing tobacco; flush doors and packing materials. Excise duty has been increased from 8 per cent to 12 per cent on packaged software.

DTA Sales

5. On DTA sales, EOU, STP and EHTP units were paying an excise duty of 25 per cent of the basic customs duty + CVD (as applicable). The said duty has now been increased to 50 per cent of the basic customs duty + CVD (as applicable). The rupee appreciation hit industries have been given one more dosage of rise in taxes by the Finance Minister. It would be interesting to know how much additional revenue is being expected by the Finance Ministry as a result of this measure. But it would definitely act as a dampener to the morale of these industries. The Government has also not talked any thing about the sunset clause with effect from 2009 for these industries from the Income-tax point of view. May be SEZ lobby is behind non-extension of the sunset clauses for EOUs, STPs and EHTPs.

Revision of abatement from MRP

6. Consequent to reduction in excise duty, the rates of abatement on all items under MRP based assessment, on which rate of excise duty has been reduced, have been revised. This has led to some anomaly in certain cases. Take for example pesticides in HSN 3808. The earlier abatement available was 35 per cent and excise duty of 16 per cent. Assuming an MRP of Rs. 100 per unit, the excise duty paid on that product prior to amendment was Rs. 10.40. Now the abatement has been reduced to 33 per cent and the duty to 14 per cent. The revised duty paid on the same item is Rs. 9.38, that is, there is a reduction in the excise duty to the extent of 9.8 per cent. But the general rebate on excise duty given from 16 per cent to 14 per cent is 12.5 per cent. Therefore, one can say that full benefit of duty reduction in case of MRP based items has not been passed on fully.

Many chapter notes under the Central Excise Tariff had referred to the words ‘manufacture’ among other things to include ‘labelling or relabelling of containers and repacking’. In many a decided cases, it was held that mere labelling or relabelling would not amount to manufacture, unless repacking was also done. Therefore, to remove the anomaly, the words have been substituted with ‘labelling or relabelling of containers or repacking’.

The petitioner company was engaged in the manufacture of fertilizers at its factory. These fertilizers were thereafter subsequently sold.

The first respondent was the State of Maharashtra, whereas the respondent Nos.2, 3 and 4 were the Officers and the Authorities exercising powers under the Maharashtra Value Added Tax Act, 2002 ('MVAT'). The respondent No.5, GAIL had been impleaded as a respondent simply because the petitioner stated that for the purposes of manufacture of fertilizers, the petitioner purchased natural gas from respondent No.5. This was an intra-state purchase. The purchase was under various gas purchase agreements. The purchase in natural gas was either utilized as fuel or as an input in the manufacture/processing of fertilizers/chemicals.

With effect from 01-07-2017, the GST regime had been implemented in India. As a matter of policy, the Central and the various State Governments chose to leave petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and alcoholic liquor for human consumption outside GST regime and continue to levy VAT/Central Sales Tax on the said commodities.

Various amendments were made to the MVAT Act vide Maharashtra Act No.XLII of 2017 to make the MVAT compatible with the GST regime. In and amongst the said amendments, was the insertion of section 16(6A) into the MVAT Act which provided that any person who was not involved in the sale of the six commodities, i.e., petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and alcoholic liquor for human consumption would no longer have a valid registration under the MVAT Act. However, the proviso to section 16(6A) provided that any person who was affected by section 16(6A), but wished to continue to do business in the aforementioned six commodities would have to apply to the respondents in the prescribed manner to have the cancellation of his registration revoked.

Prior to 1-7-2017, the sale of natural gas was governed by the residuary Entry of the MVAT Act, namely, Schedule-E and, hence, the applicable rate of tax on 30-6-2017 was 13.5 per cent. Furthermore, the petitioner was eligible to claim set off of the input MVAT paid by it subject to a reduction of 3 per cent on account of the provisions of Rule 53(1) and Rule 53(1A) of the MVAT Rules. In other words, the net effective rate of MVAT on natural gas was only 3 per cent prior to 1-7-2017 if the natural gas was consumed domestically as fuel or as an input for manufacture.

With effect from 1-7-2017, when any person purchased natural gas domestically, the seller would charge and collect full tax from him at the rate of 13.5 per cent. However, since the person was no longer a dealer under the MVAT Act due to section 16(6A), he could not claim set-off or refund of the input MVAT collected from him. Furthermore, he would be liable to pay GST on his outputs at the full rate since the GST Act only provided for adjustment of GST paid and not of VAT paid. Hence, such a person would be taxed at the full rate on his outputs without adjustment of the input tax paid by him. Whilst the effective rate of taxation on natural product prior to 1-7-2017 was 3 per cent, the effective rate after 1-7-2017 rose to 13.5 per cent.

Realizing the above, the respondents sought to provide relief to the taxpayers. The net effective rate of tax on natural gas prior to 30-6-2017 was 3 per cent. Hence, vide Notification No.VAT1517/ CR136( A)/Taxation1 dated 24-8-2017, with effect from 24-8-2017, Entry 16 was inserted into Schedule-B of the MVAT Act which made provisions for a concessional rate of 3 per cent on the sale of natural gas. In other words, the Notification dated 24-8-2017 sought to maintain quo ante.

The Notification dated 24-8-2017 also provided that for a seller to be eligible to avail the 3 per cent concessional rate, the purchasing dealer must be certified by the Respondents in Proforma-A. The petitioners duly applied and received from the respondents Proforma with effect from 24-8-2017.

5. The changes relating to customs duty are analysed below :

5.1 Rates of Customs Duty - The Base Customs Duty (BCD) remains at 10%.

Inverted duty structure was a problem for manufacturers who import raw materials since the output central excise duty on manufacture of goods utilizing such imported raw materials was much lower. In order to address this issue, on 22 key items the BCD and Special Additional Duty (SAD) which are imposed under section 3(5) of the Customs Tariff Act to offset sales tax have been either reduced or made Nil rate. This is a welcome move as the accumulated Cenvat credit on SAD (as no credit can be taken on BCD) was a cost to such manufacturers making the final product costlier or had such credits accumulated without having a chance to utilize them.

Thus, section 17A deals with the situation where any entry, or part thereof, is transposed whether under section 17 or otherwise, by its deletion from one of the Schedules and its insertion in or addition to another Schedule, then, if no tax on any sale or purchase of the goods specified in that entry, or part thereof, is leviable, the deductions provided in clause (ii) or clause (iii) of section 8 shall not apply to the resale of those goods. Therefore, there has to be a fulfilment of the pre-condition, namely, transposition, whether under section 17 or otherwise. Secondly, there ought to be no tax on any sale or purchase of the goods specified in that entry or part thereof. It is only upon such situation that there will be no deduction provided in clause (ii) or clause (iii) of section 8 and which provision deals with resale of the goods. In other words, the deductions under these clauses shall not apply to the resale of those goods. The reason for that is obvious, for the Government has exercised a power, either in terms of section 17 and clause (a) and (b) thereof, or otherwise. [Para 33]

HDPE or PP Fabrics – Whether they are textile fabrics under entry 52 of Schedule 'A' to Punjab Value Added Tax Act, 2003?

Entry 58 of Schedule B pertains to industrial inputs and packing material. At Sr. No. 162 of the list HDPE has been specified, which means that it is assessable @4% under section 8 of the PVAT Act. The parties could not deny that the goods in question were mainly used as packing material in its present form or even in its changed form i.e. bags etc. Once it is conceded position that the goods in question were nothing else but HDPE then it has to be concluded that the goods were covered under entry 58 read with items No. 162 and 202 which is assessable to tax @4%. It has been correctly concluded by the Tribunal that the goods in question are not covered by entry 52 of Schedule A, as by any stretch of imagination it cannot be concluded that it is textile fabrics including terry towels. VAT/CST - BOOK SALE AND RETENTION OF GOODS BY SELF FOR USE ON BEHALF OF OTHER PERSON - WHETHER LEVIABLE TO DUTY/TAX ?

4. A Plastic moulding company has developed a Mould for us and we have paid them for such mould. The mould will be used by the said company on our behalf for manufacture and supply of plastic parts exclusively for us. Please advise :

(1)

Since mould has not moved out of factory of the moulding company, would this be transaction of payment by us liable to excise and VAT ?

(2)

What will be treatment if after sometime we take back this mould ? Will duty or tax be leviable at that time ? If yes, on what value ?

In our view, the following shall be the consequences —

It is apparent that mould is being made/manufactured to be owned by your company. Hence, when charges for such mould are paid, it will have to be seen whether there is transfer of title of mould. As is apparent, mould becomes your property and accordingly, the same is a sale. Accordingly, the same is liable to excise duty and sales-tax. In our view, though there is no physical removal of goods from the factory of the moulding company; yet, since the title changes, it is a complete sale and would amount to 'removal' inasmuch as property belongs to you and any further use of moulds is only on your behalf. Viewed from another angle, when moulds are used inside the same factory for further manufacture, it amounts to 'captive use' and would be liable to duty in terms of the Explanation to rule 5 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The moulds must be shown as sold to you and received back on job-work basis under Rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

Since both duty and tax stand paid at the time of sale of moulds to you, no further payment of duty or tax is warranted at the time when they are returned.

Loss of input by evaporation during manufacturing processing is to be treated as ware or loss and Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such loss is not required to be reversed - CCE v. BOC (India) (2008) 223 ELT 33 (Guj HC DB).

Chlorine gas left in cylinder after use of gas in processing can be termed as 'process loss' and its Cenvat credit (now ITC) is available - CCE v. Andhra Paper Mill (2011) 269 ELT 79 (AP HC DB).

Even excess process loss is allowable if any evidence of clandestine removal is not available - Rollex Electro Products v. CCE (2016) 338 ELT 736 (CESTAT).

Loss of inputs during handling eligible - In or in relation to the manufacture covers the entire manufacturing process starting from initial stage of handling of inputs. Thus, if wastage of input at the initial handling from tank discharge due to various reasons like spillage, pipeline losses, handling losses etc., it is 'in or in relation to manufacture' and Cenvat (now ITC) cannot be denied. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. CCE (2001) 136 ELT 943 (CEGAT) - followed in CCE v. Hydrogas Plg (I) P Ltd. 2006 (196) ELT 167 (CESTAT) - same view in Zeneca ICI Agro Chemicals v. CCE (2009) 238 ELT 770 (CESTAT).

9.3-5 No credit on short received inputs but natural losses allowable

If inputs are short received and there is loss during transit, the goods short received cannot be termed as 'used in or in relation to manufacture'. Hence, Cenvat credit (now ITC) on such short received inputs is not available - Asea Brown Boveri Ltd. v. CCE 1994 (74) ELT 897 (CEGAT) - same view in Bombay Dyeing v. Total set-off of duty paid on ethylene glycol used in the manufacture of polyester fibre must be allowed even if some part of it is contained in the methanol which is a by-product of the chemical reaction during manufacture. Since the formation of methanol cannot be prevented by using less ethylene glycol, it is obvious that the final product is polyester fibre, not methanol. ".....it is clear that the Tribunal should have held that even though a part of the ethylene glycol was contained in the by-product methanol, yet the credit of duty could not be reduced to the extent of the ethylene glycol contained in the methanol as ineligible. ......ethylene glycol was used in the manufacture of polyester fibre. It appears that methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture when ethylene glycol interacts with DMT to produce polyester fibre. It is not possible to use a lesser quantum of the ethylene glycol to prevent methanol from arising for producing a certain quantity of polyester fibre. Thus, the quantity of ethylene glycol required to produce a certain quantum of polyester fibre is determined by the chemical reaction. It may be mentioned herein that it is not as if the appellants have used excess ethylene glycol wantonly to produce the methanol. It is clear that the appellants are not engaged in the production of methanol but in the production of polyester fibre. That position is undisputed. Therefore, it appears that the Tribunal erred when it held that the appellants were not entitled to a part of the credit of duty since ethylene glycol when it interacts with DMT also gives rise to methanol."

2. Set-off of duty paid on inputs can only be denied if the final product is totally exempt from duty. So credit of duty cannot be denied on non-excisable methanol which arose during the manufacture of dutiable polyester fibre. "....the only situation where the credit of the duty paid on the inputs could be denied was only where the final products were wholly exempt from the duty of excise or chargeable to nil rate of duty. In the present case, the excisable goods, namely, polyester fibre were not wholly exempt from duty nor chargeable to nil rate of duty. It cannot be read in the notification that the notification would not be available in case non-excisable good arise during the course of manufacture. In fact, the Tribunal seems to have erred in not bearing in mind that exemption notification was pressed in service in respect of polyester fibre which is excisable goods and not in respect of methanol which arises as a by-product as a part and parcel of chemical reaction."

3. Trade notice clarifying rule 56A must be considered in interpreting exemption Notfn. 201/79-CE since it is applicable to both. "On an analysis and comparison of aforesaid, it is clear that the clarification in the form of trade notice issued by the Pune Collect prate in respect of rule 56A was as much applicable to that rule as to notification No. 201/79. .....exemption notifications are meant to be implemented and trade notices in these matters clarify the stand of the Government for the trade. It is clear, therefore, that the Tribunal failed to interpret the words of the exemption notification No. 201/79 properly and fully. .....it appears further on a comparison of the rule 56A and the notification No. 201/79 that these deal with the identical situation."

4. Methanol arising during the process of manufacture of polyester fibre through chemical reaction is a product which can be said to be used to its manufacture. "Just because methanol arises as a part and parcel of the chemical reaction during the process of manufacture, it cannot be said that methanol was not used in the manufacture of polyester fibre."

The Lok Sabha passed the Finance Bill 2025 [hereinafter called 'Finance Bill (Lok Sabha)'] on March 25, 2025.While the Finance Bill,as passed by the Lok Sabha, largely retains the proposals made in the Finance Bill, certain noteworthy modifications have been made to the provisions relating to the block assessment, omission of equalisation levy and giving overriding powers to Section 44BBD over Section 115A and Section 44DA.

This article comprehensively analyses the changesmadeto the Finance Bill 2025 as passed by the Lok Sabha, highlighting their implications and the rationale behind these revisions.

1. The equalisation levy is withdrawn

Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 introduced the Equalisation Levy in respect of online advertisement services rendered to a specified person by a non-resident. The Finance Act 2020 expanded the scope of equalisation levy to the e-commerce supply of goods or services to a specified person by an e-commerce operator. However, the Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 removed the equalisation levy on e-commerce supplies of goods or services with effect from 01-08-2024.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) amended Chapter-VIII of the Finance Act 2016 and the Income-tax Act ('ITA') to withdraw the equalisation levy from 01-04-2025 entirely. The following amendments have been made:

(a)

Amendments have been made to Sections 163 and 165 of the Finance Act 2016 to provide that the no equalisation levy shall apply to any consideration in respect of online advertisement services received or receivable by a non-resident on or after 01-04-2025.

(b)

A sunset date has been inserted in Section 10(50) of ITA to provide that this provision shall not apply from the assessment year 2026-27.

2. A Proviso has been inserted into Section 44BBD(2)

The Finance Bill 2025 proposed the insertion of Section 44BBD, which provides for the computation of income on a presumptive basis for non-residents engaged in the business of providing services or technology for setting up electronics manufacturing facilities in India. Section 44BBD(2) provides that a sum equal to 25% of the aggregate of the specified amounts shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of such business of the non-resident assessee.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) inserted a proviso to Section 44BBD(2), which provides that the provisions of Section 44DA or Section 115A shall not apply in respect of the amounts referred to in this subsection. This proviso will primarily impact the taxability of royalty and fees for technical services (FTS) earned by a non-resident.

The taxability of royalty and FTS depends upon the existence of the permanent establishment (PE) of a non-resident in India. If the PE exists in India and the royalty or FTS is connected to it, the income shall be taxable under the head "Business or Profession" as per Section 44DA. If the PE does not exist, the income shall be taxable under the head of other sources at the rate specified under Section 115A, subject to provisions of DTAA.

The impact of the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) is explained below.

2.1. No disallowance under Section 44DA

Section 44DA deals with the taxability of royalties and FTS connected to the PE in India. The first proviso to Section 44DA disallows the deduction in respect of the following:

(a)

Any expenditure or allowance that is not wholly or exclusively incurred for the business of such PE or fixed place of profession in India; or

(b)

Amount paid by the PE to its head office or to any of its other offices.

As the proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 44DA, the above expenditure should not be disallowed if the royalty and FTS connected to the PE in India are taxable on a presumptive basis under Section 44BBD.

2.2. The concessional tax rate of Section 115A shall not be available

The proviso to Section 44BBD(2) excludes the applicability of Section 115A when the income is computed under Section 44BBD. Where the income is not computed under Section 44BBD, the tax rate under Section 115A will apply if the income is royalty or FTS. Therefore, the applicable tax rate for a non-resident providing services or technology in India shall be as follows:

(a)

Where the nature is business income, and the non-resident has a PE in India, the income computed as per Section 44BBD shall be taxable at the applicable rate.
